It is independent speech, because one does not utter words or preach the Dharma for the sake of seeking fame, profit, or other such matters. 6. It is non-contradictory speech, because it accords with the inclinations of others.
Because they are spoken to some extent, there are eight boundless expressions (*anantavāc*). Because they are vast and skillful, one should know that these eight briefly possess three qualities:
first, the quality of orientation, which refers to the first type; second, the quality of essential nature, which refers to the next two types;
and third, the quality of skillful means, which refers to the final five types.
Regarding the commentary on "the seven perfections" and so forth: that which is to be saved is boundless, and is thus called "immeasurable.
That which saves it transcends all else, and is thus called "supreme."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The eight purities refer to liberation by nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*”), this is the original text of the treatise.

There are two interpretations of the commentary. The first states: “Liberation in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa-vimukti*), etc. This is an explanation based on time; the dharma exists for a single moment.
It is liberation by itself. Alternatively, when the Tathāgata speaks with a single momentary sound, the dharma is also liberated.

The second statement—that the nature of the dharma is itself liberated—is explained according to its essential substance (*tattva*). Furthermore, another explanation states that the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) are called "liberation by nature."
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "successive liberation" (*saṃtāna-vimukti*), this is the text of the root treatise. The commentary also provides two interpretations.

First, concerning "succession," there are two meanings: (1) it is explained according to the self-succession of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharma; (2) it is explained in reliance upon the succession of the Tathāgata.
Second, concerning the "learner" (*śaikṣa*), another interpretation states that being in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is called "succession."
Regarding the ten pure conducts (*brahmacarya*), there are two further explanations. First, it is said that afflictions and other such phenomena are called "non-pure" (*abrahma*);

because the eight branches of the noble path can bring about separation from them, they are called "pure conduct. Second, it is said that these eight branches of the path arise from the Brahma-voice of the Tathāgata; therefore, they are called "pure conduct."
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "watching a game of go" and so forth: there was once a man who, carrying an axe, was traveling through the mountains when he saw two men playing go.
By the time they had finished a single game, the handle of his axe had completely rotted away. Furthermore, according to the *Yiyuan*:

in the past, a man was riding a horse along a mountain path when he looked into a mountain cleft and saw two old men facing each other playing *chupu* (a game of dice). As the high cliffs rose steeply above him, he dismounted and approached them.
He propped it against a pillar and knelt to examine it; he thought it had been but a brief moment, yet when he looked at his horse-whip, it was shattered and rotten.

Looking down beneath his saddle, he found the bones of his body withered and decayed. Upon returning home, he no longer saw any relatives or old friends; his former residence lay in ruins. As days and months passed, everything was utterly consumed.

Wandering about with nowhere to turn, he wept one final, bitter cry and died. Furthermore, according to the *Dongyang Ji* (Record of Dongyang), he was a person from the Jin Dynasty’s "Middle Court" era.
There was once a king named Zhi who entered the mountains to fell timber. Upon reaching a stone chamber, he saw several youths playing the *qin* and singing.

Zhi lingered there, propping his axe against a tree trunk while listening to them. One of the youths gave him an object shaped like a jujube pit; Zhi took it and chewed it, whereupon he no longer felt hunger.
He stayed for what seemed like a short while, yet it felt as though only a brief moment had passed. The youths said to him, "You have come."
"How long? Why have you not departed sooner? Startled by these words, he rose; the handle of the axe upon which he had been sitting was completely worn away and rotted.
Having returned home, several decades had passed; his young sons and infant grandsons had all become elderly, and his relatives and friends had withered away, no longer remaining as they once were.

Furthermore, regarding these two matters: although they are not explicitly cited from the *Śāstra*, their meaning concerning "prolongation" and "contraction" is identical; therefore, I have mentioned them here.
As for the term "merit" (*gōnláo*) appearing in the *Śāstra* at this point, according to the explanation in the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (*Fó běnxíng jīng*), this meaning is indeed present there.
Its verse commentary states: "Accumulating merit and abandoning all that is non-virtuous, one knows there will be no affliction in this world or the next throughout all births."
Because death has been eliminated and extinguished, one who attains this realization is called a śramaṇa.
Regarding the statement that "from the nirmāṇakāya and saṃbhogakāya up to the Buddhas," within a single saṃbhogakāya realm there are many nirmāṇakāya realms;
speaking from the perspective of these nirmāṇakāya realms, it is said that all Buddha-fields are in motion.
The commentary states that "Vaiḍūrya" is the Sanskrit term. Furthermore, another explanation says: as for the word "lǐlí" (琉璃), it is named after a mountain;
it refers to a treasure from a distant mountain, namely Mount Sumeru. This treasure is blue in color, and none of the other genuine jewels can destroy it.
Nor can it be melted or cast by fire or flame; only spirits, ghosts, or those possessing supernatural powers can break it into objects.
Some say it is the egg of a garuḍa, which these treasure-guarding spirits break open and sell to people.
Regarding the passage "The water is as clear as crystal down to the ground," the commentary states: It is not necessarily the case that there is no ice in all five regions of India.

According to the *Xiyu zhuan* (Account of the Western Regions), the Snow Mountains have abundant snow; their freezing cold and bitter hardships are far more extreme than in other places. How could it be that there is no ice?
If one speaks according to the general trend and by way of majority, it may be granted that those regions are indeed scorching hot and lack ice. Nevertheless, Master Xuansheng [cites]...
Because the Dharma Master, in his *Commentary on the Sounds of All Sutras*, made this judgment, he follows those words; however, he does not truly concede that it is so.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* that praises Puṣya Buddha while cultivating the marks and signs over a hundred kalpas: one asks, during those hundred kalpas, in how many kalpas did [the Buddha] reside?
"Seeing Puṣya Buddha" answers the sixth kalpa. How is this clarified? The answer is that according to the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha), it says:
"I recall in the past there was a Tathāgata who appeared in the world named Puṣya. At that time, that Buddha was within a cave of various jewels;
I saw that Buddha, and with a heart full of joy, I joined my ten fingers in palms-together salutation and stood upon one foot for seven [days]."
For seven days and seven nights, he recited this verse to praise that Buddha, saying: "In the heavens above and on the earth below, there is none like the Buddha," and so forth.
That Buddha then gave him a prediction: "In a future age, after ninety-four kalpas have passed, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Since it says "after ninety-four kalpas have passed," we know that he was situated within the six kalpas [of the present aeon] when he encountered Puṣya.
[He was] a Buddha. If that is so, why do certain sūtras state that he praised Puṣya Buddha and thereby transcended nine kalpas, yet later state that he attained Buddhahood after ninety-one kalpas?
Answer: This discrepancy arises because the teachings and the accounts of what was seen and heard differ; hence there is this variation. Question:

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (or *Benxing jing*) states that he passed [the period] beyond ninety-four [kalpas]. How do we know that this refers specifically to the sixth kalpa? Answer: Based on... [text truncated]
He did not leap over [the kalpas]. He should properly correspond to the sixth. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, the phrase "exceeded" refers to more than ninety-four kalpas;
the remaining six kalpas are what were leaped over. This, then, was his encounter during the first of the hundred kalpas.
Regarding the commentary on the two pure fruits: becoming a Buddha is the first; saving sentient beings is the second.
[From] the *Upāya-parivarta* (Chapter on Expedient Means).

Regarding the third commentary on "conduct being reverent": "reverent" (*sǒng*) means respect. It may be said that this refers to ceasing evil and striving to advance in goodness. Thus, the *Guoyu* (Discourses of the States) says:

"Exalting the good and suppressing the evil. The *Guangya* states: "Sǒng means 'to rise up,' that is, to ascend high. When one's conduct can honor the good and ascend, it is therefore called 'conduct that rises' (*xíng sǒng*).
Some editions read this as *shū*. The commentary explains: "*Shū* refers to spreading branches and foliage; when conduct can spread its branches and grow the fruit of the Dharma.
Although this principle exists, there is no textual authority to rely upon it; thus, the former meaning is adopted, and the character is taken as *sǒng*.
Correct.
Regarding the statement in the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Śāstra*) that the "Lotus" refers only to two meanings—cause and effect—and thus represents "wisdom" (*jñāna*), the intent is as follows:

since the treatise states that only the two aspects of "teaching" (*śāsana*) and "principle" (*yukti*) are called the "Lotus," it is therefore here [in this context] also treated as such by means of teaching and principle.
The lotus is both cause and effect; "principle" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "expedient expression" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary that the two meanings of the lotus do not contradict the underlying principle: although the lotus in the treatise serves as a metaphor for both teaching and principle while interpreting the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, that very treatise states:
"Emerging from the water and blooming—these qualities exist upon both cause and effect, and thus the principle may likewise be so."
Therefore, the lotus is taken as the example; this applies all the more to cause and effect, for it does not fail to accord with the principle of full blossoming. The commentary states:

The first interpretation relies upon the treatise to clarify the point, yet it is not the definitive one. Although the second is correct, it is based on a superior description and likewise does not exhaust the underlying principle.
The third interpretation is both exhaustive of the principle and definitive.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "Buddha-wisdom has two aspects": this generally clarifies that Buddha-wisdom consists of these two types.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the real dharma also has two aspects": as for what is called "wisdom," it must necessarily have an object. Since one wishes to clarify true wisdom, the object is presented here.
The commentary states, "The wisdom of reality is also like this. Since wisdom arises in dependence upon its object, and the real objects are twofold, wisdom is likewise twofold.
Above, two types of wisdom were indicated; here, following that text, the true wisdom mentioned above is explained. The fundamental intent is to discern the essence of skillful means (*upāya*).
If it were not contrasted with the true, how could any dharma be designated as "skillful means"? Therefore, the true is presented first, followed by the explanation of skillful means.

Regarding the commentary’s reference to "the wisdom that knows the false" and so forth: objects such as jars, armies, and forests are termed "false. This refers to the first [level], the worldly conventional (loka-saṃvṛti).
They are termed "false" because they are grasped by the mind as existing through conceptual construction, yet in their actual substance they are non-existent.
Wisdom that can know them as false is called "wisdom knowing the false. This wisdom itself is not false.

Regarding the commentary’s reference to "knowing phenomena" (*vastu-jñāna*) and so forth: the three categories (*triskandha*) and so on are termed "phenomena" (*vastu*). This refers to the second [type of] conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) based on reasoning.

Because those dharmas such as the three categories are established according to their meanings, and because their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) appear and can be known through their distinctions, they are termed "phenomena."

Regarding the commentary’s reference to "knowing the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth": this refers to the Four Noble Truths and the like, which are termed "characteristics. That is to say, it is the second [level of] realization of conventional reality;
because the causes and effects of affliction and purification can be known, they are termed "characteristics."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The knowledge that corresponds to the designating wisdom (*jñāna*)": this refers to the two gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which are termed "designation.

These are precisely the fourth [of the four truths], the conventional ultimate (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*). The wisdom of the noble ones (*āryajñāna*) relies upon these gates of emptiness to manifest the true reality; thus, they are termed "designation."
Regarding these four kinds of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*): the essence of true wisdom is one, yet there are four objects it confronts.
Because the true wisdom that confronts them is thus distinguished, it receives four names; it is not that its essence is fourfold.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the remaining four [knowledges] correspond to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)," this refers to the relationship between the subject and object—the two knowledges of the ultimate and the conventional—which exist among other noble beings as well.
However, the intent of the present commentary is to clarify specifically the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the ultimate and the conventional.
The Buddha’s subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is termed "conventional knowledge" because it is capable of cognizing the four types of conventional reality.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) knows the provisional [teachings] of the two vehicles," it may be understood as follows: either the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom knows the provisional nature of the two vehicles;

or the wisdom attained by the two vehicles themselves is called "knowing the provisional," because they understand their own vehicle to be provisional. The term "provisional" (*upāya*) refers here to the Mahāyāna discourse;

it does not mean that the two vehicles realize for themselves that their own path is provisional. Alternatively, those who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle also know this to be provisional. However, the commentary...
The essential meaning is simply to take the Tathāgata’s knowledge of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “if one relies on [the wisdom of] entering up to conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the third true [wisdom] can directly enter,” this is logically not so;
therefore, the true and the conventional are distinct. If that were the case, other conventional wisdoms would likewise not be modes of entry. Why is this not [the case]?

Correct. However, it refers only to the third [conventional wisdom]. Since the first two conventional wisdoms are entirely not expedient means for realizing the truth, the third conventional wisdom—which takes the principles of the Four Noble Truths as its object—can indeed be the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entering [the path]. Because they differ in terms of being direct or indirect, these two are contrasted with one another.

The *śāstra* states that the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are: first, the five stabilizing mental cultivations (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana-bhāvanā*); second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*);

third, the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*); fourth, the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*); sixth, the stage of patience (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Regarding the five stabilizing mental cultivations:

First, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to counteract four kinds of lust: 1. Lust for color (*varṇa-rāga*): One counters this by taking a bloated corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth as the object and performing the contemplation of impurity.
2. Lust for shape (*saṃsthāna-rāga*): This refers to the arising of lustful thoughts upon seeing a beautiful physical form or appearance.

One removes that inclination by taking such signs as a decaying body or one being devoured by animals as the object. 3. Lust for exquisite touch (*sparśa-rāga*): [This refers to] the subtle touch of the body...
When smoothness arises and one develops greedy attachment, one should contemplate maggots and the like to dispel that greedy mind.

Fourth is greed for offerings, which refers to serving others in accordance with propriety, singing, dancing, and providing entertainment to please them; because this gives rise to a defiled mind, one should contemplate a corpse that is unable to move in order to counteract it.
Second is the cultivation of the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to eliminate distraction; however, there are six causes by which it becomes perfected. First:

This refers to the counting of breaths. It means fixing the mind on the inhalation and exhalation, merely recollecting and maintaining the count of the incoming and outgoing breaths from one to ten, neither increasing nor decreasing, for fear that the mind might become excessively distracted or agitated regarding its object.

If the mental count becomes disordered in the middle of the ten, one should subsequently start again from one and count in sequence, beginning anew at the end until concentration is attained. Second is following.
This means binding the mind to the inhalation and exhalation of breath. Without applying deliberate effort, one follows the breath as it moves.

One reflects on the inhalation, asking: "To what place does this breath reach? Thus, one contemplates the entry of the breath: "Does it travel throughout the entire body, or does it travel through only a portion?

Following that incoming breath, one observes it reaching the throat, the heart, and even down to the toes; mindfulness constantly follows it. If one contemplates the exhalation, one asks: "Does it depart from the body and go out? First.
It extends one fathom. Wherever it goes, mindfulness follows it constantly. Third is *sthāpanā* (fixing):

this means that subsequent mindfulness is fixed solely upon the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even as far as the toes—wherever one prefers—one settles the mind there, observing the breath abiding in the body like a thread through a pearl, whether it is cold or warm, harmful or beneficial.
Fourth is *upalakṣaṇā* (examining): this means that although one observes...

Having examined this wind of the breath, one further contemplates the five aggregates and other phenomena co-arising with the breath as the object of focus. Fifth is "transference" (*parivarta*), which means shifting;
that is, transferring the awareness of the wind of the breath into increasingly superior and wholesome roots, up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Sixth is "purification" (*viśuddhi*), which refers to subsequent external progress by entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), or reaching the Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). This is called [the sixth stage].

This constitutes purity. The contemplation of the three conditions is for the purpose of dispelling ignorance. That is to say, there are sentient beings who are deluded regarding internal causes and effects.
To provide an analogy, one points directly to worldly examples such as the cause of grain seeds and the effect of sprouts, stalks, and so forth, which arise in an uninterrupted succession.

This serves to clarify their understanding: "How much more so in the case of that internal body; it certainly possesses causes and conditions, with ignorance and so forth as the causes, and old age, death, and so forth as the effects. Regarding that...

By contemplating this, one further attains entry into the Path. Fourth is the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), which destroys ill-will by causing one to regard all sentient beings as one would one's own children.
Fifth is the contemplation of the skillful means of the elements (*dhātu-upāya*), which treats those attached to a self;

it involves observing that this single body exists through the conjunction of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) and that, fundamentally, there is no self. "Pausing" (*ting*) means "to equalize. Among these five contemplations, whichever one is practiced according to the occasion, [it will lead to liberation].

All are able to enter the Path. Second, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) consists of practicing each of those four foundations of mindfulness individually.

Third, the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) consists of contemplating the foundations of mindfulness collectively, applying the fourfold contemplations of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self upon the Four Noble Truths and so forth.

Fourth is the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), which refers to the mindfulness of general characteristics; it is the first root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to arise within the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). This is called [the stage of Heat].
It is the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage. It is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path; thus it is established with the name "Heat.

This very wholesome dharma contemplates the four truths through their sixteen aspects. Fifth is the *mūrdhan* (summit) stage. This means that after the *uṣmagata* stage, a wholesome root arises which is named the summit stage.
Among all moving wholesome roots, this dharma is the most excellent, as it is like the crown of a person's head; therefore, it is called the summit stage (*mūrdhan*). It contemplates...

The practice is the same as before. Sixth is the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*). This refers to the arising of roots of goodness after the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), which is able to endure and accept the principles of the Four Truths;

because this is the most excellent among such states and because there is no longer any falling back, it is called "Patience. The lower and middle grades of Patience are identical in their contemplative practice to the Summits.
As for the upper grade of Patience, it contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm, as it is immediately contiguous with the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Seventh.
This refers to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). It arises immediately after "Patience" (*kṣānti*). Because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is called "mundane" (*laukika*);
because it is the most excellent, it is called "supreme" (*agra*). It consists of a single mode of activity (*ekākāra*) and lasts for only one moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), just like "Patience.

It takes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) within the Desire Realm as its object. This is a brief explanation of the essentials; for a detailed account, one should consult the *Abhidharmakośa*, though I have not included it here for fear of prolixity.

Regarding the phrase "the *shu* [commentary] attends to the real and enters the conventional": "attends" (*li*) means to confront. This refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Because it confronts the reflected image and takes the suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, yet cannot directly realize it, it is termed "attending. Because it directly takes phenomena (*dharma*) as its object, it is termed "entering the conventional."

The *Commentary on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vyākhyā*) states: "Regarding 'reaching the totality up to destruction' (*saṃkṣepa-paryanta*). According to the *Ten Stages Treatise* (*Daśabhūmika-śāstra*), within each of the ten phrases mentioned, there are six types of distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dvāra*). These are:

"totality up to destruction," "total characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), "particular" (*viśeṣa*), "common characteristic" (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*), "distinct characteristic" (*visama-lakṣaṇa*), and "increasing characteristic" (*vardhamāna-lakṣaṇa*). The "total characteristic" refers to the fundamental entry (*mūla-praveśa*).

The "particular" refers to the remaining nine entries; because they rely upon the fundamental and fulfill that fundamental. The "common characteristic" refers to the act of entering. The "distinct characteristic" refers to the increasing aspect.
Therefore, the characteristic of formation is explained briefly, while the characteristic of destruction is explained extensively, just as with the formation and destruction of the world-system.

Regarding the statement that "in all other sets of ten phrases, one should understand them according to their respective categories," the commentary explains: In the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, twenty phrases are used to praise the virtues of the bodhisattva.
The treatise explains the first ten as the "ten kinds of entry. Furthermore, based on the root sūtra, it distinguishes the six [phrases] beginning with "total equality" and so forth.

There are ten phrases. Because there are nine others based on the initial entry, the first entry is called the "fundamental. Since the fundamental encompasses the derivative, it is termed the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

The specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are to be understood as being identical to the aforementioned ten phrases; they are all equally termed "entries," which is why it is said that "the same characteristics are entries.
Within each individual entry, there are further distinct meanings, and thus the names increase in variety. This applies if one considers the eon of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*).

[It is] so. Aggregates of the four great elements and so forth form objects such as mountains; because many things are briefly subsumed within a single mountain, the *vivartakalpa* (aeon of formation) is used as a metaphor for the sense of "formation.

Because the receptacle world is destroyed and dispersed during the *saṃvartakalpa* (aeon of destruction), and the four great elements disperse extensively, the *saṃvartakalpa* is borrowed to illustrate the sense of "destruction.

However, there are those who use the actual events of the aeons of formation and destruction themselves as the names for "formation" and "destruction," but this is entirely unreasonable, as the treatise itself states: [text follows].

It says: "Formation" (*saṃvarta*) is abbreviated; "destruction" (*vivarta*) is extensive, as in the kalpas of formation and destruction. Since the word "like" (*yathā*) is employed, it clarifies that this is being used as a metaphor.
Furthermore, according to the third fascicle of that treatise, it says: "The Bodhisattva skillfully knows the formation and destruction of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

They are formed through the successive accumulation [of elements] and destroyed through their dispersal. The Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) cites these six kinds of phenomena with the intention of taking a small portion from among those six.
Regarding "containing many": this establishes the proof and integrates the skillful means. Question: While the general and the same each constitute three, what is their distinction?
Furthermore, how do they differ from the distinct and the differentiated, which also each constitute three? Answer: The "general" refers to the essence and meaning, encompassing all ten.

The "same" refers specifically to the names, following each respective phenomenon that is established. To speak briefly and exhaustively, the "distinct" relies on the nine individual [phenomena], while the "differentiated" corresponds to the one general [principle].

[The section on] "Clarification" distinguishes nine different bases. Each [base] undergoes increase and destruction as appropriate, and each is extensively analyzed and explained through its various divisions.

Therefore, there are six constituent parts (*bhāga*). As for those who lecture and read [this text], when they reach this passage, their various attempts to refute or preserve [the meaning] are all contrary to the original intent.
Therefore, I have now set them forth in full so that the former delusions may be dispelled.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra) stating, "He went to Vārāṇasī and so forth," this serves as proof for the skillful means of speech. The commentary says: Holding a vessel of excrement, he preached the ninefold Dharma;
thus body and speech were presented separately. When it says, "He went to Vārāṇasī and so forth," both body and speech are presented together. As for the term "went" (*gata*), it refers to...
This is bodily action (*kāyakarman*) that turns toward the Dharma of the Four Truths and is subsumed under vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Regarding the phrase "having already made oneself distant for the sake of convenience," there are briefly three explanations: First, to distance one's own body is called "making oneself distant" (*bāhyātman*).

This demonstrates that the Bodhisattva treats external objects as intimate and distances himself from his own body. Second, "external" refers to the bodies of others, while "self" refers to one's own essence.
To benefit others as one does oneself; thirdly, externally, to unify both self and other through these two benefits—this is termed "expediency" (*upāya*).
Regarding the "benefit of the Dharma that rescues people": "rescuing people" means benefiting sentient beings, while "benefiting the Dharma" means causing the Dharma to endure for a long time.

"Both method (*upāya*) and means (*upāyika*)" refers to those skillful perfections (*pāramitā-kuśala*). Because they possess the two meanings of "method" and "means," they are called "both method and means";
this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. It is also like Asvabhāva’s explanation of the term "Mahāyāna":
it is both a vehicle (*yāna*) and great (*mahat*), thus receiving its designation as a *karmadhāraya*.
Regarding the statement that the *śāstra* provides three interpretations by "elucidating the lower to reveal the upper" and "comprehensively manifesting," these constitute the three interpretations.

Regarding the statement that the *śāstra* combines [the topics] as the twelve skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), this refers to the combination of the three as elucidated below to reveal above, which comprehensively manifests and thereby subsumes the twelve skillful means of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "The latter four are established by means of the latter six, such as the six types of cultivation," this means that the latter six, according to their respective meanings, collectively establish the former four;
it does not mean that the latter six separately establish each of the former. Some claim they do establish them separately, but this is not the original intent of the treatise.
Regarding the commentary’s "conforming and reconciling": "conforming" means first conforming to those to be converted by manifesting signs such as warmth and smiles;
"reconciling" means resolving the doubts of those people.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “All dharmas reach [the state of] being like illusions, dreams, and so forth,” this cites a sūtra upon which outsiders are deluded.
In total, there are five phrases: first, the absence of intrinsic nature; second, the absence of substantial existence; third, the absence of arising and ceasing; fourth, equality with empty space;
and fifth, being like illusions and dreams. The commentary cites only four, omitting “equality with empty space.”
The Commentary states that the Sūtra does not say [the lack of self-nature] extends to the "self-nature" [itself]; this reconciles the first phrase.

The intention of the Sūtra is not that all phenomena—whether dependent (*paratantra*) or perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—are entirely without essence, which would be called "lack of self-nature. Rather, it refers only to the imagined (*parikalpita*).

That which is called "self-nature" has no actual essence; this is what is meant by "lack of self-nature. If that were so, there would be only the absence of the single category of the imagined; how then [does the Sūtra speak of three types]?
It is said: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature. The answer is: it is because the mind that performs pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) clings to various objects;
for this reason of pervasive conceptualization, it is also called "all."
The commentary states that "according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is not that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist," thereby reconciling the second phrase.

Although there are the two phenomena of the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) which serve as the referents for verbal expression, based upon these things, pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) arises.

The intrinsic nature of the phenomena described by such pervasive conceptualization—such as a rabbit's horn—is, according to the ultimate truth, just as [non-existent] as what is expressed by those pervasive conceptualizing words.

The nature of grasping is, in principle, non-existent; therefore, it is said to be "without object" (*avastuka*). This does not mean that the two dharmas of the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) are also called "without object.

As for the commentary’s statement, "Since that nature and object [are non-existent], how could there be arising and ceasing? this reconciles the third phrase. The aforementioned "nature and object" are all...

That which is grasped through conceptual construction has no intrinsic nature from the outset. Since its nature is non-existent, how could there be arising or ceasing? If the hide does not exist, where can the hair be attached?
The fourth point, regarding the meaning of being like space, is omitted here as it is treated briefly in the commentary.
According to that treatise: "For example, within space there are many forms and activities of form; it is capable of accommodating all forms and activities of form. This is based upon...
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is like space. The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like form and the activity of form;
due to delusion regarding the other-dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected natures, one clings to the existence of a fixed nature in persons and phenomena.

Just as when space exists, there is form and the activity of form, yet once form and the activity of form are removed, empty space appears; so too, when the two types of clinging to the imagined self and phenomena are removed, the truth [is revealed].
Just as with the two principles, they appear as pure; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are like space and so forth.
That is, the phenomena of the three natures are all like space, as explained at length in that text. There are three types of distinctions: the illustration, the application, and the conclusion.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, from 'like an illusion or a dream' up to 'therefore it is said to be like an illusion,' this corresponds to the fifth phrase.

It clarifies that those phenomena which are the objects of the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature) do not appear as they truly are according to the falsely imagined nature of inverted attachments;

nor are they entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) like the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) which serves as the basis for such imagination. This *paratantra* nature merely exists like an illusion."
Regarding the phrase “the ultimate purity,” etc., this clarifies the realization of enlightenment through the eight phases, as will be explained in detail below.
Regarding the statement in the commentary, “its nature is the wisdom that realizes the signified and the signifier,” this addresses a contradiction. An external objection states:

“In the previous explanation of the name, both the teaching and the principle were encompassed; why then, when defining its essence, is only wisdom taken? Therefore, the commentary explains: “Because of the subsequent cause...”

It is obtained. Because it can give rise to both teaching and principle, only the root is taken. Furthermore, since the nature of the signifier and the signified are each distinct, only wisdom is taken as its essence.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the contemplation of the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings is called the contemplation of true wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna-vipaśyanā*): Question: Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). Now, this [passage] clarifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Why, then, is wisdom mentioned? Answer: There are two explanations. First, it is said: The essence of contemplation is indeed wisdom associated with concentration.

Because wisdom is predominant and concentration is subordinate, the associated wisdom is cited to manifest the name of the concentration; this is an explanation based on immediate proximity (*upacāra*). Second, it is said: Contemplation is concentration.

Regarding the objects of the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): among the five specific objects of cognition (*niyata-viṣaya*), the objects of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are both termed "objects of observation" (*ālambana*).

By citing the object of observation, the concentration that performs the observation is indicated. The commentary states: "The previous explanation is superior. Even if one were to cite the object, one should simply say 'contemplation' (*vipaśyanā*).

Why then is it called 'knowledge according to reality' (*yathābhūta-jñāna*)? Therefore, the previous explanation is correct. Furthermore, there is another quality [to this]: the *Śāstra* says, "By means of according with reality..."
"Wisdom" (*jñāna*). "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to clear discernment; clear discernment means knowing the disease and identifying the medicine. Regarding "arising from samādhi":

having completed the thorough knowledge of the disease and the identification of the medicine, the time has arrived to administer the medicine; therefore, one arises from meditative concentration. The commentary states:

examining the treatise (*śāstra*), the subsequent explanation concerns "intimacy" (*sambandha*). The reason for this is that the treatise itself says: "One contemplates with wisdom as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), and then arises from samādhi."
The clear contemplation of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) is precisely that by which one arises from meditative concentration.

If, as explained in the commentary, the contemplation with the wisdom of reality as it is is itself the concentration, why would it be necessary to further state that one arises from concentration by means of the wisdom of reality as it is? The wise should reflect upon this.
The commentary states that the fact that the two vehicles do not know [this] also applies to both of these; that is, it applies to both principle (li) and teaching (jiao).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the rest specifically belong to principle and teaching": such things as the difficulty of seeing and awakening specifically belong to the teaching, while the five kinds of profundity specifically belong to the principle.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the depth of the *āgamas* is precisely the former three teachings": Question:

If, according to the various teachings, the five kinds of profundity rely solely upon *tathatā* (suchness), why does the commentary reconcile only the teachings and not the other three [profundities]? Answer: It is because [it addresses] the depth of the *āgamas*.
The Sūtra itself provides its own praise, which is why it speaks specifically [of this].

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because this exists, the other three are established as a matter of course": Question: How is it that by virtue of the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) and the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), the other three are established?
Answer: Since wisdom already exists, the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously with it are its very fruit; however, wisdom must depend upon the teaching (*śāsana*) as its cause.
The myriad practices arise; thus there is sameness. Wisdom does not arise in isolation; it must rely upon objects. Therefore, where there are two, there must necessarily be three.
As for the reason why the latter two sections are explained together in one place: it is because the second section explains that expedient means and knowledge-and-vision.

Having finished explaining the three phrases regarding "mindfulness and contemplation," the text next provides a further explanation of the three [topics] beginning with "expedient means" (upāya) as a third section.
Therefore, the commentary concludes by stating: "Within the latter two sections, the first three meanings are clarified in one place.

Having explained those first three phrases in two successive sections, it subsequently explains the fourth phrase, "words and expressions," which is also divided into two sections belonging to those three interpretations.
This is the second interpretation. The second belongs to that third interpretation; the summarized meaning can be understood.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Commentary) that "the accomplishment of the [Buddha’s] departure refers to the eightfold manifestation of enlightenment (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*) and so forth," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it says:

"By the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests various transformative appearances (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), from entering the womb up to *parinirvāṇa*. (1)
The phase of entering the womb is fully cited in the commentary. Second is the phase of infancy and childhood.
There are inferior sentient beings who, due to having few roots of virtue, are unable to behold the Buddha’s attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment and his turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma.

For their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests as an infant and acts as a youth, playing in the inner palace. If the Bodhisattva were to manifest in other forms to preach the Dharma, [the inhabitants of] the inner palace...
Women do not have faith or joy [in this]. For this reason, he manifests the appearance of an infant boy. Third, regarding the appearance of renunciation:
there are those of high spiritual practice who are still able to leave the secular world; for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests renunciation. Fourth, regarding the appearance of asceticism:
furthermore, there are devas and humans who think thus: "One cannot attain the Noble Path while sitting idly in pleasure. For their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests [asceticism].

He practiced asceticism; furthermore, in order to subdue the non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism, he manifested various difficult and arduous austerities. Fifth is the aspect of attaining enlightenment:

there were devas and humans who had made vows for a long night, praying that when the Bodhisattva proceeded to the seat of enlightenment, they, as devas and humans, would constantly present offerings.
For their sake, the Bodhisattva proceeded to the seat of enlightenment. Once the immeasurable devas and humans had made their offerings...
Having completed his nourishment, he attained all the causes and conditions for awakening. Regarding the six signs of subduing Māra:
furthermore, there were devas and humans who thought, "Evil Māras and non-Buddhists obstruct the True Dharma;

may the Bodhisattva sit upon the seat of awakening and subdue the evil Māras and all non-Buddhists, so that those with right faith may all perceive the Dharma. For the sake of these sentient beings, he sat upon the seat of awakening.
The Seat of Enlightenment. The sign of turning the Wheel of Dharma for the seventh time: there were devas, humans, and others who spoke thus:
"May we behold the Great Teacher who has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), teacherless knowledge, and self-arisen knowledge.

Although these sentient beings do not seek liberation, their faculties and natures are fully matured; they are profound vessels of the Dharma. For the sake of these sentient beings, he manifests the three turnings of the ten [aspects]."
Second, the aspect of the wheel of the unsurpassed Dharma. Third, the aspect of entering nirvāṇa. Furthermore, there are devas and humans who delight in hearing of parinirvāṇa;

for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests nirvāṇa. The commentary states: "The subcommentary (*śū*) divides [the audience] into two—infants and children—and does not mention those who have left the household life.
However, according to that sūtra, as cited previously, it is feared that the versions of the sūtra differ, or that the citations in the subcommentary are inconsistent. Further...
I have consulted various editions. Works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explain this, but fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here.
Regarding the distinction between this [section] and the fourth [section] as explained in the sub-commentary (*śūtra*), it refers to the third section of the treatise;
that is, the distinction between these two types: the third, "various cognitions and views," and the fourth, "verbal expression. This will also be explained by the sub-commentary itself later on.

Regarding the "Commentary on the Causes and Conditions of the Fundamental and the Derivative": it follows what was stated therein, that all dharmas, both fundamental and derivative, do not pertain to a single dharma alone.

Furthermore, among these six exegeses, some versions of the commentary state "turning away from the heterodox and entering [the path]," while other versions of the commentary speak of "four exegeses. There are indeed such variations.
To say there are five [turnings] is entirely erroneous. At the beginning of the commentary, the explanation of the treatise states:

"Manifesting the heterodox teachings of the non-Buddhists and the orthodox teachings of the Buddhas" refers to the first and second turnings, which involve turning away from error and entering into the correct path. The commentary further states: "There are four additional instances of skillful means;

together with the preceding ones, there are six, which form three pairs in total: (1) the pair of turning away from error and entering into the correct path; (2) advancing in goodness and destroying..."
"An evil counterpart. Third, "awakening oneself and awakening others.

Regarding the phrase "the body touching the ground": one asks about those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Only those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have realized it through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) attain this;

how then can it be said that they still possess views such as attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? In response, there are briefly four explanations. First, regarding afflictions, views, and precepts... [text breaks off].
Furthermore, it is equal to non-existence. As for the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is neither [existent] nor non-existent.

Prior to attaining the state of an Arya, one hears of this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and gives rise to views and attachment to precepts (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), grasping it as supreme and then training, cultivating, and realizing it; such a person is in fact still an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*). Third, regarding the general meaning of the three texts:
although they generally speak of "clinging to this samādhi," they ultimately refer to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and worldly types, because of their attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

And so forth. They cling to their own states of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the like, asserting that these are not [the states] of the noble ones (*ārya*). There are those who, having attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), give rise to such clinging.

Regarding the four gates of conforming reasoning (*anuvartana-yukti*), as in the Sarvāstivāda school, they likewise give rise to grasping and clinging toward the precepts of liberation (*prātimokṣa-śīla*) and other matters.

The commentary states: Of the first two interpretations, there is no contradiction with the teachings or the principles. Although the third is generally consistent, it relies merely on inferential intent.
The fourth is difficult to fully accept, as there is no clear evidence for it.
Regarding the phrase "the object-condition has immeasurable realms," according to the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, it says:

"Immeasurable great loving-kindness" refers to those bodhisattvas who, while practicing the bodhisattva path for the sake of enlightenment, pervade the entire realm of sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness.
That is to say, as far as the realm of empty space extends—the measure of sentient beings—just as the realm of empty space is all-pervasive, so too is the great [loving-kindness] of the bodhisattva.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is likewise. There is no sentient being, nor any category of conscious beings, that is not pervaded by it.

This constitutes its objective sphere (*ālambana*) and its practice of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are five general meanings: first, the basis (*āśraya*); second, the objective sphere (*ālambana*);

third, the aspect of activity (*ākāra*); fourth, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); and fifth, the accompanying factors (*sahāya*). With meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as the basis and sentient beings as...

The object (*ālambana*) is the wish for others to be endowed with happiness; this constitutes the aspect of the mental application (*ākāra*). Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute its essential nature (*svabhāva*). All primary minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) constitute its attendants (*sahāya*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Desiring equality so as to cause [beings] to leave all evils behind": the term "equality" (*samatā*) reveals the aspect of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Although it...
Sentient beings' relinquishing of all defilements is also termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). However, the meaning of equanimity is established through impartiality, or it may encompass both meanings.

Thus, the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-siddhi-śāstra* states: "Equanimity refers to casting off; it causes the abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, abiding in the middle is also designated as equanimity."

Regarding the phrase "the commentary [states] that its essence is samādhi and prajñā," etc.: Question: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* takes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. Why is this different here? Answer:

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (or *Abhidharma-sāra-śāstra*) relies on the general essence that induces [the result], whereas the present commentary relies on the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and other texts, which focus on specific antidotes.
This is a separate exposition of the essential nature [of compassion]. Answer: They are distinct in terms of their referential meaning, yet they are not mutually contradictory.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "compassion without objects" (*anālambana-maitrī*) and so forth constitutes the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), why is it called "without objects"? Answer: "Without objects" refers to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
The essence is suchness (*tathatā*). The dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is beyond words; its essence is without arising or ceasing. All phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are termed "non-existent.
The first two [categories], sentient beings and dharmas, are likewise objects.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that the first three [perfections] are "peaceful" (*anurakṣa*) and the last one is "beneficial" (*hitārtha*): it is called "beneficial" simply because it causes one to be free from afflictions such as greed and delusion;

it does not necessarily mean that one immediately attains a state of composure and stability, which would be termed "peaceful. This is because the meanings of "peaceful" and "beneficial" are distinct.
The meaning of the first three being "peaceful" can be understood by analogy. If this is so, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (attributed to Vasubandhu) state: "Equanimity..."?
Regarding "immeasurable": does this mean one desires for sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness? The answer is: there is that which is a benefit but is not called happiness;

there is that which is both a benefit and is called happiness. The *Śāstra* (the commentary) relies on the individual [aspects of the] phrases, while the *Vibhāṣā* (the treatise) relies on the combined statement;
thus, they do not contradict one another.

Regarding the phrase "bestowing all kinds of benefit and happiness" (*sarvākāra-hita-sukha-ādi*), there are briefly two interpretations. The first states: This refers to the person who benefits others.

Because the beings to be benefited are not one, the merit of the benefactor is likewise not one; thus, it is termed "all kinds" (*sarvākāra*). The second states: This refers to the sentient beings to be transformed.
Because those to be benefited are not one, it is termed "all kinds. The commentary says: Although the latter interpretation is comprehensive, the former...

The explanation is based on the root [text]. Because the Buddha is named "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) and "One with Knowledge of All Aspects" (*sarvākārajñā*), the commentary states that when cause and effect correspond, it is termed "the possible" (*sthāna*), and so forth.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva, "place" (*sthāna*) refers to that which has the capacity to contain or receive; if there is no such capacity for containment or reception, it is called "the impossible" (*asthāna*). That is to say, there is none.
There is no room for [the notion that] various classes of sentient beings could possess dissimilar causes for evil and yet obtain results that are either pure or impure;
this is what is meant by "locus" (*sthāna*). The commentary explains: Pure karma is the locus from which pleasant results arise.

Impure karma is the source from which the fruit of suffering arises. The likes of Maheśvara and others are called "unequal," referring to those among the non-Buddhists who reckon that Maheśvara and so forth can produce all phenomena and act as their causes; yet the phenomena thus produced are unequal in terms of their excellence or inferiority.
The *Zhengfa zhe* (Critique of the True Dharma) asks: "Since the cause is one and the same, why are the fruits so different? To disparage the other on this account is called 'inequality.

The commentary on the phrase "the cause that turns according to reality" (*yathābhūta-parivartaka-hetu*) explains: "According to reality" (*yathābhūta*) means to correspond with reality; "turning" (*parivartaka*) means to arise.

It is necessary that, based on reality, one personally gives rise to good or evil as the cause, thereby producing the fruits of pleasure or suffering. This is not the same as the non-Buddhist [schools].

Because it is reckoned as equal, it may be called a "basis" (*sthāna*). In the commentary (*śāstra*), the original name is given as "like a transformative cause" (*pariṇāma-hetu*); this is an error in the manuscript.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "this concentration is pervasive of both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), and is therefore termed 'defiled' (*saṃkleśa*) and so forth," this is based on a general classification of tainted and untainted.
However, to explain in detail, there are two types within the defiled: first, because they act as obstacles, they are defilements. As the treatise says: "One attains..."

Regarding that which has not yet been attained, there are obscurations and afflictions; this refers to the manifestation of any one of the following: a lack of skillful means, preparatory application (*prayoga*), or hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The commentary states: when one initiates preparatory application in order to seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is due to a lack of skillful means and the presence of various hindrances.
Because they arise interspersed [with other states]. Second, regarding the defilements of one’s own stage that have already been attained and those yet to be attained:
the defilements of one’s own stage refer to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). The commentary explains:

although one has abandoned the desires of the lower realms and attained the dhyānas and so forth, one still remains defiled by the active outbursts and latent tendencies of one’s own stage and thus does not attain purity. As for what is called "purity," the treatise states: furthermore, there are four.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics should be understood as being the opposite of the above," the commentary explains:

First, skillfulness and purity, which refers to the manifestation of skillful conduct and all virtues in a state of complete purity. Second, freedom from entanglements and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which refers to the total purification of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth that arise from being free from both manifest entanglements and their latent seeds.
Third, the understanding of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), which refers to the induction [of states] based on the dhyānas and so forth.
Various merits are generated; according to their functional capacity, provisional names are established. Fourth is purity of liberation (*vimokṣa-viśuddhi*).

Furthermore, once these various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth have been fully realized, one subsequently advances further, cultivating them to perfection until they are obtained according to one's desire, without difficulty or impediment, and without rigidity or harshness; this is called purity.

Regarding the "faculties of the roots" (*mūlendriya*), namely the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*): Question: Does this refer exclusively to these five faculties beginning with faith, or does it include others as well?
Answer: Since this section specifically clarifies the faculties for entering the Path (*mārga-praveśa-indriya*), it refers only to faith and the others.
However, if explained in a general sense, all twenty-two faculties—including those that are the roots of birth and death (*saṃsāra-mūla*)—are included.
The commentary states "eighty thousand practitioners," which refers to eighty thousand. This merely cites the rounded number; to speak fully, there are eighty-four thousand.
"Elements" (*dhātu*) refers to causes; they are the seeds.
Regarding the phrase "the gates of the various destinies" (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*) among these: the practices to be known here are, in total, of four kinds.

First, the practice leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*), such as the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity by one whose temperament is dominated by desire. Second, the practice leading to the destinies of sin, merit, and immovability, which refers to the conduct that conforms to the five destinies.
Third, the practice leading to the various individual factions, which refers to conduct based on conflicting views. Fourth, or...

All other categories of distinctions—namely, the blameless courses of conduct leading to this world and the next, as well as those pertaining to the three vehicles and the indeterminate nature—which give rise to the blameless practice for proceeding toward nirvāṇa throughout the three periods of time; the commentary text follows these points in sequence across four lines.

Question: What is the distinction between the power of knowing all paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*) and the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*)? Both are able to discern what is correct and what is incorrect.

The answer is: that [power] knows a broad range of objects, whereas this power of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī pratipad*) only knows those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are capable of leading somewhere.

The power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) does not merely know this; it also knows other phenomena, namely the number of drops in the ocean, the dust motes on the earth, the mental states of sentient beings, matters of truth and falsehood, and so forth—all such immeasurable things are penetrated by the power of the possible and the impossible.
Regarding the "two types of birth": these refer to the kṣatriya and so forth.
Regarding the "three types of lineage": these refer to such notions as "this is my father" and "this is my mother."
Regarding the commentary on "longevity reaching its limit": a lifespan that reaches old age is called "longevity"; a lifespan that extends even further is called "abiding for a long time.
The exhaustion of the length or brevity of a life as induced by karma is called "reaching its limit."
Regarding the "abbreviated six practices": among the eight modes of discourse (*aṣṭau vyavahārāḥ*), the last three are combined into one, as they are identical in being measures of lifespan;
thus, there are only six. The eight modes of discourse refer to that which has arisen in the past and consists of the designating names and so forth.

The six abbreviated practices refer to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are the objects designated by those [names] within the first six of the eight. Question: Do Bodhisattvas also attain these ten powers (*daśabala*)? Answer: They do.

It is obtained, yet it is not complete. If so, why is it called the "exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*)? The answer is: because both total exhaustion and partial exhaustion are termed "exhaustion.

Alternatively, it may be because one knows that the outflows of others have been exhausted; or, on the eight stages [of the bodhisattva path], the outflows never manifest again, which is also termed the "exhaustion of outflows."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “I have no basis for right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) in response to this objection”: according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it says, “In this matter, I have no object for right view.

The meaning is similar: when faced with various objections based on false accusations, seeing that there is no real cause [for such charges] is called “having no object for one's view” (*dṛṣṭir nirālambanā*).
Here, “object” (*ālambana*) refers to the “cause” (*hetu*). Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says: “The Tathāgata is able to provide the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to this.”
"In all these criticisms and difficulties, not a single instance of a valid reason (*yathābhūta-hetu*) is to be found. The commentary explains:
"Not a single instance of a true principle (*tattva-yukti*) capable of constituting a valid objection is to be found."
Regarding the statement, "The obstacle of deviant conduct obstructs all noble paths," another commentary explains: there are two kinds of afflictive obstacles to the path.
Namely, the afflictions of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) obstruct the path of seeing, and the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) obstruct the path of cultivation.

Although one has already attained the first fruit (*phala*), the afflictions of the path of seeing will never again arise; however, because one has not yet fully perfected the path of cultivation, one still gives rise to [afflictions regarding] wives and children.
"Equal love.
Regarding the commentary’s statement on "the path of renunciation," etc., it is explained in full within the commentary. Furthermore, another explanation states:

although an Arhat has perfected the path and, having exhausted the karma for future births, will ultimately not undergo the physical suffering of illness and so forth that would otherwise repay prior karma, they must still experience [such results].

The commentary states: Among the explanations in the *Śāstra*, the initial one is most superior in principle; furthermore, the *Sūtra* contains instances of manifested phenomena, and the *Sūtra* explicitly states that he is an Arhat.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* (Commentary) that says, "Not yet having subdued and eliminated [the perception of] internal [form], one contemplates external form," this is likely the Master of the Commentary’s interpretation of the intent of that treatise, rather than the actual text of the treatise itself.
"Internal" refers to one's own body. The "seer" is the conventional person who is the agent of seeing.

To have a craving for the perception of form within one's own body is called the "perception of form. Because one has not yet eliminated this perception regarding the internal body, one performs the first contemplation. And...
One eliminates it by this means. Question: Since greed arises internally, why is external impurity observed as its remedy? Answer: The external is easy [to observe], while the internal is difficult.
Furthermore, because internal greed does not cease due to external objects, one observes the external in order to still internal defilement.
Regarding the commentarial note, "Now it is not so": [The questioner asks,] "The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also states: 'Within, one has not yet subdued the perception of form regarding what is seen.

The Master of the Commentary (*Sūzhǔ*) adopted this to explain the *Abhidharmakośa*. How can you now say, 'It is not so'? [The answer is: "They are slightly similar in that [the perception] has not yet been subdued."
Because the radiance is impure, there are many differences.

Regarding the phrase "beginners and so forth" in the Commentary: the question is raised based on the root treatise, which states, "Within, one has not yet subdued the perception of forms as being seen."
"Or it manifests the perception of form in the viewer. The commentary explains this as follows:

"That is to say, within one's own body, before relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to suppress and eliminate the perception of form in the viewer, the perception of form in the viewer is established and made manifest.

Neither of the two treatises contains the phrase "initial practice" (*ādikarmika*) and so forth; upon what basis, then, is [your] statement made? Answer: Although the text is not explicit, the principle admits of both interpretations. If it were only one...

[The author] explains: Why resort to the word "or"? Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "One who is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), has already abandoned desire for the desire realm, but has not yet abandoned desire for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), is called the first liberation.
Based on this commentary, which synthesizes the two treatises, there is no contradiction in principle.

Regarding the phrase "within the internal body," there are briefly three interpretations. First, "internal body" refers to the mind (*manas*) and the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*), which have not yet relied upon the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): that which is seen by one who has subdued [the senses] is form (*rūpa*). The two types of grasping—the five sense faculties (*indriya*) and their corresponding objects (*viṣaya*) that support them—are collectively termed the "internal body.
Based on this very body, the cognition of form arises; this cognition has not yet been subdued by the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Thirdly, desire-realm and form-realm forms—including those manifesting shape and so forth, as well as those pertaining to sentient and non-sentient beings—are all designated as "body" because they are all aggregations. Regarding these, the practitioner has not yet...

Being free from desire for form, one remains in this very body; that which is within the sphere of the characteristics of desire is called the "internal body. Regarding the observer of form-perception (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), there are briefly two explanations.
First, as for the "observer," this refers to the conventional person (*pudgala*), who is the agent capable of perceiving form and so forth; this is the conventional person’s perception of form.
This refers to the conceptualization of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) based on seeing form; the name is established in reliance upon the object, hence it is called "conceptualization of form.
Regarding the second, "the seer": this refers to the thought "I am able to see," which is termed "the seer. The conceptualization of form is the same as before.

Some say that not observing the sense faculties and objects belonging to one's own body, but only observing the sense faculties and objects of another's body outside oneself, is called "internal [defilements] not yet subdued" regarding the seer and the conceptualization of form. This statement is an extreme exaggeration.
This can be fully understood through reflection.
As for the commentary stating that if one’s long-practiced karma reaches the stage of "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*), it manifests before one:

the question is, since the explanations in the *Abhidharma* have already been cited above, on what basis is this proven, given that the text does not mention the phrase "separation from desire for form"? The answer is: it must be so according to reason; otherwise, it would not be the case.

Regarding these two interpretations, neither relies upon the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and since one has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), what difference is there between them?

The treatise divides this into two explanations and employs the word "or" (*vā*). Furthermore, if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the realm of form, the forms themselves would naturally appear to the mind; why then wait for them to be "established"?

Since it says they are "established" and then "manifest before one," it is clear that this refers to one who has abandoned the defilements of the realm of form. Question: Since [one] has already abandoned...

Regarding the defilement of form (*rūpa-rāga*): why establish it provisionally and observe it repeatedly? Answer: It is to make the observation pure and refined, so that obstacles are turned away and distanced.

As for the statement that one observes the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as light and so forth, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one forms a mental attention toward the luminous aspect within the forms of the desire realm and generates resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Furthermore, it asks: "One who observes all forms—what kind of forms does he observe?"
Answer: Regarding the phrase "the various forms of the desire realm," the term "forms" (rūpa) encompasses both internal and external. Question:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) based on what is already liberated, having practiced for a long time from the beginning and being free from attachment to form (*rūparāga*).

Why, then, does it observe only the internal and external forms of the desire realm, rather than observing the forms within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks only in reference to beginners; it explicitly states that one observes the desire realm. This is according to the *Abhidharma*.

Since this applies both to those newly practicing and those who have long practiced, the observation of all forms is said to encompass the objects of both realms (*dhātu*). The commentator, following a broader perspective, speaks only of observing the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) for the time being.
Furthermore, because the desire and form realms are coarse and defiled, and the power of their hindrances is more predominant, he speaks specifically of them.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “By means of the first three liberations,” etc.: Question: The treatise states that the object of the first liberation consists of “all forms” (*sarvarūpa*).
Why, then, is it now said to “comprehend the few and the many”? Answer: The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) specifically cultivate meditations on the few and the many;

here, those are subsumed collectively as “luminosity. Therefore, this does not contradict the treatise’s statement that one contemplates “all forms. Question: Which liberation induces the spheres of mastery? Answer: [The first three liberations.]
The first liberation induces the first two [mastery-spheres]; the second liberation induces the third and fourth; the third liberation induces the latter four kinds.
Why is this so? It is because the first sphere of mastery involves having the perception of internal forms while contemplating external forms that are limited.
Whether beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior—regarding those various forms, one attains superior knowledge and superior vision, and achieves a perception that accords with reality.
By way of the path of *śamatha*, it is called "superior knowledge"; by way of the path of *vipaśyanā*, it is called "superior vision.

Within these two types—the superior and the non-superior—one does not harbor increased conceit; this is called "perception according to reality. This is the second sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Internally...

There is the perception of internal form. One contemplates external forms as manifold, until one attains the perception of things as they truly are. Because in these two cases there is internal form, one emerges from the first liberation.

The third sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) involves the absence of the perception of internal form; one contemplates external forms as few, until one attains the perception of things as they truly are.
The fourth sphere of mastery involves the absence of the perception of internal form; one contemplates external forms as manifold... until [one attains the perception of things as they truly are].
One attains the perception of things as they truly are through the next two bases (*āyatana*). Because in both cases there is no internal form, they flow from the second liberation (*vimokṣa*).

As for the remaining four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), one possesses the perception of no internal form while contemplating external forms—blue, yellow, red, and white—and so on, until one attains the perception of things as they truly are.
These four colors correspond respectively to the latter four bases. Through these latter four bases, one possesses the perception of no internal form while contemplating...
Because there are four pure forms (*rūpa*), they emerge from the third liberation (*vimokṣa*). This is explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. Question:

Although the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth are induced by means of the liberations, even if their objects differ, what fault would there be [in this]? Answer: It is like the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), which, in order to induce the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), again performs the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) and true suchness (*tathatā*).
Although they differ in being proximate or remote, the name of the object of focus (*ālambana*) is the same. Furthermore, because...

Liberation arises from the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth; furthermore, liberation is perfected by means of the spheres of mastery and so forth because they serve as mutual causes.

Thus, the objects of observation are the same. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "One practices based upon liberation. The commentary explains: "By means of the first liberation, one merely gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and only then does one initiate the subsequent practice;

hence it is called 'practicing' (*bhāvanā*). By means of the spheres of mastery, one initiates the application of skillful means (*upāya*). The commentary explains: [This refers to] the actualization of the path through the power of the spheres of mastery.

Next, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are able to master the preceding objects; this is the power of initiating the preparatory application (*prayoga*), which is called "arousing the means" (*upāya*).

Through the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), they reach fulfillment. The commentary states: subsequently, by means of the spheres of totality, the activity regarding the object becomes universal;

therefore, it is called "fulfillment. This is liberation (*vimokṣa*). It was previously stated that [the spheres of mastery] arise as its cause. Furthermore, it says: if one attains fulfillment regarding those [spheres of mastery], then one reaches the ultimate limit regarding liberation.
[End of section]. The commentary states: Furthermore, by means of both "excellence" (*viśeṣa*) and "pervasiveness" (*vyāpti*), one is able to liberate oneself from all hindrances.

Therefore, this excellence and pervasiveness are the causes of liberation. Consequently, once fulfillment is achieved through the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the aforementioned liberation finally attains its ultimate consummation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "By removing the obstacles to transformation (*nirmāṇa-āvaraṇa*) and so forth," there are briefly two explanations. First: Transforming various forms to make them appear or disappear is called "transformation.
When performing such transformations, the inability to exercise mastery is termed the "obstacle to transformation"; it is subsumed under the cognitive obstacle (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Second:
