Regarding the path of the Bodhisattva: why would the wholesome qualities cultivated herein not be skillful means and causes for enlightenment?
If they were not causes, the analogy of the jewel within the garment could not be established. If they are indeed skillful means, then since they have already been cultivated, why say they have not?

In brief, there are three explanations: First, it is said that "not yet cultivated" refers to this present life; even if one has cultivated them previously, it was not the signless (animitta) cultivation.

Therefore, the analogy of the jewel in the garment is based on the existence of mutual causality. Second, it is said to be based on the fact that untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) have never yet arisen;

since untainted wholesome dharmas are the very root of Bodhi. Third, it is said to be because [the jewel] has never been cultivated under other Buddhas previously. Of these, the first two meanings are superior.
Regarding the phrase "because the arrows within are sparse," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "These arrows within the womb gradually increase. The commentary explains:
When a child is in the womb, the fetus harms the mother just as being struck by an arrow; because the arrow can damage the body, it is named after this metaphor.
It is called the "arrow within the womb. Because it first coagulates as described above, it is termed "internally thin" (*antara-sāra*).

This discusses its physical form. As for the question in the commentary regarding the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*), this meaning is explained extensively in the sūtras, śāstras, and commentaries.

The commentary extracts the essential points to form these verses; thus, those who are widely learned can understand them easily based on these [verses] without requiring further detailed exposition, as follows:
Beginners find it difficult to realize [the truth] upon merely seeing it; they require detailed exposition. Therefore, for those who have just begun their practice, this is briefly unfolded.
Regarding the verse stating that "those who see birth and death as pervasive and eternal throughout two, four, eight, or ten kalpas," this explains these four types of pervasive eternity.

It refers to various non-Buddhists who, having attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) and are thus able to remember the events of twenty eons of cosmic evolution and dissolution (*saṃvarta-vivarta-kalpa*). Consequently, they cling to [these views].

Both the world and the self are eternal. One observes that those who die here are born there; this is merely a matter of concealment and manifestation, not of annihilation. Therefore, they cling to the view of permanence.
[The views of] forty-eight and ten [kalpas] involve varying lengths of memory, yet the meaning of permanence remains the same; this constitutes the third [category].
Fourth, by obtaining the divine eye, one sees at the time of the death and birth of sentient beings that the succession of the aggregates (*skandha*) continues. Thus...
They maintain that both the world and the self are eternal.
Regarding the verse’s phrase "a portion [of those] up to Brahmā," this explains these two lines to clarify that one portion is eternal. First, there are those who pass away from the realm of Brahmā.
Having been born in this world, he attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and formed this conviction:

"We were all created by Brahmā; Brahmā is eternal, while we are impermanent. Alternatively, it may be that they were in the Brahma-world, or perhaps they heard a report that Brahmā held such a view, saying:

"The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal, while consciousness (*citta*) is non-existent. Or, having heard this principle—that [Brahmā] was either eternal or the opposite—they [concluded]: "I..."
Taking the Brahmā King as their standard, they believe what he says; therefore, they cling to the view that one portion of the world is eternal.

Third, there are those who previously passed away from the Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka*) and were reborn here. Having attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they give rise to this clinging:

"While those gods remain in that state without playing and so forth, remaining eternal, we are impermanent. Fourth, there are those who passed away from the Heaven of Anger through Thought (*manah-pradūṣaka*) and were reborn here.
The intervening sections are the same as the third.

Regarding the verse from "possessing form" (*rūpin*) to "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*), this explains these four phrases to clarify that there are sixteen types of those possessing perception. The treatise contains four sets of four phrases.
As for the first set of four: (1) "I possess form; after death, I possess perception. Here, the self-substance being form is termed "possessing form."

Form (*rūpa*). That which is able to grasp the characteristics of phenomena is called "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*). This includes the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and a portion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).

If one allows that there is also form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), then it refers to the first three heavens [of the formless realm], excluding only the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception;

these are collectively termed "possessing perception. Having died, all are reborn in these places of possessing perception, which is called "possessing perception after death. Second, those who are formless (*arūpin*): after death...
There is one who possesses perception (*saññin*). Excluding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), they hold the remaining four aggregates to be the self (*ātman*). The rest is the same as before.

Third, there is one who holds that the self is both with form and without form, and that after death it possesses perception; this takes all five aggregates collectively as the essence of the self. The rest is as explained previously.

Fourth, there is one who holds that the self is neither with form nor without form, and that after death it possesses perception; this excludes the third view and has no further distinct doctrine. The rest is also [as before].
The same as before. These four [views] can all arise based on *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) within meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Regarding the second set of four propositions: first, one clings to the self as being finite and possessing perception after death. If one clings to form (*rūpa*) as the self, its substance has limits;

it may reside within the body, measuring the size of a finger joint or similar. If that which is non-form (*arūpa*) is taken as the self, it likewise has limits, such as those of its basis (*āśraya*) or its object (*ālambana*).
Because it has limits. The rest is the same as before. Second, they cling to the self as being infinite and possessing perception after death.
If they take form (*rūpa*) to be the self, which pervades all places, then that which is not known is all said by them to exist;

it is not something they have seen, yet they claim to know its infinity across the three thousandfold world-systems and so forth. Because it actually has limits, the following cases should be understood accordingly: because their wisdom is unable to know its boundaries.
Because it has no limit, it is called "boundless. It is not that one knows the boundless through distance; rather, because there is no boundary to its boundlessness, it is called "boundless.

The rest is as previously explained. Third, [the view] that the self is both finite and infinite: after death, there is perception, and one clings to the self as following the body, expanding and contracting without fixed measure;
when the body is immeasurable, the self is likewise immeasurable. The rest should be understood by analogy with the above. Fourth, clinging to the self as being neither finite nor infinite.

"Not infinite" excludes the third [view]. These four [views] depend upon the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of vitarka and vicāra. Regarding the third set of four propositions: first, "I have the notion of unity;
after death, I shall have a notion," referring to the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). Second, "I have manifold notions;

after death, I shall have a notion," referring to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*). Third, "I have the notion of smallness; after death, I shall have a notion."
Apprehending a limited amount of form as "self" and perception as "mine," such that "I am conjoined with it," is called the "limited perception" [attainment].

It exists in the desire realm and the form realm, excluding the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva). If one allows for the existence of form in the formless realm, then the first three [realms] are included.
The fourth is the "immeasurable perception" [attainment]: after death, there is perception, and one takes immeasurable form as "self" and perception as "mine. The rest is as previously explained.
These four [statements] also depend on the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) with vitarka and vicāra. Regarding the fourth set of four propositions:

first, "I am purely possessed of pleasure and shall have perception after death," which refers to the three lower dhyānas; second, "I am purely possessed of suffering and shall have perception after death," which refers to being within the hells.
Third, there is the existence of suffering and pleasure after death, accompanied by perception, among animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the gods of the desire realm.

Fourth, there is the existence of neither suffering nor pleasure above the fourth dhyāna. The rest is as previously explained; these also arise based on the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) involving vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the verse: "There are those who hold that there is form, those who hold to the extremes, and those who arise [in the realms of] non-perception and neither-perception-nor-non-perception," the commentary states:

These two lines clarify the arguments for the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the arguments for the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Each of these contains eight propositions, totaling sixteen.

First, regarding the eight propositions concerning non-perception, there are four concerning "having form" (*rūpin*) and four concerning "extremes" (*antavān*). As for the four concerning having form: first, "I have form."

After death, there is no perception. Taking form (*rūpa*) as the self, one attains the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Seeing others attain that attainment and be reborn there, one consequently forms this calculation:
"The second self is formless; after death, there is no perception. Taking the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the self, the rest is as previously explained.

The third [self] is both with form and without form; after death, there is no perception. Taking both form and the life-faculty collectively as the self—[at this point, the text continues:]... upon...
Within these two [views], one gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*); the rest is as explained previously.

Fourth, the attachment to a self that is neither material nor immaterial and is non-percipient after death excludes the third [view]. There is no separate entity; rather, based on meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), both vitarka and vicāra arise.
Regarding the four views beginning with "having limits": 1. The self has limits; after death, it is non-percipient.

One clings to form as the self, which is narrow and small. The rest is as previously explained. 2. The self is limitless; after death, it is non-percipient. One clings to form as the self, which pervades all places.
The rest is as previously explained. 3. The self both has limits and is limitless; after death, it is non-percipient. One clings to form...

For the sake of the self, there may be contraction and expansion; the rest is as previously explained. Fourth, the self is neither finite nor infinite, and after death it is non-perceptual (*asaṃjñin*).
This negates the third position. The basis for its arising is the same as before. Regarding the eight views that maintain "neither [of the two]," there are likewise two sets of four propositions.
First: the self possesses form (*rūpin*), and after death it is neither-perceptual-nor-non-perceptual; this is the attachment to form as the self. One observes sentient beings entering...

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Perception is not clear; one dwells with such an attachment, arising solely based on vitarka and vicāra, and so forth at length.
Second, the attachment to a self as being formless: after death, as before, one clings to the formless aggregates (*ārūpyaskandha*) as being the self and so forth.
One enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because it is not clearly manifest, one forms this conception: "Only vitarka and vicāra arise.
Third, one holds that the self is both with form and without form, and after death it remains as before; thus one clings to both form and formlessness as the self.

Seeing that the perceptions of sentient beings are not clearly manifest, one forms this clinging: "It depends solely upon vitarka and vicāra. Fourth, one clings to the self as being neither with form nor...
Formless. After death, it is as before. This excludes the third proposition. Regarding the four propositions beginning with "having limits": first, "I have limits;
after death, I am neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," and so on, up to the fourth: "I have neither limits nor no limits; after death, I am neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
All such cases take the formless as the self. Having already attained [the state of] neither-... [perception].

Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), such attachments may indeed exist. First, because the duration of that meditative absorption is brief, one takes each individual aggregate (*skandha*) as the object and clings to the self as being finite.
Second, because the duration of that meditative absorption is long, one takes the four aggregates collectively as the object and clings to the self as being infinite.
Third, because the duration of that meditative absorption is either short or long, one [takes] each individual aggregate...
Because it is taken as a whole for the sake of "me," it constitutes the third proposition. The fourth [proposition] is established by way of negating the third. Regarding the verse’s statement:
"The person, the desire realm, the form realm, the four formless realms, and cessation"—the commentary explains that these two lines clarify the seven doctrines of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
First: "I possess form; having the coarse four great elements as its derivative nature, it ceases after death. It concludes: "It is annihilated."

Ultimately, none exist. Because one perceives that after the body dies, what existed becomes non-existent: if the self, others, or the "I" are all merely coarse matter, they are annihilated after death;
this present body, or even another body, both undergo annihilation. This is the first "self," that of humans in the desire realm, who are annihilated after death.
The second "self" is that of the gods of the desire realm, who are annihilated after death. The third "self" is that of the gods of the form realm, who are annihilated after death.
1. My self is the sphere of infinite space; 2. my self is the sphere of infinite consciousness; 3. my self is the sphere of nothingness; 4.
my self is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—all of which are annihilated after death.

Regarding the verse on those who, having passed away from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), speculate that [existence] is without cause: the commentary explains that this clarifies two theories of non-causality.

First, there are those who, having passed away from the Heaven of No-Thought and been reborn in this world, attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), yet are unable to remember all the stages prior to their emergence from that state.
Consequently, they cling to the view that all phenomena were originally non-existent and arise [de novo], asserting that "all phenomena, like myself, should be non-existent."
Due to the arising [of thoughts], they then cling to the notion that the self and the world arise without cause.
Second, due to vitarka and vicāra, they do not remember their previous lives and thus form this clinging that [the self] arises without cause; this is explained at length.

Regarding the verse’s mention of “recalling the destruction of the lower, upper, and lateral [realms], having limits, and so forth,” the commentary explains that this clarifies the fourfold theory of finitude (*antavāda*).
First, by being able to recall from below as far as the Avīci Hell and from above as far as the fourth dhyāna, one holds that the self pervades all within these realms.
One then thinks: “Beyond this there is a self; I ought to be able to see it. Thus, one concludes that it has limits. Second...
Third, because one can recollect the infinite [directions] laterally while grasping at the self as being all-pervasive, one clings to it as being infinite.

Fourth, because one can recollect the states of the eon of destruction (saṃvarta-kalpa) just as before—recollecting the near and far above and below as in the first case, and the lateral directions as in the second case—one fails to find a limit;

thus, one conceives of the existence of limits regarding the vertical directions, while conceiving of infinity regarding the lateral directions. Fifth, because one can recollect the specific stages of the eon of destruction, one gives rise to the notion that it is neither finite nor infinite.
Regarding the "notion of extremes": because the various vessel-worlds (bhājana-loka) are non-apprehendable.

As for the verse beginning with "fearing ignorance" and ending with "confused equivocation," the commentary states: these two lines clarify the four types of equivocal discourse regarding immortality (amarā-vikkhepa).
The "Immortal" refers to the gods (*deva*). Because the gods possess long lifespans, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to them as being eternal and immortal.
Since one obtains rebirth in those heavens by answering questions concerning the Immortal Gods without equivocation, to now disparage that practice is called "equivocation" (*vibhāṣā*).

First is the fear of ignorance: thinking, "I do not know what is wholesome or unwholesome; if others question me, I shall not be able to give a definitive answer. If one were to give a definitive answer...

[Regarding] the first: lest others perceive my ignorance and consequently mock me, I should speak words such as, "The secret meanings of the devas should not be disclosed in their entirety," and so forth.

Second, regarding those who act with deceit: they think to themselves, "It is not that my pure deva permits the disclosure of all secrets—namely, what has been personally realized and the cultivation of the path to purity"—and thus they speak as previously described. Third, regarding those who harbor fear...
He is afraid, yet he does not provide a definitive explanation, lest his own dullness and inferiority be known by others. For this reason, he is unable to explain.
Taking this fear as his dwelling, he settles within it; therefore, he is called "one who harbors fear. He speaks as previously described.
Fourth, there is the one who is foolish and ignorant, who exclusively cultivates right practice and cannot utter deceptive words, but merely thinks thus: "Should anyone ask..."
I shall counter-interrogate them. Whatever they may ask, I shall respond to everything according to their words without deficiency, thereby confirming and conforming to it.

Regarding the verse on humans, devas, and up to meditative absorption and nirvāṇa, the commentary states: this clarifies the treatise on the five types of manifest nirvāṇa; first, the manifest [nirvāṇa] through vision.

1. Experiencing the fivefold sensual pleasures of humans and devas, they take this to be *nirvāṇa*. 2. Loathing the fivefold sensual pleasures, they dwell in the first dhyāna and take this to be *nirvāṇa*;
as it arises within their bodies, they call it "attaining bliss. Seeing others currently dwelling in concentration likewise, they do the same; the following cases should be understood by analogy. 3.
Loathing applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), they dwell in the second dhyāna and take this to be *nirvāṇa*. 4. Loathing all... [text truncated]
Because of desire, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and joy (*prīti*), one currently dwells in the third dhyāna and takes it to be nirvāṇa.

Being weary of the five desires, up to and including inhalation and exhalation, one currently dwells in the fourth dhyāna and takes it to be nirvāṇa. The above verses clarify the distinctions among the sixty-two types of views and conduct.
Regarding the verse “pervasive, unitary, and extending to the prior limit,” the commentary explains: “Pervasive” refers to the four [theories of] eternalism that are pervasive;

“unitary” refers to the four [theories of] eternalism that are partial; “causeless” refers to the two [theories of] being without cause; “finite” refers to the four [theories of] finitude; and “equivocal” refers to the four [theories of] equivocation.
Both the past and the present are termed “prior,” because the present is dependent upon the future; therefore, these are also termed “prior. These constitute the four [categories].
It is evasive. Although it arises in the present, because it takes the future as its form, it is called "prior. Alternatively, having heard prior teachings, one gives rise to this attachment;
based on those teachings, it is termed "prior."

Regarding the statement that the remaining forty-four [clinging-aggregates] mentioned in the verse are all subsumed under the "subsequent limit" (aparānta), the commentary explains: their number can be known through calculation;
they are all reckoned as the future, which is termed the "subsequent limit."

Regarding the verse’s statement that "pervasive views see everything," the commentary explains: Among the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there are the distinctions of annihilationism and eternalism.

Specifically, there are four theories of universal permanence, four theories of partial permanence, sixteen theories concerning perception (*saṃjñā*), eight theories concerning non-perception (*asaṃjñā*), and eight theories concerning neither [perception nor non-perception].

These combined constitute forty theories known as the extreme view of eternalism (*śāśvatāntadṛṣṭi*). The seven theories of annihilation (*uccheda*) constitute the extreme view of annihilationism (*ucchedāntadṛṣṭi*). Thus, the two pervasive extremes together comprise forty [theories].

7. Regarding the verse stating that "those two [views] which lack a cause for reaching [the goal] are both subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)," the commentary explains: In total there are fifteen categories;

those that do not arise subsequent to the view of selflessness are all termed false views. A brief expansion of the gloss on this verse follows; for the many other textual meanings, they are fully analyzed as presented in the chapters.
Regarding the statement in the sutras that "one may use glue, lacquer, cloth, and so forth," a question is raised: since the *Upāsaka-sūtra* does not permit the use of glue, why is it permitted here?

Briefly, there are two explanations. The first says: what is prohibited is glue made from skins, bones, and the like, whereas glue derived from wood is permitted. The second says: [the prohibition refers to animal-derived glue, while this permits plant-based glue].
The distinction between permitting and prohibiting has a specific underlying intent.

Regarding the passage in the sutra that says one should cause others to make music and so forth: it is asked whether there are sutras stating that musical instruments should not be given as gifts because they destroy the pure mind.
"Why do you now hold this [object] to offer as a gift? He replied: "The pleasure of sexual misconduct damages the pure mind;
true and correct pleasure praises virtue and fosters goodness. Therefore, there is a distinction between what is offered and what is not.
It is also like the music of Zheng and Wei in this land, which is called 'deviant,' while the ancient music of Da Xia and Da Shao is called 'correct. As for the deviant..."

The ruin of states and the extinction of families occur because one fails to manifest virtue through rectitude and to admonish oneself with integrity. According to the *Chunqiu Ganjing Fu* (The Spring and Autumn Annals:

Symbol of the Refinement of the Essence), "The high ministers and great officers shall employ men of the eight abilities to strike the *huangzhong* drum, offering congratulations for their virtue to the sovereign.

It further states, "In performing the eight musical rites, one must always take solemnity and reverence as the admonition. Furthermore, according to the *Han Shi Waizhuan* (Outer Commentary on the Han Poetry), "Tang composed the *hu*; 'hu' means..."
The name "Yue" (Music) signifies protection and salvation. Hearing the sound of Gong causes people to become gentle, kind, and magnanimous.
Hearing the sound of Shang causes people to become upright, frugal, and righteous. Hearing the sound of Jiao causes people to become sympathetic and benevolent. Hearing the sound of Zhi—
It causes people to delight in nurturing others and to enjoy giving. Upon hearing the sound of the *yu* (feather) pitch, it causes people to be respectful, frugal, and fond of ritual propriety.
Furthermore, according to the records, when King Wen of Wei asked Zixia about the meaning of "new music," Zixia replied: "When this new music is performed, it leads to excess in sensual desires."
This is detrimental to virtue. Furthermore, the *Shiji* states that King Zhou composed the "Music of the Northern Border of Zhao-ge," and as a result, he perished and his state fell.
Moreover, the *Liji* states that the music of Zheng and Wei is the music of a chaotic age, while the music of Sangwen Jian is the music of a ruined state.
By comparing these cases with the present matter, the principle becomes clear.
The commentary explains the five notes. According to the *Hanshu*: "Notes cleanse away a person's depraved intentions and lead them toward their fundamental nature.
*Shang* means 'to manifest,' for when things are accomplished, they can be clearly defined. *Jiao* means 'to touch,' for when things emerge from the earth, they bear sprouts and tips.
*Gong* means 'central,' for it dwells in the center, pervades the four directions, initiates the beginning, and bestows life; it serves as the net for the other four notes. *Zhi*..."
It is secret. When things are bright and expansive, it is secret. "Yu" means "feathers"; when things cover and conceal, the character "fu" (to cover) is used.

Regarding the eight musical tones (*bāyīn*): according to the *Lèjì* (Record of Music) in the *Lǐjì*, it says: "The arising of all sounds originates from the human heart. The movement of the human heart is caused by external things.
Stirred by things, they move; thus they take form as sound. From this, the various directions [of pitch] are established. This is what is meant.
Regarding the term "sound" (yin): the commentary states that "fang" refers to literary composition. Question: Why are eight precepts employed? At what points do these eight sections apply?

Answer: According to the *Guoyu*, it says: "Metal and stone instruments move [the spirit]; strings and flutes carry it forth; gourds proclaim it; earthenware assists it; leather and wood provide the rhythm.

When things attain their proper measure, it is called the ultimate of music (*leji*). Where this ultimate gathers is called sound (*sheng*). When sounds pair with one another, it is called harmony (*he*).

That the minute and the great do not exceed their proper measure is called music (*yue*). Thus, it is rubbed with metal, struck with stone, played upon with strings or wood, and regulated by gourds and bamboo;
it is then drummed forth and performed to regulate the eight winds—that is, the winds of the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*).

Regarding "the shields, axes, feathers, and yak-tail plumes": according to Zheng Xuan’s commentary, "shields" (*gan*) are bucklers; "axes" (*wei*) are battle-axes, held by those performing the martial dance (*wu*);
"feathers" (*yu*) are pheasant plumes; and "yak-tails" (*mao*) are the tails of the *māo* ox, held by those performing the civil dance (*wen*).
Regarding the *jingxiao* (flute): according to the *Tongsu*, Shun created the *xiao*; its shape is notched like the wings of a phoenix, consisting of ten tubes and measuring two chi in length.
The *Yiji* states that the *xiàzhī* music of the Xia dynasty used the *bǔxiao*; this *xiao* was fourteen inches long. Zheng Xuan’s commentary notes:
"The number of fire is seven, and it is the season of summer; since fire is active, two sevens make fourteen, and the length of the *xiao* is derived from this. Thus it is explained.
It is named *xiāo*, which is *sù* (solemn). Its sound is *sù-sù* (reverent), flowing with clarity. Furthermore, regarding the *shāo* and the *dì* (flute):

the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states that the sound of the *dí* is *dí* (to cleanse). Moreover, the *Fēngsú Tōng* (Comprehensive Account of Customs) says that during the reign of Emperor Wǔ, it was created by Qiū Zhòng.
"Dí" means cleansing; it is so called because it cleanses away depravity and filth, leading one toward the refined and correct. It is fourteen inches long and has seven holes.
Regarding the *qín*: furthermore, according to the *Baihūtong*, "Qín" means "prohibition," for it prohibits licentiousness and depravity, thereby rectifying the human heart.
Moreover, the *Erya* states that the *qín* of Fuxi was seven feet two inches long and had five strings.
Regarding the *konghou*: the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names) states that it was created by Shi Yan as a form of decadent music (*mimi zhi le*).

Later, it emerged from the lands of Sangjian and Puchang, likely remaining there during the period when the state of Kong was empty. Furthermore, the *Xu Hanshu* (Continued History of the Han) records that during the reign of Emperor Ling, he favored foreign dress and had the "barbarian *konghou*" made.
Additionally, the *Fengsu Tong* (Comprehensive Account of Customs) states: "The *konghou* is also called *kanhou*. According to [the records of] Emperor Wu’s sacrifices..."
Emperor Taiyi of Mount Tai and the Goddess Houtu commanded the musician Hou Tiao to compose the *Kanhou* based on the lute;
it was called *Kanhou* because its rhythmic beats were "kan-kan" in response to the musical measures, and the surname "Hou" was used to head the title.

Regarding the term "pipa" mentioned in the sutra: according to the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names), it originally originated from among the Hu peoples and is an instrument played while on horseback.
Pushing the hand forward is called "pi," and drawing it back is called "pa. It is named after these actions performed during its playing.
Regarding the *jing-niao* (cymbal-bell): the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states that its sound is "khak-khak.

Regarding the two *simas* (officers) holding the *duo* (gong): the *Sanli tu* (Illustrations of the Three Rituals) states that the *duo* is the same as the bell (*ling*) of today; its frame is made of copper.
A wooden tongue constitutes a wooden *duo*; a golden tongue constitutes a golden *duo*. Furthermore, the *Shuowen* states: "A *duo* is a large bell. The *Shiming* says:
"A *duo* means 'to measure' (*du*); it serves as the standard for proclamations and commands."
Regarding the term "singing" (*gē*) in the sutras: according to the *Shìmíng* (Explanation of Names), human voice is called "song. "Song" (*gē*) is "branch" (*kē*).

Because one chants and intones with the voice through ascending and descending pitches, it is like plants and trees having branches and leaves; thus, the singing voice is said to be like a branch. One may ask: what things are appropriate for song?
Answer: According to the *Liji*, Zigong visited Master Yi and asked him, saying, "I, Ci, have heard that when one sings, there are names appropriate to one's character.
As for someone like me, what would be appropriate? Master Yi replied, "Now, singing is the means by which one expresses oneself and manifests one's virtue.
When it moves, heaven and earth respond; the four seasons harmonize; the stars and constellations are regulated; and the myriad things are nourished. It is expansive yet tranquil, gentle..."
As for those who are upright, they should sing the *Eulogies* (*Song*). Those who are expansive yet tranquil, and distant yet trustworthy, should sing the *Greater Odes of Elegance* (*Daya*).
Those who are reverent, frugal, and fond of ritual propriety should sing the *Lesser Odes of Elegance* (*Xiaoya*). Those who are straightforward, tranquil, and incorruptible should sing the *Feng*.
Those who are open, direct, and compassionate should sing the *Shang*. Those who are gentle, kind, and capable of resolute judgment should sing the *Gong*.

Regarding the phrase "Koṭikarṇa and others" in the commentary: according to the *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions), his name is Śrutasomakotī, which in the Tang language means "Hearing Two Hundred Billion.
The ancient translation as "Yier" (億耳, Koṭikarṇa) is erroneous. He was from the country of Ilāvadradvīpa.
Long ago, there was an elder who was noble, prestigious, and immensely wealthy. Late in life, he had an heir. Whenever someone reported this news, he would immediately bestow two billion gold coins;
consequently, the son was named Erbaoyi (Two Hundred Billion). By the time he reached maturity, he had never walked upon the ground, so his feet were raised off the floor.
His body hair grew to over a foot in length, glossy, fine, and soft, with a color like refined gold. Later, Bimbisāra...
When the King heard of this, he wished to see him. The elder went from his home to the city, where he dug a canal and filled it with mustard seeds to stabilize the royal barge.
He then sent the barge safely to deliver his son, hoping to avoid the disaster of the elephant-ship sinking or capsizing. Before departing, the son first paid homage to the World-Honored One.

The Buddha, regarding the matter of the husband presenting his feet, approved of his conduct; consequently, the King released him to return home, and he followed the Tathāgata to leave the household life.
He attained the fruit. The rest is as detailed in the *Biographies* (Zhuan); fearing prolixity, it is not recorded here.
Regarding the phrase "In all dharmas, there are briefly two kinds," etc.: the preceding portion explains according to the text;
the following portion points to the dharmas to clarify the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), providing a brief summary rather than a separate commentary.

Regarding the passage in the sutra from "At that time, the various Brahma kings came and requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma" until "Since you have appeared in the world for the sake of sentient beings, you may speak of your own accord;
why wait for a request?"—the answer is: although the Buddha has no need [for such a request], it is for the sake of generating merit in those who request it that he speaks only after being entreated.
Therefore, the *Saptakṣaṇa Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states: "Requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma."

This can extinguish the sin of slandering the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Question: For what reason is it the devas who make the request? Answer: There are two explanations. First, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) mostly serve Brahmā; once Brahmā has made the request, the minds of the non-Buddhists are thereby subdued. Second, because the devas are superior beings, the request is made by them to clarify this point. Answer: [The text continues: ...because the devas are superior beings, the request is made by them to clarify this point. Question: In the case of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, his sons made the request first and Brahmā’s request came later. How does the present case differ from that? Answer: [The text continues: ...because the devas are superior beings, the request is made by them to clarify this point. Question: In the case of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, his sons made the request first and Brahmā’s request came later. How does the present case differ from that? The commentary on the sutra states: "The previous Buddha appeared in a fortunate age; thus, the son’s succession of his father's legacy was profound. Śākyamuni appeared in an evil age;
thus, the son’s succession of his father's legacy was meager. Therefore, there is a distinction between them."
Regarding the term "xiàoliè" (校獵), there are two interpretations of "xiào" (校). First, Li Qí stated that it refers to using five types of military units to conduct a hunt on foot.

Yán Sīgǔ stated that it refers to wooden stakes pierced through one another to form a general enclosure or barrier (*lánxiào*), which serves to block and contain birds and beasts so they may be hunted.
Regarding the term "zòng liáo" (縱獠): the pronunciation of "liáo" is *lì yǔ* (力予反). According to the *Ěrzǎo* (爾疋), "xiāo tián" (霄田) is called "liáo.
Guō Pǔ states that in Jiangdong, hunting is called "liáo," which is the same as tonight's hunt; it refers to carrying a brazier (*lú*) [to light the way] and illuminating [the area].
The commentary’s mention of *Udraka Rāmaputra* is erroneous; the correct form is *Udraka*, which means "Fierce" (*Mingsheng*).
The commentary’s mention of *Ārāḍa Kālāma* is erroneous; the correct form is *Ārāḍa*, which means "Encountered" (*Fengyu*).
Regarding the commentary’s tradition that explains the five individuals and so forth: according to the *Buddha-mūla-prakaraṇa-sūtra* (佛本行經), fascicle 34, they are:
first, Aññā-Koṇḍañña; second, Bhaddiya, which means "Small Virtue" (小賢); third, Vappa, which means "Arisen Breath" (起氣);
fourth, Mahānāma, which means "Great Name" (大名); and fifth, Assaji, which means "Tamer of Horses" (調馬).
Regarding the "śrāmaṇya" (the state of a śramaṇa) mentioned in the Commentary: that treatise, having already explained that śrāmaṇya, further clarifies its synonyms.
All untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) constitute śrāmaṇya; one who harbors these paths is alone called a śramaṇa.
"Brahmins" and so forth are merely different names. If one relies on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), Brahmins and others are distinct from śramaṇas;
however, according to the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*), the sūtras also state that one who possesses the true nature of a śramaṇa is called a "Brahmin.

Why is this? One is called a "Brahmin" because they have dispelled the afflictions (*kleśa*). If one can exert diligent effort to pacify all afflictions, that is the meaning of a "śramaṇa. Therefore, based on this...
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). That is precisely this.
As for the commentary stating that it is also called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakra*) and so forth, it is another name for the state of a śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇya*);

it is termed the "Brahma-wheel" from the perspective of its being turned by [the Buddha]. Thus, that treatise states: "It is also called the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the power of the True Brahmā King. The Buddha is the unsurpassed Brahmā.

He is endowed with such virtues. Therefore, World-Honored One, you alone should be named Brahmā. As it is stated in the sūtras, the Buddha is also named Brahmā, also named Tranquil, and also named Cool.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "Only the Path of Seeing, etc., [is seen] therein": within this wheel turned by the True Brahmā, it is only based on the Path of Seeing that it is designated as the Wheel of Dharma; all else is not so designated.

The commentary states that the "Dharma-wheel" is so named because right view reaches its goal. Right view and the other three [limbs of the path] must rely upon ethical discipline (*śīla*) to arise in relation to their objects;

thus, they resemble spokes that exist by depending on a hub. Right speech and the other three [limbs] take ethical discipline as their essence, for ethical discipline is the foundation upon which all practices depend, just as the hub of a worldly wheel is the support for everything else. Right concentration is able to encompass right view.
These four [factors] prevent scattering, just like the rim of a worldly wheel; therefore, only these eight receive the name "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*), while other dharmas do not correspond.
Regarding the phrase "How is it known, etc.," this is the interrogative statement from that treatise. "Kauṇḍinya and others" is the answer given in that same treatise. Kauṇḍinya...
When the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises, the terrestrial devas proclaim: "The World-Honored One has turned the Wheel of the True Dharma.

Therefore, it is known that the Path of Seeing is called the Wheel of the Dharma. Otherwise, how could it be said that it has been "turned"? This is because the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) had not yet been turned at all.
This [statement] refers to [the turning] for the sake of others; it does not concern the Tathāgata’s own turning of the Dharma. [This] was already attained previously.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is designated as the "turner" so that those to be converted may conceive a sense of reverence; for this reason, he does not speak of himself [as the turner].

Regarding the commentary by Vasubandhu up to the point where the name "Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma" is established, the intent of this objection is as follows: according to the tenets of our own school, [it is said that] eye and wisdom...
The clear awakening reveals and displays the three paths; therefore, it is called the "turning of the twelve aspects. Consequently, an objection is raised:

since the twelve aspects pertain not only to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) but also extend to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), how can it be said that the name "Wheel of Dharma" is established solely for the path of seeing?

The Commentary states: "Therefore, one should proceed only so far as it accords with correct reasoning. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, relying on the Sautrāntika school—or perhaps expressing his own view—set forth this correct interpretation.

According to that treatise: because one cultivates and traverses the four noble truths through three cycles, [the first cycle]—"this is suffering," and so forth—constitutes the four aspects of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
[The second cycle]—"this should be fully known," and so forth—constitutes the four aspects of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). [The third cycle]—"this..."
"Having fully known," and so forth; because there are four [moments] for each of the paths of no-more-learning, twelve are established. The commentary states:

These very three revolutions and twelve aspects constitute all the verbal teachings of the Dharma-gate of the Four Truths; each is the essence of the Wheel of Dharma and may be correctly applied according to reason.
The *Śāstra* states that all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are termed the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*); this is the second interpretation of Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.

It universally includes the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), asserting that all such paths constitute the Wheel of Dharma, which differs from the position of the Sarvāstivāda school.
"The transformation within the manifested body" explains the meaning of "transformation.
"Reaching the name of 'already transformed' within the mental continuum of another" addresses the objection raised previously regarding that which has already been transformed.

In the commentary on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it states: "Regarding the passage 'one who practices emptiness alone,' upon examining the *Satyasiddhi* from beginning to end, no such text as cited in the commentary is found.
Only in the twenty-third chapter, 'Seeing the One Truth' (*Eka-satya-vibhāga*), it says: 'Question: If one does not attain the Way by means of the Four Truths...'"
"By what dharma is the Path attained? He replied, "The Path is attained by means of a single truth, namely, cessation (*nirodha*). As it is said in the Sūtra:
'Because the practitioner contemplates these five aggregates as empty and selfless, it is called an "empty jar," just as a jar that contains no water is called an empty jar.'"

Thus, because there is no self (ātman) within these five aggregates (skandhas), they are called "empty. One who contemplates in this manner is also said to be "empty," and is likewise termed "possessing knowledge and vision" (jñānadarśana).
Furthermore, the subsequent section on the three types of wisdom states: "The three types of wisdom arise in mutual dependence. [The author] comments:

The Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) has merely taken the general purport of the treatise to formulate his words; he has not transcribed the treatise in its entirety. This is the judgment established by the Master of the Commentary. Its...
The bestowal of realization is for the most part like this. However, if one examines it more closely:

regarding the statement that "the former serves as the cause for the latter," it is like how hearing serves as the cause for reflection, and how both hearing and reflection together can serve as the cause for cultivation.

Vision is the cause for cultivation; name and so forth are the subsequent causes. Vision and cultivation together can serve as the cause for the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); name and form together constitute the cause of the fruit.
The remaining [categories] should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "the insights of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning correspond in sequence," this means that the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of knowledge and vision are respectively assigned to those stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
Thus, that treatise states: "The three cycles proceed correctly; according to their sequence, the clear realizations of knowledge and vision are called the attainment of the means.
It should be understood that at the time of entering the clear realization of the truths, knowing them as they truly are—as the truth of suffering and so forth—is what is termed [attainment]."

The stage of knowledge (*jñānāvasthā*). From this point onward, regarding the various truths, there remains further that which is to be done, such as "that which is to be fully known" (*parijñeya*) and so forth;

because of this contemplation, it is called the stage of vision (*darśanāvasthā*). On the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*), one understands in accordance with reality: "I have fully known," and so forth.
This refers to the stage of "manifest realization" (*abhisamaya*).
Regarding the statement in the commentary that this is a "conventional designation for *brahman*," there are three brief explanations: First, the Tathāgata is neither *brahman* nor non-*brahman*.

Because he is designated by force as a name, it is called "conventional" (*adhivacana*). This is because all phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be reached by verbal expression; they are all transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). [They are merely] provisional...

First, the designation of names is called "augmentation" (*āgama*). Second, although the two dharmas are fundamentally beyond words, they are augmented by means of names and phrases within sounds so as to have something expressed;
therefore, it is called "augmentation. Third, "augmenting speech" (*adhivacana*) refers to names; that is, the Tathāgata possesses these Brahma-names.
Therefore, it is called "Brahma.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that these four types are either suppressed or abandoned, etc., these refer to the four dharmas: teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that one attains the means up to the cause of bodhi: [this] asks whether the paths of seeing and cultivation may be termed "means," and how one attains bodhi...
Question: Regarding the cause, at the stage of perfection of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this itself is bodhi. Against what, then, could it be called a "cause" or a "skillful means"?
Answer: Briefly, there are two explanations. First, both bodhi and nirvāṇa are termed "bodhi. That which can realize [it] is the cause; that which is realized is the fruit.

Based on this principle, at the stage of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), they are designated as "causes" and "expedient means. Although both have already reached the state of no-more-learning, they must still first arise;
thus, the four—fully realized knowledge (*parijñā*) and so forth—are designated as "aspects" (*ākāra*). These four aspects serve as causes for the subsequent stages.
For these two reasons, the commentary states: "The former serves as the cause for the latter."
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "based on the gate of the expressive [term], it exists throughout the three periods of time," there are briefly two interpretations. The first says:

This refers to the Truths of Suffering and so forth, which belong to the three periods of time; however, the principle of cessation through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) underlying those Truths of Suffering and so forth does not belong to the three periods of time.

Because one realizes that principle by means of abandoning the Truths of Suffering and so forth—which do belong to the periods of time—the Truths of Suffering and so forth serve as the expressers. Therefore, it is based on the expresser [that the term is said to exist throughout the three periods].
It explains the principle that is revealed, which pervades the three periods of time. Second, it says: "This distinguishes the principle of the third truth, cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

It is that which can manifest [the truth] by means of the realizing wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) that severs the afflictions to be abandoned; therefore, it is called the 'expressive' (*vācaka*). Based on this expressive [wisdom], it is said that there are the three periods of time.
For this reason, within each truth, there exist those four kinds of aspects (*ākāra*), such as the eye and so forth. The commentary states: "Although the previous explanation is acceptable..."
This is not the intended meaning of the *Śāstra* (Commentary). The latter interpretation is correct, as can be understood from the text.

Regarding the statement that "the stage prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is different from the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)," it is because the stage prior to the Path of Cultivation contains those untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the Path of Seeing, and furthermore, because [the practitioner] personally gives rise to untainted dharmas [at that time].
Therefore, even the suppression (*vibhava*) by means of the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) is termed "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*). As for the Path of Seeing...
Prior to the Path, there is absolutely no untainted (anāsrava) state; therefore, [the afflictions] are suppressed but not abandoned.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "those [afflictions], from the stage of Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) up to the stage of Suchness (tathatā), constitute the four [levels]"—however, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* does not explain the eye and so forth in this manner, nor does it correlate them with the Dharma-patience and other stages.
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 79, there are two explanations, the first of which...

The first interpretation assigns the four—dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) and so forth—to the four [faculties] beginning with the eye, as cited in the commentary. The second interpretation states: "Eye" has the sense of observing and seeing;

"knowledge" (*jñāna*) has the sense of decisive judgment; "clarity" (*vidyā*) has the sense of illuminating and comprehending; and "awakening" (*buddhi*) has the sense of startled discernment. The commentary explains:

the former interpretation refers to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), while the latter interpretation applies to all three paths. Now, the commentary cites that statement from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle... [number].

This is one interpretation. According to this view, because one performs the contemplation of the eight truths (*aṣṭasatya*) solely during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are the four [moments] beginning with patience (*kṣānti*).

However, when cultivating the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), one contemplates only the four truths and does not perform the contemplation of the eight truths; therefore, there are neither subsequent patiences (*anvayakṣānti*) nor subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).
Consequently, the four aspects for each truth would be insufficient.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This refers to the Buddha’s three turnings for others,” it is asked: Do all śrāvakas rely upon the Tathāgata’s three turnings of the Dharma?
The answer is: Not necessarily. For example, those who attain the four fruits in the presence of the World-Honored One have them turned by the Buddha;
however, those who attain the fruits without seeing the Buddha do not have them turned by the Buddha. Depending on the circumstances, they receive one or two turnings from the Tathāgata.
Regarding "turning" (*parivarta*) and so forth: some do not receive it at all because they do not encounter a Buddha; others do encounter a Buddha, yet the results obtained differ.
This can be understood through reflection. If this is so, why is it called "turning by another"? There are two explanations: first, based on encountering a Buddha;

second, although one does not encounter [a Buddha], one nevertheless encounters the teaching of the Tathāgata’s three turnings and thereby attains the fruit. Thus, by subsuming the teaching back into the Buddha, it is also so designated.
The Buddha is said to have performed the "three turnings.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "causing others to reach deep faith and understanding":

one might ask, while Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained the principle and could thus develop faith and understanding regarding what the Buddha realized, how could those earth deities and others—who had not yet attained the state of an *ārya*—develop such faith and understanding regarding what Kauṇḍinya realized?
Faith and Understanding. Answer: Because the Buddha proclaimed, "Cunda has understood the Dharma," and through his divine faith in the Buddha’s words, he conceived faith in what Cunda had realized.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 41) states: "The Buddha told others, 'I have turned the Wheel of Dharma;

the bhikṣu has seen the Dharma. Therefore, they were able to hear it. Question: For what reason did he tell others? Answer: The World-Honored One manifested himself among the ninety-six [non-Buddhist teachers]...

Within the teachings of the Dharma, it is supreme and unsurpassed. Furthermore, it is to manifest the true merits of Cunda and others, and because they serve as excellent fields of merit for the world, he informs others of this.
Question: Since there were other celestial deities and so forth present in the assembly, for what reason did the earth deity first proclaim this?
Answer: Because that earth deity was the first to utter the sound. Question: For what reason [did she do so] first?

He replied: "Because they constantly follow the Buddha and act as his guardians, now that they have seen the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma, they rejoice and celebrate, thinking, 'Our previous efforts have brought this fruit to fulfillment.
Therefore, they were the first to announce it. Furthermore, because the nature of the earth deities is to leap [with joy].
Furthermore, according to the principle of proximity in sequence: the earth deities are close to the Buddha; therefore, they were the first to announce it."

Regarding the statement that "its wheel is able to pacify, for its nature is inherently quiescent": "inherently quiescent" refers to the principle of the quiescent essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The objective realm of the Wheel of Dharma may be called the "Wheel of Dharma. Previously, when it had not yet been turned, it was shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*);

now, as the Wheel of Dharma is turned, the Noble Path arises, whereby afflictions are entirely exhausted. Consequently, the principle of the inherently quiescent True Suchness is revealed; therefore, it is said to be "able [to pacify]."
Quiescence. Its intrinsic nature is quiescent.
Regarding the "rare Dharma-knowledge realized by devas and humans": the untainted, correct knowledge obtained by those of the three vehicles is called "Dharma-knowledge.
It is termed "realization" because it is only at this time that devas and humans are able to attain it.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that the Pratyekabuddhas attain the dharmas such as *uṣmagata* (Heat) and so forth: Question: There are also sūtras which state that Pratyekabuddhas are born by transformation (*upapāduka*) and yet also attain the state of an Arya.

How can these two accounts be mutually contradictory? Answer: If they manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to cause others to attain the fruits [of the path], then such a principle is indeed possible.
However, this is not the case when it concerns their preaching of the Dharma. Thus, the second fascicle of the *Mahādharanī-dharmolkā-sūtra* states: "Those Pratyekabuddhas are fully endowed with..."
He possessed wisdom; yet, he was unable to preach the Dharma to deliver others. [Question: Was it that he did not preach at all, or did he preach even slightly?
[Answer: It was because he did preach slightly. The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states: "At that time, King Brahmadatta went to the presence of a Pratyekabuddha.
Then the Pratyekabuddha preached the various Dharmas briefly, causing the king to rejoice and leap with immeasurable joy, manifesting virtuous matters. If...
Regarding the statement in certain places that "the Dharma is not taught," there are two intended meanings. First, it is called "not taught" because [the Buddha] does not teach extensively.

Second, it is also called "not taught" because although he teaches the Dharma, he is unable to cause others to attain the state of an *ārya*. Question: The fourth fascicle of the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states:
"The various *pratyekabuddhas* cast their alms bowls into the void and perform the eighteen transformations. Each of these *pratyekabuddhas*..."

Your Excellency, all [of these] texts fully explain the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). In response to that, the sutra does not state that all *pratyekabuddhas* fail to teach it;
it is possible that some may indeed attain it.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddha Śuklodana and others, there are two traditional explanations. First, it is translated here as "Beloved by His Father";
because he was the youngest son, his father’s affection was particularly focused upon him, hence the name "Beloved. Second, it is translated here as "Weeping";
because he heard that all his elder brothers had already attained Buddhahood, he wept constantly, grieving that he would not be delivered [to liberation], and thus the name was established.

Regarding the statement that "the solitary king [Śākyamuni] alone [endures] one kalpa": this refers to the present Bhadrakalpa. In total, there will be two cycles of eighty aeons of increase and decrease.
While nine hundred and ninety-nine World-Honored Ones each abide for eighty aeons, the final Tathāgata alone shall occupy one full cycle of eighty aeons.
This is called one kalpa.
Regarding the statement in the commentary that after twelve kalpas there is the Kalpa of Adornment (*Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*): Question:

According to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra*, there were formerly three thousand people who recited the names of the thirty-five Buddhas. By virtue of this merit, one thousand people [attained birth] in the Kalpa of Adornment.

They shall attain Buddhahood. One thousand people will attain Buddhahood in the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon), and one thousand people will attain Buddhahood in the Nakṣatrakalpa (Constellation Aeon).
According to the text of that sutra, the *Vyūhakalpa* (Adornment Aeon) is a past aeon; thus, it should be understood that the various explanations in these scriptures differ.

Alternatively, this commentary may be erroneous, for in the Master’s *Commentary on the Sutra of Maitreya’s Ascent*, he also states that the *Vyūhakalpa* is a past aeon. Therefore, we know that the commentary is mistaken.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that Kāśyapa Buddha lived for seven days:

A questioner asks, "According to the *Sūtra of the Names of Ten Thousand Buddhas*, the lifespan of Kāśyapa Buddha was two intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), whereas the lifespan of our Śākyamuni Buddha is the shortest, being only one hundred years. How can these accounts be reconciled?"
Answer: There are differences in what has been seen and heard, and the various teachings are not uniform; such examples are not limited to one.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of “the rarity of the Dharma” and so forth: it is like the case of the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa and Pradīparāja, who, following the first Buddha, waited until after twenty thousand Buddhas had passed before Pradīparāja finally preached the sutra; therefore, it is considered rare to hear.
It is difficult to encounter the Dharma after a long interval has passed, as stated in the sūtras.

During the time of the Buddha, there was a brāhmaṇa whose wife was beautiful and whom he loved deeply; thus, he was unwilling to renounce the world. He thought to himself, "If a Buddha appears in every generation, it will not be too late for me to go forth later.
When he eventually encountered the World-Honored One, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "Will there be another Buddha in future ages? The Buddha...

He answered him, saying, "The number of future Buddhas is like the sands of the Ganges. Upon hearing this, he departed. Not long after he had gone, he thought to himself, "Were there Buddhas in the past?
If there were, why have I not encountered them? He returned and questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said, "The Buddhas of the past were likewise infinite.
Having heard this, he attained awakening: "There were Buddhas in the past whom I did not meet; there will be Buddhas in the future [whom I may encounter]."
...how could he know that this was a transgression? He immediately requested ordination and thereby attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
*Puyupin* (The Chapter on Similes), Commentary, Scroll Five.

Regarding the discussion of the seven types of sentient beings who possess afflictions (*kleśa*), there are briefly two interpretations. The first states they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). As the text says:
Because they are fully possessed of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*). If one is a noble being (*ārya*) still in training (*śaikṣa*), one cannot be said to be fully possessed of afflictions.

Second, it is said that this also applies to those in training. How can a person in training be called "fully possessed"? The answer is: there are two ways of being "fully possessed. First, in terms of the realms (*dhātu*);

second, in terms of the number and substance of the afflictions. If we rely on the explanation in terms of the realms, for those who have attained the first two fruits, [afflictions] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been abandoned.

It may be said that they possess [the afflictions]. Speaking in terms of their essential nature (*tattva*), because the afflictions of the lower realms have not been entirely eliminated, they are also called "possessing" them.

The commentary states: "The former is correct, while the latter is erroneous. How is this verified? The treatise says: "As for the first type of person, they seek the fruit and retribution of the wondrous realms of humans and devas;
therefore, they are called 'inverted' (*viparyāsa*). How could one who studies the Path of the Sages seek such things? Furthermore, regarding the first two fruits...

There is absolutely no such thing [as a person who possesses all fetters]. For one who has attained the second fruit, both innate and acquired fetters are present; for one who has attained the first fruit, they are not so.

Since there is already a deficiency in the defilements, how can it be said that they are "complete" in terms of their substantial nature? Therefore, it is known that [the opponent's position] is erroneous.
Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "The following twenty-six chapters collectively clarify these three meanings," etc.:
although these three meanings are present, absent, or entirely lacking within the subsequent chapters—as indicated in the Commentary—their scope varies in breadth and narrowness.

While it is not difficult to establish four logical permutations (catuṣkoṭi) by comparing them against one another, this is included here for the sake of providing a complete and elegant exposition, even though the meaning itself is not obscure. This applies to both the meaning and the text.

The "Remnant" and so forth constitute four sets of four statements (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the first set of four—where there are seven parables and three equalities—the four statements are as follows: 1. There are parables that are not equalities; these consist of five chapters:

the *Śraddhā-bhaiṣajya* (Faith-Medicine), the *Nirmita-nagara* (Transformation City), the *Sukhavihāra* (Abiding in Bliss), the *Āyuṣpramāṇa* (Life Span), and the [final chapter]. 2. There are equalities that are not parables; these consist of seven chapters:

the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prediction), the *Śikṣāpada-dharmabhāṇaka* (Teaching the Dharma according to the Precepts), the *Ratnastūpa* (Jeweled Stupa), the *Devadatta* (Devadatta), the *Parīndanā* (Entrustment), and the *Anuparīndanā* (Further Entrustment).

Light [parables] have three shared characteristics and two categories, namely the *Upamā* (Simile) and the *Śatapañcāśatka* (Five Hundred). Those lacking all four [characteristics] comprise twelve categories, namely:

the *Abhyudgata* (Emergence), *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis), *Anumodanā* (Rejoicing), *Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa* (Qualities of the Dharma-preacher), *Prabhāva* (Spiritual Power), *Bhaiṣajyarāja* (Bhaiṣajyarāja), *Gadgadasvara* (Gadgadasvara), *Avalokiteśvara* (Avalokiteśvara), *Dhāraṇī*, *Suśobhana* (Excellent Adornment), *Samantabhadra* (Samantabhadra), and *Parindana* (Entrustment).
The second set of seven parables is correlated with the ten unsurpassed qualities to form four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

1. There are those that have similes but are not unsurpassed; these consist of two chapters, namely the *Dṛṣṭānta-parivarta* and the *Adhimukti-parivarta*. 2. There are those that are unsurpassed but do not have similes;

these consist of fifteen chapters, namely from the *Stūpa-samudgama-parivarta* up to the tenth, the *Anuttara-parivarta*, which consists of fourteen chapters, excluding the single *Sukhāvati-vyūha-parivarta*.

3. There are those that possess both; these consist of five chapters, namely the *Oṣadhi-parivarta*, the *Nirmita-nagara-parivarta*, the *Pañcaśatika-parivarta*, the *Sukhāvati-vyūha-parivarta*, and the *Āyuḥpramāṇa-parivarta*. 4. There are those that possess neither.

There are none. There are four categories: namely, the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the instruction of the Dharma-master, Devadatta, and the third, equality. In contrast to the ten unsurpassed [categories], there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there is equality that is not unsurpassed; this consists of five categories: namely, the parable, the prediction of enlightenment, the instruction of the Dharma-master, Devadatta, and Viśākha.
Second, there is the unsurpassed that is not equality; this consists of sixteen categories: namely, the medicinal herbs and the transformation [bodies].

The *Anurādhapura* (City of Peace and Bliss), the *Udgata-āyus-pramāṇa-vibhaṅga*, the *Anumodanā-dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-anubhāva*, the *Bhaiṣajyarāja*, the *Gadgadasvara*, the *Avalokiteśvara-dhāraṇī*, the *Suśobhana*, and the *Samantabhadra-pariṇāmanā* each possess three [elements] and four chapters;

that is, the five hundred Dharma-preachers and the *Ratnastūpa* which encourages upholding [the teaching]. Four [elements] are absent; there is one chapter, namely the *Adhimukti*. The fourth [section] consists of the upper and lower parts.
The two remaining sections are paired to form four propositions: 1. There are six chapters that belong to the higher [division] but not the lower:

namely, "The Medicinal Herbs," "The City of Transformation," "The Five Hundred Jewel Stūpas Emerge," and "The Lifespan. 2. There are thirteen chapters that belong to the lower [division] but not the higher:

namely, "The Dharma Master Encourages Retention," "Distinguishing the Merits of the Dharma Master," "Rejoicing," "The Supernatural Powers of the Dharma Master," "Bhaiṣajyarāja," "Gadgadasvara," and "Avalokiteśvara."
The *Dhāraṇī-alaṃkāra* and the *Samantabhadra-pariṇāmanā* possess all three [features]. There is one chapter that possesses one [feature], namely the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha*. Four possess none.
There are six chapters that possess [all] six, namely: the *Upamā*, the *Adhimukti*, the *Vyākaraṇa*, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, the *Devatā*, and the *Aparājitā*.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "the ten unsurpassed [vehicles] comprise twenty-one chapters," etc.: Question: It is taught that the Great Penetration (Mahābhijñā) constitutes the unsurpassed practice (*caryā-anuttara*), as it clarifies the cultivation of the great path.
Since the metaphor of the ox-cart is also a cause for the Mahāyāna, why is it not considered unsurpassed? Answer:

The metaphor primarily clarifies that while within the triple world (*tridhātu*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are taught in order to gradually lead beings out of the house. It does not exclusively distinguish the ox-cart; therefore, it is not [itself] unsurpassed.
Above.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra-commentary), "The ten unsurpassables are the seven similes and three equalities; as for the remainder," the question is:

does the term "remainder" refer to the meaning of the ten unsurpassables, or does it refer to the sūtras that speak of those unsurpassable points? The answer is: judging by the wording of the *Śāstra*, it appears to refer to the meaning of the unsurpassables.
According to the *Śāstra* based on the *Vyākhyā*, this refers to that sūtra. It clarifies the *Anuttara-sūtra*, which is a supplementary sūtra to the *Saptopama-trisamatā-sūtra*.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "The meaning of 'unsurpassed' (*anuttara*) refers to the remaining *sūtras* that clarify the meaning of being unsurpassed."

According to this treatise, the term "residual" (*śeṣa*) refers to the *Sūtra* that explains both [the residual and the non-residual], yet it does not explicitly designate the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Because the commentary (*śāstra*) is somewhat brief, many readers are confused;
therefore, I have repeated these words.

Regarding the phrase "upper remainder" (shàng-cán) and "lower remainder" (xià-cán) in the Commentary (*śāstra*): the word "remainder" (*cán*) is mentioned in two places within the treatise, yet its placement differs between the former and the latter;

therefore, the Commentary designates them as "upper" and "lower. Question: The *Jiǎn píngděng jīng* (Sūtra on the Selection of Equality) also appears after the analogy; why is it not termed a "remainder"?
Answer: The metaphors (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the equality (*samatā*) both speak of curing illness; because their intended meaning is similar, they are not called "residual" (*śeṣa*).
Only when the supreme intention (*anuttara-abhiprāya*) is distinct is it designated by the term "residual. Question: Since the supreme is situated at the end, it may be called "residual.

But there are also cases where it is spoken of before the metaphors and the like; how can it be called "residual" in those instances? Answer: The treatise establishes the seven metaphors, the equality, and the supreme as its primary sequence. Even if [the supreme] were placed elsewhere...

There are one or two unsurpassed [qualities] that are manifest before one; speaking in terms of the majority of categories, these are collectively termed "residues" (*śeṣa*). The subsequent "residues" are to be understood accordingly.

The commentary states that the mention of "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*) and "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) serves to distinguish them from noble ones who are still in training; thus, the term "ordinary" is employed because they possess something to aspire toward and seek.
Because they cultivate and practice [the path], they are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*). This is not the same as the common explanation;

for these ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are in reality not "those in training," as they have not yet attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*). Rather, they are called "those in training" in contrast to those who are "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), who possess the three types of equanimity.
The commentary states, "From 'as if grasping at a conjured city' to 'having nothing to seek,' this intention is raised to clarify the seven types of metaphors;
these all correspond to those in training (śaikṣa), not to those beyond training (aśaikṣa). The city will be explained below."

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* stating, "The person without afflictions reaches such a meaning," this is a general explanation of the intent of the treatise, which may be understood from the *Śāstra*.

As for the detailed interpretation of the textual passages, they are difficult to understand based on the *Śāstra*; therefore, I shall now provide an explanation for those sections where the *Śāstra* merely cites the text without further commentary.

The *Treatise* says: "The three kinds of defilement and the person without afflictions. This clarifies the intended audience (the person for whom the teaching is addressed). It continues: "Samādhi, liberation, vision, and so forth... [and so on].

"Defiled pride" (*māna-saṃkliṣṭa*) clarifies the disease to be treated; it explains the aforementioned "defilement. Concentration (*samādhi*), liberation (*vimukti*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and so forth are the bases from which defilement arises.
Defiled pride is precisely the defilement that arises therein. Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others..."

Being obscured and obstructed by the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), one does not abandon those dharmas that ought to be abandoned, nor does one attain those dharmas that ought to be attained.
Therefore, the ground of the abiding of ignorance accumulates and gives rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*):

namely, the afflictions regarding correct reception (*samādhi*), the afflictions regarding the fruit, and the afflictions regarding gnosis (*jñāna*). These correspond, respectively, to the samādhis, liberations, and views within this context.

The word "etc. (ādi) includes other [categories]. That is to say, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* contains fourteen phrases concerning the general and specific causes and conditions that clarify the locus where defilement arises;

these include the remaining eleven [phrases] regarding those who have not attained the ultimate goal but consider themselves satisfied, and because they are thus haughty, this is termed "pride" (*māna*).
Question: Since the original intent clarifies that grasping at the distinctions of saṃsāra and so forth is called the "three types of defiled pride," why is it necessary to cite those three samādhis?

Regarding the passage beginning with "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*), the response cites seeing and so forth as being accompanied by defiled pride (*māna*). This proves that these three bases are also subject to defilement.
If this clarification were not cited, one might fear that there is doubt regarding those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who are thought to lack such defiled pride.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “the subsequent delusions of view and so forth arise after suffering,” this means that the mind of subsequent attainment is coarse;

it cannot apprehend either fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) or suchness (*tathatā*). Consequently, one perceives that the delusions regarding the practices and stages previously cultivated do not arise.

Therefore, the mind undergoes a transformation, giving rise to the conceptual understanding that one has attained *nirvāṇa*. This transformative capacity is pointed out and designated as the "chariot.

Regarding the commentary's statement from "Now it is said" up to "playing with them," this can be fully understood from the text itself. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The arousal of the bodhicitta and the stages such as the ten levels of faith have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*); these are all termed "worldly.

The virtues and so forth belonging to these stages are called "worldly merits. The absence of greed, hatred, and delusion is termed "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). Tainted meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the like are termed "samādhis.

Because they still correctly crave the three realms and so forth, they are described as being free from greed and so on [only relatively], while remaining attached to the external worldly pleasures of the five desires.

Therefore, he preaches the samādhi for them, instructing them so that they may rely upon it; this is called "causing them to sport. By means of this, they subsequently attain entry into Great Nirvāṇa. The commentary states:

Both the *Śū* (the sub-commentary) and other meanings are difficult to comprehend. Regarding the difficulty of understanding the *Śū*, the Sūtra speaks of the burning house where there are three sons, and it is announced that they shall be given vehicles;
the vehicles are also said to be threefold. The *Treatise* (*Lun*) explains the intent of the Sūtra by stating in general that they are given "wholesome" [vehicles]. It does not...

To determine their number: why are only the conceptual understandings (*saṃjñā-vijñapti*) capable of transformation belonging to the two vehicles taken as the "chariots" and termed "worldly roots of goodness," while Bodhisattvas are excluded?
