This refers to the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering, as explained extensively above. Regarding the three characteristics of emptiness:
when something does not exist in a particular place, one correctly perceives it as empty by virtue of that principle. Question: In what place does what not exist? Answer:

Within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), such things as a permanent, eternal, and unchanging self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) do not exist; by virtue of this principle, they are all empty. Furthermore, there are three kinds [of emptiness].
Emptiness: first, emptiness of intrinsic nature; second, emptiness of suchness; third, emptiness of true reality.
The first is observed in relation to the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) definitely do not exist.

The second is observed in relation to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because all things are non-existent in the manner they are conceptualized. The third is observed in relation to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The contemplation of nature (*dharmatā-vipaśyanā*): because it is the very reality of emptiness itself. Fourth, the characteristic of selflessness (*anātman-lakṣaṇa*):

that is to say, the characteristics of a self as established by proponents of the theory of self (*ātmavādin*) do not apply to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). This is because the characteristic of a self does not exist within the aggregates, elements, and bases.

Furthermore, non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who propound the theory of self conceptualize various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being the self; however, those conditioned phenomena do not possess such a characteristic. Therefore, they are called "selfless. [This concludes] the four aspects of the origin [of suffering].
Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): first is the characteristic of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to the causal habituation that can bring about future existence;

this is called the characteristic of the cause, because karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as the causal habituation that can bring about future existence. Second is the characteristic of accumulation (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to those various sentient beings.
The accumulated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that serve as the equalizing cause for various classes of sentient beings are called the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*).

Because the habitual tendencies accumulated by sentient beings act as the cause for the equal arising of similar physical forms and types among the classes of sentient beings, such as gods and humans, this constitutes the third characteristic:
the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to the immeasurable varieties of differences within each individual internal body.
The cause of distinct arising is called the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

It is the cause for the distinct internal continuities of all sentient beings, determining their rebirths in various realms and the distinctions among all categories of existence, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

The characteristic of conditions (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the causes by which sentient beings individually obtain or abandon [states]. It is that which enables sentient beings to obtain what they have not yet obtained...

There has been [a time when this was attained]. Because one has already abandoned the body previously acquired, yet that previously acquired body still exists, there are four aspects of cessation (*nirodha*).

First, the aspect of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the dissociation from afflictions (*kleśa-visaṃyoga*). Since it is the cause of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), the dissociation from those afflictions is called "cessation.

Second, the aspect of tranquility (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the dissociation from suffering (*duḥkha-visaṃyoga*). Because it is dissociated from the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*)—which are characterized by the unsatisfactoriness of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and lack the aspect of non-tranquility—it is called "tranquility."
It is quiescent. It possesses three sublime characteristics (*māṇa*): namely, the matters of bliss and purity; the ultimate liberation from all afflictions and suffering;
and having natural bliss and purity as its very essence. Therefore, it is called "sublime. Fourth is the characteristic of being free [from marks].

Because it performs the work of constant benefit, it never regresses and is supremely secure. Accordingly, it is termed "constant benefit" and "supreme excellence," and is thus called "virtuous nature."

Regarding the four aspects of the path (*mārga*) for the sake of abandonment: first is the aspect of the path (*mārgatva*). This means that by means of this path, one seeks the true meaning. Why is this so?
Because this noble path is the route by which all noble ones (*ārya*) realize the true meaning; therefore, it is called the "path."
Second is the aspect of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*). This means it is able to counteract all afflictions (*kleśa*). Why is this? All afflictions are irrational;
since the Path can eliminate them, it is therefore called "suchness. Third is the aspect of activity (*ākāra*). This means it is well able to accomplish the mind.

It is for the purpose of preventing perversity. Why is this? Because the mind does not awaken to the true principle and gives rise to perversions such as permanence regarding phenomena that are impermanent and so forth.
By being well able to cultivate and purify this perverted mind, one causes it to be free from perversion and to awaken to the true meaning;
therefore, it is called "practice. The four characteristics of emergence refer to proceeding along the path to true permanence. Why is this?
By means of this Noble Path, one is able to proceed toward renunciation and the ultimate, eternal way; therefore, it is called "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*).

In the commentary, regarding the passage from "to eliminate the four inversions" up to "eliminating [the view of] self": Question: Why does the single [inversion of] suffering eliminate two inversions, while the two [inversions of] emptiness and non-self each eliminate one—the inversion of self?
Answer: That which is called "suffering" must, by its very nature, be *sāsrava* (with-outflows). Phenomena that possess outflows are exclusively...
Impurity: by knowing this as suffering, one immediately knows it as impure; thus, a single practice regarding suffering can eliminate two inversions.

Within the aggregates, elements, and bases, there is no such eternally permanent self as is grasped [by others]; this is called emptiness. Within these very aggregates, elements, and bases, there is no characteristic of a self as imagined by the non-Buddhists;
this is called non-self. By means of these two practices together, the inversion of the self is counteracted.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that the Truth of Origination culminates in "exclusive craving": the four modes of craving have already been analyzed above. Based on these four inversions, the four types of craving arise;
their modes of activity can be fully understood. Question: Regarding the four modes of the Truth of Origination, does one contemplate each of the four types of craving individually?

Answer: These four numbers represent the general characteristics; they are established as the four aspects of origination (*samudaya*) taken collectively, rather than each individual aspect being matched separately with those four types of craving.
This is because each of those four cravings possesses the fourfold principle of cause, origination, arising, and condition.
This can be understood through reflection. Regarding the four aspects of cessation and the path, they are applied to the four types of craving and so forth based on their general characteristics;
for the cessation of each individual craving possesses the fourfold principle of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation. The path is likewise. Both can be realized through reflection.
Regarding the phrase "accumulated by action within a single kṣaṇa" and so forth:

just as in the duration of a single kṣaṇa, acts such as killing constitute a kṣaṇic action that can accumulate the seeds for the five fruits of future suffering retribution; wholesome actions are to be understood in the same way.
In some places, the *Śāstra* (Commentary) also states that [the members] do not extend to the seeds of the pervasive [causes].

Since that Sūtra says that "arising" (*jāti*) and "leading" (*ākṣepa*) are simultaneous, and since the leading causes—consciousness and so forth—are seeds, it is clear that the branches of "birth" (*jāti*) and "aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) also extend to seeds. However, in reality they are not seeds;

they are called seeds only in a figurative sense. Question: When examining the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one finds that it accords with that Sūtra in explaining why the five factors, beginning with consciousness, pertain to the manifest state.
It is not said that this sūtra teaches that the factors of birth and aging are also seeds. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Alternatively, it is based on the state of future manifestation;
furthermore, because of this teaching, birth and projection are simultaneous, yet it speaks only of consciousness and so forth, referring to the stage of their impending arising."
This is the reason why they are said to manifest simultaneously. How is this known? That sutra also states that [the factors] such as arising (*jāti*) pertain to the seeds.
Although the text does not explicitly state this, it can be understood through reasoning.

Since it speaks of "arising" and "projecting" existing simultaneously, it implies that the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) mentioned in that sutra are subsumed under the category of actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), because those projecting members (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*) are identical to the members of arising (*abhinirvartaka-aṅga*). Thus, they too should arise [simultaneously].

The link of arising (*jāti*) and the projecting [link] (*ākṣepaka*) occur simultaneously; the link of arising is identical to the projecting [link], and it also includes the seeds (*bīja*). Because this principle exists, the Commentary states:
"The Sūtra speaks of birth and old age; death includes the seeds. Otherwise, it would be difficult to understand.
The commentary states: "Because this exists, that exists" reveals the meaning of dependent origination without agency (*anabhisamskāra*).

Because phenomena exist by virtue of conditions such as ignorance, those resultant phenomena, such as formative forces (*saṃskāra*), come to exist. This principle applies to all subsequent links in relation to one another.

Non-Buddhists and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) cling to the notion that conditions possess an active efficacy; the present refutation of them is termed "without agency. Although there is no false attachment to a [substantial] reality, [the teaching remains].
Because the actual functioning is still able to produce an effect, it is called "dependent arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "this arises, therefore that arises" reveals the meaning of impermanent dependent arising:

because these factors such as ignorance arise from causes, those effects such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are then able to arise from ignorance and the other factors; the same principle applies to the mutual arising of the remaining members.

This [teaching] differs from the false attachments of non-Buddhists who hold that Īśvara, Brahmā, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and so forth, are eternal entities that do not arise from causes yet can act as causes to produce other resultant phenomena.
To distinguish itself from those views, it is called "impermanent," because it arises from causes;
its arising through conditions is the same as previously explained.

Regarding the phrase "The Commentary clarifies that [factors such as] potentiality, function, and dependent origination... and so forth: Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to factors such as time and space, asserting that they can serve as causes for manifold effects.
Here, those views are refuted. It is clarified that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors possess the sense of having the potentiality and function to give rise to *saṃskāra* specifically;
they cannot universally produce all other members [of the twelve links]. The same applies to the successive mutual relationship between the remaining members. Question: If it is only...

Regarding the statement that because there is the capacity for production in immediate succession, it is called "dynamic efficacy" (*śakti-vṭti*): why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that the link of ignorance serves as a condition even for old age and death?

Answer: There are two kinds of conditions: first, the proximate (*āsanna*), and second, the remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*). The preceding passage of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium of Abhidharma) rely upon proximate conditions;
therefore, they state only that ignorance serves as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). However, the subsequent passage of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* [accounts for] both...
Because it depends on proximity and distance, the text says "up to and including," which also serves as a condition for old age and death;

thus, there is no contradiction. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Ignorance has two aspects... until the maturation fruit arises": "Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the evil retribution of the three miserable realms.

Because of the delusion of not believing that unwholesome conduct can induce the maturation of the three miserable realms, this "delusion regarding maturation" is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. For this reason...

Because of ignorance, one engages in various unwholesome actions. This directly contradicts the right view regarding the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three miserable realms (*apāya*), which is based on faith and understanding.
Thus, the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Due to ignorance regarding maturation, one initiates non-meritorious conduct (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

It is impossible for one who does not accept and believe in the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the maturation that accords with right view to [attain liberation]. The true meaning refers to the Four Noble Truths; because of delusion regarding these, one does not know them.
The three realms are all suffering; yet, through false attachment, humans and devas take them to be happiness, as well as [the states of] nirvana and so forth.
Consequently, they give rise to immovable karma and meritorious karma, aspiring for those fruits. This ignorance regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*) is also based on the primary [ignorance].
Thus, the *Abhidharma* says: "The true meaning refers to the Four Noble Truths; delusion regarding them is called 'ignorance of the true meaning.'"

When one does not know the suffering of the three realms as it truly is, one is able to give rise to the nature of the causes for future existence: meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya-āniñjya-saṃskāra*). Question:

Do these formations project ignorance as a manifest state (*sammukhībhūta*) or as a seed (*bīja*), and are they simultaneous or asynchronous? Answer: They apply to both seeds and manifest states, and they apply to both simultaneous and asynchronous times.
Therefore, the Abhidharma states: "By way of non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*), which are defiled in nature, at the time they are conjoined with ignorance..."
This refers to its manifestation arising simultaneously with non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*). Furthermore, it says:

"Even though one gives rise to a wholesome mind, because it is bound by those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is also called delusion. This clarifies that the seeds coexist with both the immovable and meritorious formations.
It further states: "By their power, one does not know the suffering of the three realms as it truly is, and thus gives rise to meritorious and immovable formations."
This clarifies that the power inherent in the preceding moment of ignorance initiates the subsequent moments of meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇyāneñjya-saṃskāra*).

Regarding the ignorance of the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*), since it plants seeds simultaneously with its activity and manifests in the subsequent moment, it is capable of initiating both types of formations. Within the ignorance of maturation (*vipāka-moha*)...

It should also be understood in this way. Because the shadow [of the meaning] is explained in brief, only ignorance is manifested; meritorious and immovable formations do not arise simultaneously, because they differ in their clarity and obscurity.

Question: If it is based on the Truths (*satya*), it is called the "meaning of reality" (*tattvārtha*). Since the essential bodies of the fruits of the five destinies are all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), they are collectively termed "reality.
If, however, it refers to the side of repaying causes, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*); thus, the dharmas that are fruits within the three realms are all maturation.

[Question: Why is delusion regarding the retribution of humans and devas called "delusion regarding reality" (*tattva-moha*), while delusion regarding the fruits of the three miserable realms (*apāya*) is called "delusion regarding maturation" (*vipāka-moha*)?

[Answer: When non-meritorious action (*apuṇya-karman*) coincides with delusion, one fails to understand the evil causes and thus obtains an evil maturation (*vipāka*). Because one is deluded regarding the maturation fruit that is experienced, one initiates non-meritorious action.
Meritorious and immovable actions (*puṇya- and āniñjya-karman*) are likewise initiated by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), which deludes one regarding the [rebirth as] humans and devas.
"Result" (*phala*) refers to the retribution of pleasure and renunciation; one initiates practice with the desire to seek these.

Although the fruits of humans and devas are also maturation (*vipāka*), the maturation of the three miserable realms is likewise subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). However, when initiating non-meritorious conduct (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*), one does not realize that a retribution will be obtained;
therefore, suffering within the retribution is not explicitly explained. This is termed "suffering by inversion," which arises solely from being deluded regarding the maturation that is experienced.

Regarding the delusion concerning maturation (*vipāka-moha*): those who are deluded regarding the realms of humans and gods certainly know that their karma can induce its fruit; therefore, it cannot be called delusion concerning maturation.

Rather, it is because they do not understand that the fruits of the human and heavenly realms are suffering and are not *nirvāṇa*, yet falsely designate them as "pleasure" and "nirvāṇa," giving rise to practice in order to seek birth therein;
for this reason, it is termed "delusion regarding the true meaning" (*tattvārtha-moha*).

Regarding the phrase "the *vibhaṅga* (discrimination) of the dependent origination of self-nature (*svabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*)": "Discrimination" (*vibhaṅga*) has the meaning of distinguishing and differentiating.
That is to say, because the causes of all phenomena cause the resulting effects to arise by being categorized and differentiated individually, it is called "discrimination.
This does not mean "discrimination" as the act of cognitive apprehension or conceptualization. As for "self-nature," it refers to the essential substance of the causal seed; or...

Regarding the resultant entity produced from these seeds, the latter interpretation is superior. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "As for 'causal condition' (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is so designated because it is manifested by the conditions of its own-seed (*svabhāva-bīja*).
As for 'discrimination' (*vikalpa*), it is the function of that cause; its self-nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely the resultant entity produced [therefrom].

The name is established based on this function and its constituent element (*dhātu*). The term 'discrimination of self-nature' (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Regarding self-nature...
The dependent origination of discrimination is also explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Regarding "the pleasant and the unpleasant":
the maturation of the happy realms is called "pleasant" because it is desirable; the maturation of the miserable realms is called "unpleasant" because it is not desirable.

Dependent origination is precisely the cause for these two destinies. Discrimination is as previously described; furthermore, it serves as the cause by way of its function and its fruit. This is based on...
This is the Master’s explanation. Question: What constitutes the essence of these two types of dependent origination? Answer:

Some say that regarding the first, the causal condition of self-nature (*svabhāva-pratyaya*), if one follows the general theory, the three types of perfumed seeds each produce their own respective fruits, and all are causal conditions of self-nature.

However, what is clarified here primarily takes the indeterminate seeds of designations (*nāma-kalpa*) as the causal condition of self-nature in relation to the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). Commentary says: Observe the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The three types of perfumed seeds, when viewed in relation to their own respective fruits, constitute the self-nature (*svabhāva*) as their essence; they are not merely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

When viewed in relation to the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In this context, the arising of all phenomena based upon the ālayavijñāna is called the dependent origination of the differentiation of self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*).
As Vasubandhu explains: "Because it is able to differentiate the nature of all produced defiled phenomena."
Regarding the phrase "to effect differentiation," according to the *Mūla-śāstra*, it says that "all phenomena arise. The *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Commentary) states:

"All that has birth"—how could this refer only to phenomena that are *vipāka* (maturation)? By calling them "all phenomena" and "all," one knows that they take the three types of perfumed seeds as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
this is what the treatise refers to when it speaks of "mind. As for the essence and specific nature of the conditions of the desirable and the undesirable:
It is solely by means of the arising of contaminated seeds—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that the fruits of maturation (vipāka) as wholesome or unwholesome are produced;

these are thus "desirable" or "undesirable. Therefore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "By means of wholesome and unwholesome karma, the distinctions between the three miserable realms, humans, and devas are brought about.

Furthermore, the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Merit and the imperturbable [karma] are desirable; non-merit is undesirable. This is according to the general [definition].

Treatise: Regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), both their manifest and seed states consist of the agreeable and the disagreeable. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:

"The subsequent twelve-linked dependent origination is called the dependent origination that discriminates the agreeable and the disagreeable (*iṣṭāniṣṭa-vibhāga-pratītyasamutpāda*), because it functions as the causal condition capable of discriminating the various individual existences (*ātman*)—both agreeable and disagreeable—within the good and evil realms of rebirth.
Both the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and its commentaries rely upon this general definition.
The commentary’s reference to the *ālaya-vijñāna* and so forth indicates the substance of the conditions (*ālambana*).

Since the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is the locus for all those [dharmas], it cites the supporting consciousness to reveal the supported seeds. The phrase "the arising of all dharmas" cites the fruits that are produced.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and so forth”: as for the term “*ālambana-vijñāna* (object-condition consciousness),” it refers precisely to the *ālayavijñāna*, because it is the generative condition (*pratyaya*) for the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Since the *ālayavijñāna* serves as the condition, the evolving consciousnesses produced by it are termed the “experiencer” (*bhoktṛ*), as they are the subjects who experience [objects].

Regarding the objects of experience, sensation (*vedanā*) is predominant. Because it arises simultaneously with consciousness, it is designated by the name "the experiencer" (*vedaka*); this is an *upapada* (dependent) compound.

As for the phrase "in this context," it refers to "within these" among the six evolving consciousnesses; alternatively, it may point to both the preceding consciousness that perceives the object and the sensation that experiences it.

Regarding this point, the commentary states: "The latter explanation is superior. [Objection: Is it not the case that the consciousness which serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) must also have associated feeling (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and so forth?
[Response: That which experiences is precisely the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). That which discriminates is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

As for those mental factors (*caitta*) that drive the mind, these refer to volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); they cause the mind to act and exert itself. Therefore...

It is called "investigating the mind" (*cittābhyūhanā*). It refers to all mental factors (*caitta*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), such as volition (*cetanā*) and attention (*manasikāra*).
Because these minds and mental factors are all capable of experiencing their respective objects, they are termed "experiencing conditions" (*ālambanopabhoga*).

The Commentary states that "the three aggregates co-arising with consciousness" excludes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), as it is itself a constituent member [of the dependent origination].

This refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) in its entirety, and a partial portion each of the two aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and form (*rūpa-skandha*). Regarding form, this excludes the five sense faculties and the materiality of bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti-rūpa*) as well as non-intimation (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

These correspond respectively to the members of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the branch of existence (*bhava*), excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), because these latter three are subsumed within the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of shamelessness and dreadlessness.

Furthermore, volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), lethargy (*styāna*), agitation (*auddhatya*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), arising (*utpāda*), and cessation (*nirodha*) are established as distinct branches; therefore, only a limited portion [of the factors] is included.

Regarding the statement that "abiding in name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): "name-and-form" is the general category, while the "faculties" (*indriya*) are its specific instances.

Because the specific depends upon the general, it is said to "abide in name-and-form. Question: Since the mental faculty (*manas*) is past and there are currently only five [senses], how can a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) possess all twelve links?

It would lack the link of the six sense bases. Answer: Just as with the link of name-and-form, this does not exclude non-material phenomena; rather, it includes all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) without exception.
By abiding in this state, it receives the name "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). The same applies to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); although their number is fewer, they are not deficient.
Alternatively, because the five faculties can fulfill the six bases, a portion of the six bases is also called the "six bases," just as one speaks of "burning a garment."
Because one portion of the robes was burned, it is called "burning the robes. Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The material sense-faculties are designated as the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the arising of all phenomena is called 'arising-action' (*jāti-karman*)," a question is raised: Since the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) belongs to the future, while aging and death (*jarā-maraṇa*) exist only in the present, and the time [of their occurrence] is thus divided into two, how can a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) possess all twelve links?
There are two explanations. The first says: This is based on the four characteristics (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*).
The completion of its function is termed "one moment. Therefore, the twelve links possess the sense of being complete [within that single moment]. Second, it is said:

the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are explained by combining their essence and their function. "Arising" (jāti) refers to their essence, while "aging-and-death" (jarāmaraṇa) shares the same function as the present. One may adopt either of these two interpretations.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) that "there is another explanation which differs from the previous meaning," this is the teaching of a different master. [He asserts that] both the momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and the continuous (*prabandhika*) [conditions] pervade all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), encompassing both sentient and insentient entities, as well as the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). However, while all masters agree that the continuous condition (*pratyaya-prabandha*) pervades all conditioned phenomena, they differ regarding the momentary condition; thus, he sets forth a distinct explanation in contrast to the continuous one. Question: What is the meaning of "continuous" (*prabandha*)? Answer: [It refers to] the uninterrupted succession of similar states. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, a stalk, a leaf, and so forth, until the fruit is finally produced, the continuity of the series is called "continuous. Furthermore, when a person dies in one location and is reborn in another, the continuity of the series is likewise called "continuous. Moreover, when a person enters the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the continuity of the series is also called "continuous. This is because, although the mind and mental factors are temporarily suspended during that state, the seeds of the mind and mental factors remain within the body, and the seeds of the body also reside within the mind and mental factors; thus, their continuity is never severed. Therefore, it is termed "continuous. Furthermore, even when a person has attained the fruit of Arhatship and entered the state of final Nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*), the continuity of the series is still called "continuous. This is because, although the mind and mental factors have ceased, the seeds of the mind and mental factors remain within the body, and the seeds of the body also reside within the mind and mental factors; thus, their continuity is never severed. Therefore, it is termed "continuous. It is for these reasons that it is called "continuous. As for the momentary condition (*kṣaṇika-pratyaya*), it is the capacity of a phenomenon to produce its own effect immediately after it arises. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, the seed is the momentary condition for the sprout. When a sprout produces a stalk, the sprout is the momentary condition for the stalk. When a stalk produces a leaf, the stalk is the momentary condition for the leaf. And so on, until the fruit is produced. This is called the momentary condition. Furthermore, when a person dies in one location and is reborn in another, the dying consciousness is the momentary condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*). When a person enters the state of cessation, the mind and mental factors prior to entry are the momentary conditions for the emergence of the mind and mental factors upon exiting that state. When a person attains the fruit of Arhatship and enters final Nirvana, the mind and mental factors prior to that moment are the momentary conditions for the final cessation of the body. This is called the momentary condition. It is for these reasons that it is called "momentary. Thus, the momentary condition and the continuous condition are distinct. The momentary condition does not include the continuous, and the continuous condition does not include the momentary. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition applies to all conditioned phenomena, whereas the continuous condition applies only to those that persist over time. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that produces a phenomenon at the very first moment, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that maintains the phenomenon throughout its subsequent duration. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the arising of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its persistence. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the transformation of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its continuity. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its non-interruption. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the differentiation of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its similarity. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the diversity of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its uniformity. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the impermanence of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its apparent permanence. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the suffering of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its apparent pleasure. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the emptiness of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its apparent selfhood. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the non-self of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its apparent selfhood. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the tranquility of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its apparent agitation. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the ultimate truth of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its conventional appearance. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the liberation of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its bondage. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the transcendence of a phenomenon, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its worldly involvement. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of craving, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of craving. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of grasping, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of grasping. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of existence, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of existence. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of birth, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of birth. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of old age and death, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of old age and death. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the aggregates, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of the aggregates. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the sense bases, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of the sense bases. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the elements, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of the elements. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of dependent origination, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about the increase of dependent origination. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the cycle of rebirth, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its continuation. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of saṃsāra, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its persistence. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of suffering, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its accumulation. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the origin of suffering, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its proliferation. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of the path, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its cultivation. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of cessation, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its maintenance. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of wisdom, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its development. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the momentary condition is the cause that brings about the cessation of liberation, whereas the continuous condition is the cause that brings about its attainment. Therefore, they are explained separately. Furthermore, the moment

"Uninterrupted" (*anantara*) means "continuous. To be joined together is called "binding" (*bandhana*). Alternatively, being in immediate succession is called "continuous," and being mutually connected is called "binding.

Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The dependent origination of continuity and binding refers to the uninterrupted and mutually connected arising of causes and effects, whether of the same or different categories."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This very [process] is called ‘distant continuity’ (*dūrasaṃtati*): this refers to the third stage of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

It is termed “distant continuity” because, although there is an interval between its occurrences, it continues in a connected sequence. This is stated with reference to the future limit and in terms of indeterminate [karma].

Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says: “Distant continuity refers to the past and future limits; it consists of karma and afflictions that are to be experienced in subsequent lives or are indeterminate.”

Therefore, there is beginningless saṃsāra. Question: What are the distinctions among these types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Answer: Regarding momentary dependent origination (*kṣaṇika-pratītyasamutpāda*), two explanations differ, as has already been analyzed above.

As for continuous dependent origination (*saṃtānika-pratītyasamutpāda*), it applies to both the sentient and the insentient, and to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the sequential continuity of states (*avasthika-pratītyasamutpāda*), it pertains only to sentient beings and is exclusively contaminated. Furthermore, in the case of continuous dependent origination, the preceding and succeeding moments are immediately adjacent and connected.

Regarding continuity (*saṃtati*): if it refers to the condition of states (*avasthā-pratyaya*), it arises as a continuous succession based on the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) within the sequence of states, as well as being described as indeterminate.
If it refers to the condition of distant continuity (*dūra-saṃtati-pratyaya*), it is based on the latter [links] among the states, as well as being described as indeterminate.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Alternatively, [it refers to] the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) and so forth”: Question: Even if one relies on the established truths, why does one first contemplate suffering (*duḥkha*)?
Answer: Among the four established truths, the truth of suffering comes first; therefore, one first contemplates suffering.
The commentary states: "Regarding 'the practitioner who proceeds toward the cessation of old age and death,' the Four Noble Truths correspond respectively to the contemplation of old age and death.

That which corresponds to the link of old age and death is called the Truth of Suffering. The link of birth is called the Truth of the Origin of Old Age and Death, because it is the cause of old age and death.
Cessation and the Path are to be understood accordingly. This applies to all remaining links: each subsequent link constitutes suffering, while each preceding link constitutes its origin."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because ignorance is without cause, it lacks the seeds of wisdom”: here, ‘seeds’ (zhǒng) refers to causes. Since wisdom would lack a cause, the forty-eight [factors] could not be established.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vasubhāṣa), fascicle 110, it asks: “For what reason is the knowledge of the absence of ignorance not mentioned? It answers:

“If a dharma is subsumed under the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), takes the members of dependent origination as its cause, and is the fruit of the members of dependent origination, [then it is so designated].”

This is explained here: although ignorance (*avidyā*) is also subsumed under the "links" (*aṅga*), it does not have the link of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) as its cause, nor is it the fruit of the link of existence;
therefore, it is not mentioned here. Furthermore, this is explained here because, by relying on these factors, all four types of knowledge (*jñāna*) arise;
whereas by relying on the link of ignorance, only three types of knowledge arise, and the knowledge of the origin of the link of existence does not arise. Therefore, it is not mentioned here.
It is said:

regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "the teaching as an object is not included among the members," this refers to the fact that the teaching itself is not one of the twelve members; thus it is said to be "not included among the members.

The first six types of knowledge are knowledge that takes principle (*tattva*) as its object; "principle" here refers to the ultimate truth. The seventh type of knowledge takes phenomena (*vastu*) as its object.

Question: Why is it called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*)? Answer: It refers to conventional knowledge (*sammutiñāṇa*). Having heard the Dharma as established by the Buddha, this knowledge is non-erroneous knowledge;
thus it is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena. Because this knowledge is free from error, it abides in the Dharma. The Dharma here refers to the Four Noble Truths.
This is the principle of cause and effect. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 94, states:

"To be able, by means of sublime wisdom, to awaken to and resolve with faith that suffering is truly suffering, and so forth, up to the path being truly the path—to establish these within the dharma according to their respective causes and effects—all such sublime knowledge is called 'knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (*dharmasthitijñāna*).
Alternatively, 'dharma' refers to the fruit and 'stability' (*sthiti*) refers to the cause; thus it is named."
Regarding *dhammatthitiñāṇa* (knowledge of the stability of phenomena): because it is similar to the minor vehicle (*hīnayāna*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol.

110) states: "Phenomena (*dharma*) refers to the fruit; 'stability' (*sthiti*) refers to the cause. Wisdom that knows the causal basis upon which the fruit-phenomena rest is called *dhammatthitiñāṇa*.
This wisdom only knows the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the causes, and not the characteristics of noble practice (*āryacaryā*); therefore, it is [not the path]."
This is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). The Commentator accepts this as the correct interpretation.

The Sub-commentary states that both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) possess this knowledge. Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga), fascicle 94, it says:

"Abiding in the stage of an ordinary being, one is able to enter into and gain conviction through sublime wisdom regarding the Dharma of the Four Truths; this is called 'knowledge of the abiding of phenomena' (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*). Furthermore...
Question: It is said that one should know that seventy-seven types of knowledge are established, and immediately following this, one enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).

According to this sacred intent, these refer only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); why then is it said that they apply to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) alike? Answer: Regarding the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), ordinary beings have much of it while noble ones have little;
regarding true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*), noble ones have much while ordinary beings have little. Since the treatise bases its statement on the majority, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement that "this *sūtra* is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and is therefore called the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthiti-jñāna*)," a question is raised:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 94, it states that when one dwells in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), one is able to contemplate correctly through mental attention (*manasikāra*) produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

By means of sublime wisdom, one awakens to and gains conviction in the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths; this is called the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena. Why, then, does this [text] contradict the teaching?

[Objection: It is only the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). [Response: Since the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) states that it is present in both the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), how could he possibly not allow for the presence of the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)?
This is merely stated with reference to ordinary beings, who constitute the majority; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the "dependent origination in direct and reverse order": Question: On what basis are the names "direct" (*anuloma*) and "reverse" (*pratiloma*) established? Answer: There are three pairs [of criteria]. First, the pair of cause and effect:
when the cause comes first and the effect follows, it is called "direct," as it accords with the principle of sequential arising.

Conversely, this is called "reverse. Second, the pair of the subtle and the coarse: when the subtle comes first and the coarse follows, it is called "direct," as it accords with the principle of accumulation. Conversely, this is called "reverse."

Third, regarding the relative proximity and distance: to proceed from the near to the distant is called "conformable" (*anuloma*); such conformable contemplation accords with reason. To do the reverse is called "inverse" (*pratiloma*).

Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 23, states: "To infer the effect from the cause is called conformable observation; to infer the cause from the effect is called inverse observation.
Furthermore, to enter from the subtle into the coarse is called conformable observation; to enter from the coarse into the subtle is [called inverse observation].

Reverse observation (*pratiloma-anupaśyanā*). Furthermore, observing the distant by means of the proximate is called forward observation (*anuloma-anupaśyanā*); observing the proximate by means of the distant is called reverse observation.

Although the *Śāstra* does not explicitly state that [the sequence] extends to the twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra*), this serves as a rebuttal to the objection. The objection states: "The twelve causes..."
The "Conditions" (pratyaya) section originally addressed the Pratyekabuddhas; the following clarifies the benefits obtained.
Since there were originally no Pratyekabuddhas present, and the intended audience was not assembled, how could the nectar of the Dharma descend in vain? Therefore, the Commentary answers:

it causes those of the Śrāvaka vehicle to hear the teaching on dependent origination, whereby they also attain realization of their own vehicle—just as one might realize the inner school through external treatises—and by relying upon that Hīnayāna, they proceed toward the Mahāyāna.

Yun said: "There are also pratyekabuddhas. Although the sūtra merely states that at the time of preaching the Dharma, 'nayutas of people did not receive any dharmas,' this can generally be understood as including pratyekabuddhas;
what loss is there in this? If that is so, why does the sūtra state next:"
From this point onward, there are immeasurable śrāvakas. The answer is twofold: first, from the perspective of the majority; second, from the perspective of a general explanation.
This is because the term "śrāvaka" applies generally to pratyekabuddhas as well. If it were not so, there would be the fault of over-extension by analogy.

Why is it that when the Buddha teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, there are those who are reached—both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas—yet when he teaches the twelve links [of dependent origination], why are there none?
Because they are objects of transformation, there is no contradiction in their being universal.

Regarding the "Three Assemblies of Maitreya" and so forth: if one asks why both [Maitreya’s] Great Pervasive [Assembly] and these [three] are called assemblies and are equally emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), yet the number of those born through transformation differs, the answer is:
while there are three assemblies of Maitreya, those that are listed here are merely cited as examples from the Śākyamuni [era].

The disciples of the bequeathed Dharma do not conform to such a number; some are selected for their preeminent virtue, while others are distinguished by their specific spiritual resonance. Why must they be identical?
It is because the latter interpretation is superior.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that Śākyamuni does not speak of "assemblies": it may refer to the three periods of teaching—the empty, the non-empty, and the neither-empty-nor-non-empty—which are termed the "three assemblies.

Regarding the phrase "because he waits for the faculties [of beings] to ripen, thus passing twenty thousand kalpas": it means that he causes them to give rise to a sense of rarity and difficulty in encountering the Dharma.

Therefore, regarding the passage where the Buddha states that this sutra was taught over eight thousand kalpas: it is asked, "When the Buddha preached the Dharma, why were there so few śrāmaṇeras? The answer is:

because he responded to the specific spiritual capacity [of his audience], or perhaps because the Tathāgata spent much of his time in meditative absorption (samādhi). For these reasons, the śrāmaṇeras were numerous when the Dharma was extensively proclaimed.
Regarding the commentary’s demonstration of the four kinds of reasoning, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle eleven, it states:

"Because one is able to contemplate those phenomena by relying on four kinds of reasoning: first, the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), which means that when conditioned phenomena arise, they necessarily depend upon a multitude of conditions."
Just as when a sprout arises, it depends upon the seed and so forth, so too when the various consciousnesses arise, they depend upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

This is the principle of dual function: that distinct phenomena each have their own specific function. For example, the eye faculty and so forth function as the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness and the rest;

visible forms and other objects function as the focal point (*ālambana*) for visual consciousness and the rest; and the various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, perform the function of discernment (*vijñapti*).
Form and so forth; goldsmiths and the like; the thorough cultivation of gold and so forth.

The three principles of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*) refer to the proclamation of statements that do not contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish the meaning that is to be proven. "The meaning to be proven" refers to the specific nature of the entity itself.

"Statements that do not contradict" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, as well as the non-contradictory presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so on. These are called the four natural laws (*dharma-tā*).
"Principle" (yukti) refers to that which has been established throughout beginningless time regarding the phenomena abiding within their own and common characteristics;
it is the intrinsic nature of dharmas (dharmatā), such as fire being able to burn. As the Sūtra says: "Though the eye is perfectly clear, it is empty and lacks permanence," and so forth.
Why is this? Because its nature is intrinsically so (dharmatā).

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'excluding those who have already abandoned desire' in this context: within this sutra, those who have abandoned desire are omitted because their abandonment of desire and their manifestation [of the path] are both intended to lead to practice;
thus, the Translator combined them. However, this is actually incorrect, for although both involve practice..."

First, one causes them to become free from defilement; second, one manifests [the truth] to cause them to develop faith and understanding. These two meanings are distinct. Furthermore, the gradual method of transformation requires five stages.

Moreover, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 54: "One shows them what is wholesome and unwholesome, instructing them to abandon evil and follow the wholesome.
When they have not yet attained the flavor of the Dharma, their minds may fall into despondency; [the teacher] can then explain the superior fruits for them, causing them to practice."

It is called "benefit" (*hita*) because it causes one to see what is advantageous through wholesome causes. It is called "joy" (*sukha*) because it praises [the path] according to what each person delights in, thereby causing them to rejoice.
According to another interpretation, taking the intent of this present sutra, these four are explained as follows:

first, it is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it demonstrates that the three vehicles are expedient vehicles, while the one vehicle is the true vehicle. Next, it causes one to abandon the three [vehicles] and enter...

Thus, the teaching of the One Vehicle is issued. Furthermore, it is taught that the retribution of the Three Vehicles is inferior while the fruit of the One Vehicle is supreme, so as to cause beings to cultivate the single cause and perceive its benefits;
this is called "beneficial. Moreover, observing the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, he may teach by means of the Dharma or by means of parables.
It describes causes from past lives; according to what each person delights in, it causes those who are suitable vessels to rejoice, and is thus called "joy. The commentary states:

Although there is no such teaching [in the sutra], the principle may be observed. However, the claim that it causes one to abandon the three [realms] by describing the inferiority of the three types of retribution is logically untenable.
One should simply state: "It causes one to abandon the two. To say that the two retributions are inferior is logical, as explained in the Chapter on Vehicles (*Yāna-varga*).
Alternatively, it may be a scribal error for the character "wei" (爲) resulting from the confusion of the three strokes in "xue" (學). Please further consult other editions.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The cause is long and the principle is [profound]," it is like saying that because there is a *hetu* (cause), a *śāstra* (treatise) arises.

Regarding the commentary’s current explanation up to the phrase "is named nirvāṇa": Question: Prior to the turning of the mind (*cittavivartana*), those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) originally had not yet attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Why, then, does the text now state that they have obtained *sopadhiśeṣa* prior to the turning of the mind? Answer: This is spoken in reference to them...
Regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*): if they do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they will certainly realize the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* of their own vehicle.
The present sutra speaks of what they are made to realize prior to turning their minds, designating it by the name "nirvāṇa" and calling it "abiding. Question:

Why is there such a vast disparity in the number of kalpas required for these noble ones to turn their minds? Answer: This inequality arises from the distinction between those with afflictions and those without, as well as the difference between those of sharp and dull faculties.

Question: The afflictions (*kleśa*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) are many; they reach enlightenment over many eons (*kalpa*). When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) suddenly arouses the aspiration for enlightenment, one should consider this as "sudden awakening" (*tongwu*) in contrast to gradual realization. Answer:

For an ordinary person, the two types of delusion (*moha*) are complete, and their inclination toward [the mundane] increases while their inclination toward [the supramundane] diminishes; therefore, it is called "sudden awakening. Those in training lack these afflictions, and their inclination toward renunciation increases while their inclination toward compassion diminishes;

therefore, they require many eons. Question: Since the afflictions are few and the inclination toward renunciation is weak, why must they pass through many eons? [This applies to] those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whose afflictions...

[The former] is entirely absent; [the latter] lacks "turning away" (*parāṅmukha*) for many *kalpas*. Answer: For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is entirely absent; for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is entirely present.

Turning away increases, yet there is no manifestation of many *kalpas*. For those in training (*śaikṣa*), there are obstructions and no increase in turning away; they are neither entirely present nor entirely absent, and many *kalpas* pass. Question:

When those in training approach the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles (*yāna*), much time does not elapse. Even if they subsequently turn their minds toward them and attain the two types of non-learning, would this not be a reduction [in time]?

Regarding the hardships of those long kalpas, the answer is: once they have already turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they loathe the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) as if they were enemies;

who would be willing to take them up again? A sutra states: "A bodhisattva fears turning toward the two vehicles as much as one who cherishes his life fears returning to a butcher’s shop," as will be cited extensively below.

Regarding the passage "The commentary states that they have already passed through seven births, etc.," the intention of the ancient masters is as follows: The first five types of persons are all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Because the number of births they must pass through is not fixed, the Sūtra consequently designates them by names such as "those who have attained the first fruit" and so forth. Although they are all beyond training, their faculties differ in being either sharp or dull;
therefore, the number of kalpas they must pass through is not fixed.

Regarding the phrase "an ordinary body attaining the fruit" (*phala*) and so forth: when one first attains the noble fruit (*āryaphala*) from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "an ordinary body attaining the noble.

After having attained the noble state, if one undergoes further births, the body that subsequently arises is called a "noble body" (*āryakāya*); it is precisely based upon this body [that the following occurs].
Thus they realize the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and enter parinirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said in general: "The ordinary body attains the fruit; the noble body enters nirvāṇa.

If one proceeds from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and no longer undergoes further rebirth, one immediately attains the fruit of no-more-learning of the two vehicles and enters parinirvāṇa.
This refers precisely to such cases as being called "an ordinary person attaining the fruit" or "attaining nirvana in an ordinary body.
Regarding the commentary on the eighth fascicle, from "the ten afflictions" up to "all mutually support one another," there are briefly two explanations. The first states: "Afflictions and karma..."
Each of the ten categories of their respective types mutually supports one another; it is not that afflictions and karma themselves mutually support one another.
Because the karmas capable of producing [retribution] and so forth mutually support one another in a hundred ways, the suffering produced is likewise of a hundred kinds.

It is not that the substance of the fruit itself can mutually support itself; rather, it is supported by means of the afflictions and so forth. If this is so, since both afflictions and karma each have a hundred varieties, the suffering that they support—

[Objection: The result should logically amount to two hundred. [Response: In principle, it should indeed be so. However, because the two [factors] that support suffering support a single fruit, it is simply called "one hundred.

It is not because there are two supporting factors that there are two [results]. Regarding the three—afflictions, karma, and suffering—they are divided into two types of suffering; now it should be the same here. Second, it is said:
the ten categories of what is produced each mutually support one another to constitute those one hundred. Question: Do they each act as...?

[Question: As for the fruit, what further reliance is required? How can it be said that they mutually assist one another? [Answer: They are called "mutually assisting" because they rely on each other’s power;
it does not mean that once something has become a fruit, it no longer requires reliance. For example, the present sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are their fruit;

since they arise through mutual dependence, how could they not be termed "mutually assisting"? There are many such instances. The commentary states: Both interpretations are acceptable. However, the subsequent explanation is as follows:

Following the commentary, [the author] himself states that the three—afflictions, karma, and suffering—all mutually support one another, whereas the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) does not so support them;
why then would it need to be listed? Since the subsequent explanation follows this point, it is consistent [with the commentary]. One may accept or reject [this view] according to one's own judgment.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that the *pariṇāma-śīti* (death through transformation) extends to two hundred [verses]: Question: Why is the karma that invites [this state] not also taken as three hundred?
Answer: Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma is not termed "perilous. Contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma is not the direct cause that evokes the fruit of *pariṇāma-śīti*; therefore, it is excluded.
According to another interpretation, the five hundred [verses] represent the three realms and the two vehicles; those exceeding three hundred are those who have transcended them.

This refers to the three realms (*tridhātu*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, stating: "Having crossed four hundred *yojanas*, one is not far from the city.
Nāgārjuna’s commentary explains: "Three hundred is a metaphor for the three realms; four hundred is a metaphor for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
If this is so, since the numbers four and five differ, how can it serve as proof? Answer: In the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the two vehicles are combined under a single name.

One hundred. This sutra elucidates it. Although the methods of elaboration and condensation differ, their essence is without distinction. What fault is there in employing this analogy? The commentary states:

Although the terminology of this [text] and the *Śāstra* differs, their underlying meaning is no different. It is clear and easy to understand; thus, the *Śāstra* and its commentary are worthy of contemplation.

Regarding the passage "the wise and sagacious," there is one interpretation: wisdom residing in the ears is called "acute hearing" (cóng-huì), while residing in the eyes it is called "clear penetration" (míng-dá).

Furthermore, acute hearing is a metaphor for the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and clear penetration is a metaphor for the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividyā). The knowledge of all modes illuminates the myriad dharmas horizontally, while the three types of supernormal knowledge reflect the three periods of time vertically.

The commentary states: if explained according to worldly convention, the principle that the ears and eyes are sharp and clear is indeed intelligible. However, if one relies on the Buddhist scriptures...
It need not necessarily be so; there is no contradiction in the subsequent explanation.

Regarding the phrase "now desiring to retreat": if one asks why it says "now desiring" when [the person] has not yet actually retreated—since they are merely intending to retreat—and since there is no further mention of actual retreat in the following text, and if [retreat] were to occur at that very moment, how could one say "desiring"?
The answer is: according to one interpretation, it is for the sake of the faculties (*indriya*).
Their nature is indeterminate. Some regress to become ordinary worldlings; some regress to abide in the Two Vehicles; others advance to become Bodhisattvas.

Because they are thus indeterminate, the term "desire" (or "seeking") is employed. In reality, however, they have already regressed. Question: Since there are these two types of regression, when one now speaks of "regression," at what stage does this regression occur?

Answer: This refers to retreating to the station of ordinary beings within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). For this reason, the Teacher established the "transformed city" (*parinirmita-nagara*) for them. The commentary states:

Based on the differences in their faculties and dispositions (*indriya-gotra*), their intentions are not fixed; thus, while it is not without reason to speak of "desire," when examining the scriptural text, it merely mentions their "retreat.
There is no distinct characteristic of a specific faculty or disposition seeking retreat. Such statements as "I now desire [to enter]" addressed to the Buddha are all...
This is explained according to the underlying meaning (*artha*). The Buddha, knowing their intention, spoke of it in terms of that meaning.
Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) that "it may be requested for explanation at a later time," this is cited as an example to establish the point.

For instance, the three fetters—view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—are eliminated upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Nevertheless, when it is said that a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) eliminates the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), this is based on that [specific context].

This refers to the "limit" mentioned later; that is, those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and so forth. Having emerged from the three evil realms, they are also granted this designation.

Although they have surpassed three hundred [births], they have not yet emerged permanently. Those who have emerged permanently are the *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training). One who is entirely free from the five [lower fetters] is said to have emerged permanently.
Therefore, it is said that the *aśaikṣas* surpass the three hundred. Question: In reality, those in the first fruit have fully severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Why...

What does the Noble Teaching mean when it speaks of severing the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*)? Answer: According to the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, there are two brief explanations.
First, they obstruct liberation; second, they cause delusion regarding the three objects. Because these faults are severed, only the severance of the three is mentioned. That same treatise states:
"Because these three types most significantly obstruct the attainment of liberation—due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one clings to the five aggregates."

Regarding what is "mine" and "I," they develop deep attachment and delight; consequently, they do not feel revulsion toward this great mass of suffering, nor do they give rise to the resolve to set out toward supreme liberation.

Or, even if they do set out, because of their adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), their doubt and perverse clinging to wrong paths, and their uncertainty regarding the right path, they achieve either a false deliverance or an improper deliverance.
Furthermore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is deluded regarding the objects of knowledge.

Because of this mass of great suffering, one falsely superimposes the characteristics of "I" and "mine. Thus, through the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one is deluded regarding the cause that enables vision;
because one regards perverted views as the cause for purification and liberation. Through doubt (*vicikitsā*), one is deluded regarding the cause of the antidote.
Because there is no certainty regarding the Three Jewels. If one follows the Hīnayāna, the meaning differs from this;
as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 21.
Although the commentary also mentions those among humans and devas, even those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are included among humans and devas; this, therefore, should be...
It is said to exceed five hundred [kalpas]. However, this refers only to birth through transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*), which is subsumed under the realms of humans and devas.

Since those of the two vehicles have not yet escaped such birth through transformation, it cannot be said that they have transcended the realms of humans and devas. Therefore, it is simply stated that they exceed three hundred [kalpas].

The Commentary states that it is called "one" in contrast to the vehicle of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is based on the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):

since the conditioned knowledge of all modes consists of three types, whereas the unconditioned principle of cessation (*nirodha-tattva*) is singular, it is designated as "one. Alternatively, it may be because the essence (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge of all modes is one;

thus, in contrast [to the other two], it is called "one. If this is so, how can it be said that there are three vehicles? The answer is: although they are three according to their names, when discussing their essence, they are but one.

The two vehicles of the sheep and the deer are fundamentally without intrinsic substance. Question: Since the principle of cessation is non-dual and naturally one, why must it be designated as "one" only in relation to wisdom?
Answer: That the principle of cessation is non-dual is one sense of "one"; that it is in relation to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is another sense of "one.
These two textual passages are distinct; though they may at first glance appear identical, they differ.
The commentary states that one actually attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) at the final completion of the stage; this is established by analogy.

When one is about to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one has already realized the unconditioned state of the non-existence of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) during the proximate preparatory stages.

Nevertheless, the statement that "one attains the unconditioned in the absorption of cessation" is made based on its manifest location. This is because within that absorption, both perception and feeling do not function, and thus the expression "cessation of perception and feeling" is manifest at that time. If...
If it were not so, then once one has entered meditative absorption and the six consciousnesses no longer function, who could be said to realize the cessation of perception and feeling?
For there must be a realizing mind before there can be anything realized; how much more so, then, for the mental faculty (*manas*) to be awakened! Some say that within this ninth absorption...

Because there is no perception or feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*). Although one may have developed aversion toward them in the preceding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it is not yet called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
A critique states: This reasoning is highly contradictory. Furthermore, does one obtain this unconditioned state of perception and feeling through the preceding absorption?

If you say one does not, the analogy is invalid, because it would imply that [the cessation] is obtained prior to the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*). If you say one does obtain it, then both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures unanimously [state... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
It does not say that one first attains the cessation of perception and feeling through the eight meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called an erroneous teaching.
Regarding the passage in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* stating that they are "far from the realm of nirvāṇa," this clarifies why the two vehicles do not possess the four wisdoms.

As for the phrase "other births" and so forth, it reveals that while their births have come to an end, they have not yet reached ultimate perfection; this refers to the wisdom of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), which, although it eliminates the coarse, segmented existence (*bhavāgra-cheda*), is not yet final.
Because the transformation [of existence] still persists, it is said to be "with remainder. Since it is not yet exhausted, there shall be further birth.

Although one no longer undergoes birth in a subsequent existence, this transformation-birth is nonetheless a phenomenon of birth and death; because such birth and death exist, it is called "having birth."
Because it is received after the [birth] division.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “furthermore, because other Brahmās are established,” etc., this clarifies that the practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established but is not yet ultimate.

That is to say, the knowledge of the realization of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is called the “Brahma-realization” (*brahma-sākṣātkriyā*). The “practice of Brahma” (*brahma-caryā*) is a name formed by the *tatpuruṣa* compound. There are two types of holy practice (*brahmacarya*): first, ...

The exhaustion of the causes of the *paricchinna* (segmented) existence manifests the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder); the exhaustion of the fruits of the *paricchinna* existence manifests the *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).

The exhaustion of the two types of *pariṇāmika* (transformative) fruits manifests the *anupadhiśeṇa-nirvāṇa*; the persistence of the untainted basis (*anāsrava-āśraya*) manifests the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
