Those of the fixed lineage (*niyata-gotra*) among the two vehicles attain only the former; those of the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) attain only the *sopadhiśeṣa* within the former; and those of both fixed and indeterminate lineages have not yet attained either.

Thereafter, there is the wisdom of non-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-jñāna*). Although it has that which is accomplished, it is called "impure" because it is intermingled with the causes and effects of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
In comparison to what one has personally attained, it is termed "accomplished. Because this subsequent wisdom is residual, it is called "with remainder" (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*).

Alternatively, this subsequent wisdom has not yet been attained by those of the Two Vehicles; for those who have attained it, it is residual. Since this is that which ought to be accomplished, it is termed "accomplished. As for the statement regarding "matters," it is not...
"Ultimate equality" clarifies that what was to be done has already been accomplished; it is not "non-ultimate. This refers to the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*).

There are two types of the path of cultivation: first, the antidote for the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*); second, the antidote for the realm of transformation (*pariṇāma-bhava*).

Since the two vehicles have not yet cultivated the latter antidote, this path of cultivation is said to be "not ultimate" because its task is as yet unfinished. Because there is still further practice to be undertaken, it is called "having something to be done. Thus it is said:

"Those who do not cross over" clarifies that they have not yet attained freedom from future existence (*punarbhava*), nor have they reached the ultimate goal. This refers to the knowledge that abandons the origin of suffering (*samudaya-jñāna*).

There are two types of abandonment regarding the origin: first, the cause of the fragmented existence (*pariccheda-hetu*); second, the cause of the transformational existence (*pariṇāma-hetu*). Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have abandoned the cause of fragmented existence, the cause of transformational existence remains;
thus, they are said to "not cross over. Because they have not crossed over, [the cause] must necessarily be abandoned. The above provides a general explanation of those four knowledges.

It is not ultimate. The statement that they are "far from the realm of nirvāṇa" and so forth reiterates the fourth point and applies it by analogy to the other three, demonstrating that their nirvāṇa is not yet fulfilled.
The Great Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha is called the "realm of nirvāṇa.
Since the merits of the two vehicles are not yet perfected and must still require three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before they can reach it, it is said that they have merely "attained" it.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* that says, "What has been done is not yet accomplished," etc.: this scriptural text belongs to the meaning of those four wisdoms (*jñāna*) not being ultimate;
the scripture is brief, while the *Śāstra* explains it fully. One may realize this by careful investigation, and thus I have not annotated it here.
However, the *Śāstra* states, "The holy life (*brahmacarya*) is not accomplished"; the character "not" (*bu*) is an error, for that scripture does not contain the character "not."

Regarding the phrase "contemplating emptiness as the ultimate meaning of the house": "contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to that which contemplates; "emptiness as the ultimate meaning" (*śūnyatā-paramārtha*) refers to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) that is contemplated—the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
This principle serves as the "house," because it is the family of the Tathāgata. Thus, the treatise states: "Abiding in the Stage of Extreme Joy, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

By citing that which contemplates, it reveals the essence of what is contemplated and takes that as the house. This is an analysis of the name according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]

"Thought belongs to that which is thought of"; this is a *karmadhāraya* (possessive) compound. The meaning is thus understood. Abiding in the *tathatā* (suchness) of emptiness may also be termed the "emptiness of ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is attained by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The commentary states that the "Chapter on Awakening" up to the "Eight Liberations" constitutes the bathing ground; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment serve as the flowers, for they both possess the significance of flourishing and manifesting the fruit.
Dharanis are able to sustain and maintain all practices, resembling a garden that guards against external [distractions].
Because it can sustain what is internal, the Dharma of the Mahāyāna causes ten thousand virtues to flourish; thus, it is equal to a forest.

Just as flowers, stalks, trunks, and fruits are all fully present in their lush abundance, although the merits of the Two Vehicles are not called "great," they also flourish and are therefore likewise called a "forest."

Therefore, taking that sūtra as a model, it is appropriate to draw this comparison. Furthermore, in the Āgama-sūtras, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the garden and the various outflows-free states (*anāsrava*) are the groves;

these are distinguished by their respective meanings. Since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can thoroughly moisten and nourish, and liberation (*vimukti*) is free from defilement, they are compared to flowing streams and ponds.

Regarding the commentary on "successive gates" (*chóngmén*) and so forth: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) all pertain to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); this is the reason for their being abandoned [as objects], hence they are called "successive. "Successive" implies they are not singular.

One interpretation holds that "successive gates" is the same as before, while the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are termed the "high pavilion.

Others say that the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths are assigned to the three gates of emptiness; the meaning is as assigned in the commentary on the *Śraddhā-vimukta-parivarta*. First, one contemplates the object...
One takes [the object] and regards it as empty; subsequently, one contemplates the subject that grasps it and finds that it, too, is empty. Therefore, this is called "repetition" (*guru*).

The two repetitions regarding signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are also to be understood according to this principle. Furthermore, the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) are subsumed into three:

because one contemplates the objects of the Four Noble Truths as empty, one practices the wisdom of emptiness and enters into nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), wherein both mind and mental objects are empty. Taking this as the gateway is called...

The "double gate" (*dvāra-dvaya*)—namely, the two [gates] of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*)—should also be understood according to this principle. However, those who enter cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are exclusively those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).
Those of unfixed nature (*aniyata-gotra*) can also attain this meaning of the "double emptiness. Thus, the Sarvāstivāda school says: "It is like a staff used to turn a corpse;

once the corpse is exhausted, the staff is also discarded. [The author] comments: The intent of this metaphor is entirely erroneous; it is not a sound explanation. The Sarvāstivāda school relies merely upon...

The emptiness of both subject and object is called "repeated emptiness" (chóngkōng). This does not clarify the meaning of the "gates" (mén); rather, it illustrates that all three types [of emptiness] can enter into principle, and are thus termed "repeated gates.
This can be fully understood through reflection.
Regarding the statement that the true dharma of the truths is the "Element of the True Wisdom of Emptiness for Men": through hearing the teachings on the truths, the wisdom of emptiness arises;
this arising wisdom is able to perpetuate the Three Jewels and is thus termed a "dhatu" (element). The term "Element of the Truths" (*satya-dharma-dhātu*) is established as a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Regarding the passage in the *Commentary on the Chapter of the Five Hundred Disciples* concerning those who give rise to false interpretations from an inferior mind: "those who harbor an inferior mind" refers to the two fruits they seek; "giving rise to the false" refers to the grasping mind that seeks them.
Alternatively, the character "mind" (*xin*) may belong to the following phrase, in which case it refers to the mind that performs the grasping. Consider this further.

The Commentary states: "These are those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Question: Regarding the seven types of defiled conceit (*māna*), all are ordinary persons. Why, then, does it further say they include those in training? Answer:

Although they are called "those in training," they are nonetheless subsumed under the category of ordinary persons. Question: If that is so, why is the conjunction "and" (*ca*) used? Answer: There are two kinds of ordinary persons:

first, those who seek and aspire toward [the path], who thus receive the name "those in training"; second, those who do not seek or aspire toward it. It is for this reason that the word "and" is placed there.
They are merely designated as "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana). These two types of people both lack a concentrated mind and both cling to the two extremes.

To distinguish between them, the word "and" (ca) is used. Alternatively, because their cultivation may differ in duration—whether long or short—they are described as "those in training" (śaikṣa) and "ordinary persons."

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "from those of inferior faculties down to those who have already received it": at the point where Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra received [the teaching], the assembly of five hundred followers likewise received it in full.
The remainder is as stated in the text.

Regarding the commentary’s second point, “Receiving the Prophecies and so forth”: A question is raised concerning the end of the *Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*, where it is stated in general that all disciples shall receive prophecies;
this [section] now takes up that very point. Furthermore, at the end of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*, it is also said that the śrāvakas who hear even a single verse shall all become Buddhas.

"Why did he not comprehend it? [The answer is: Although it was stated in general terms in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*) that they would attain [enlightenment], he had not yet seen a specific prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) granted to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), and thus he still harbored hesitation.
It was only after the "Bestowal of Predictions" (*Vyākaraṇa-paṭala*)—where Śāriputra and others received their individual predictions—that he attained certainty;
therefore, he comprehended it. This is not the same as Śāriputra, who, being a person of superior faculties (*agratīka*), was able to comprehend the "Expedient Means" [upon its initial teaching].
The commentary states that from the passage concerning Śāriputra onwards, the bestowal of predictions encompasses the accounts of all four great śrāvakas; hence the phrase "and those below.

Regarding the mention of the four leaders’ supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, it asks: how did he employ such skillful means as the "City of Transformation" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) to guide those who were weary of the lofty path?
This is precisely what is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*). The parables of the burning house, the impoverished son, and the medicinal herbs have the same meaning;

why then are they not included? Since both are established as such, [the objection is raised]. The answer is: In truth, both are indeed subsumed under the realization of supernatural power. However, regarding the "Transformation City" (*nirmāṇa-pura*), the text itself states:
"That which I have conjured. This is not the case for the other parables; therefore, they cannot serve as a precedent.

Regarding "because of being detached from the referent (*abhidheya*)," this means that one does not give rise to attachment toward the phenomena that are the referents; thus, it is called "detached from the referent," and is therefore termed "pure.
Regarding "cultivating the Brahma-conduct and constantly upholding the Bodhisattva's threefold aggregate of precepts": "Brahma" refers to *nirvāṇa*, and "conduct" has the sense of a cause.
The three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) are the cause of *nirvāṇa* and are called the "Brahma-faring" (*brahmacarya*).
Regarding the mention of the "seven Buddhas" and so forth in the commentary: Question: Since the Buddhas are actually infinite in number, why speak of only seven? Answer:

Tradition states that the Buddhas' manifestation of transformation is fundamentally for the benefit of sentient beings. Because worldly delusions are established based on secular customs, such as the practice of establishing seven ancestral temples, [the Buddhas] now conform to those [customs], and thus establish the number seven.
The Buddha, wishing to transform them gradually so that they might return to reality, [composed this].

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the Bhadrakalpa has four [assemblies]," why is this so? The answer is: the number seven mentioned refers to a count that includes both himself and others.
It is for this reason. Later, [the lineage] reaches Maitreya; [the succession] from Vipaśyin is superseded by adding Maitreya. Question:

On what basis is the name "Bhadra-kalpa" (Auspicious Aeon) established? Answer: According to the fifth fascicle of the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (*Beihua jing*), it says: "For what causes and conditions is the aeon named 'Good and Wise' (*Shanxian*)?
Within this great aeon, there are many sentient beings characterized by greed, anger, ignorance, and pride. There are a thousand worlds..."

“World-Honored One, because you have appeared in the world having accomplished great compassion, the name of this eon was established. In most other sutras, the word ‘excellent’ (kuśala) does not appear.
Question: Since the seven Buddhas already include Śākyamuni, why do you further say that he is also the foremost among those who preach the Dharma under my guidance?
Answer: The seven Buddhas are mentioned in terms of the general; what I refer to as ‘under me’ is spoken according to the specific.”

Since he is now the Master of Transformation, he is explained further in detail. Regarding the phrase "the Worthy Aeon" (*bhadrakalpa*) mentioned below, both the general and specific meanings should be understood accordingly.

Concerning the passage on "protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma," it is asked: Since the responsibility of one who protects the Dharma is so grave, what kind of person is capable of such a task?

Furthermore, what are the principles of the Dharma? The answer is that there are many categories of meaning, but briefly three types may be clarified: first, the conduct by which one protects people; second, the intention by which one protects the Dharma;
and third, the benefits obtained. Regarding the first, there are again two parts: first, a general clarification of that conduct; second, a specific analysis according to individuals.
Regarding those who protect the Dharma in general: from the Buddhas above down to the common people below, the Buddhas possess all merits and are certainly able to protect the Dharma;

yet it is not known what practices others must employ to be able to protect it. Now, one who wishes to protect the Dharma should revere and honor those of noble virtue, never treating the lowly with contempt;

they must not contravene the scriptural teachings and should accord with correct principles. They should practice generous giving to nurture all beings, harmonize the mind, guard the sense faculties, and expose faults and evils.

Excellent! You have interred [the remains] at the *jia* tree and set them upright; your words and deeds correspond, and you are able to accomplish such practice. Truly, you are a protector of the Dharma. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 571 and 572, states:
"One's actions do not contradict one's words; one respects teachers and elders; one accords with the True Dharma;
one’s mental conduct is harmonious and supple; one’s disposition is pure and sincere; the sense faculties are tranquil; and one remains far removed from all that is evil and unwholesome."

The Dharma. One cultivates supreme roots of goodness. Furthermore, it is said: "One would rather sacrifice body and life than abandon the True Dharma. One is humble toward others and does not give rise to arrogance.
One is able to endure being treated with contempt, degradation, or disgrace. To sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst, one gives excellent food and drink;
to those in peril, one bestows fearlessness; and for those who are ill, one provides medical treatment according to the Dharma. One adorns and decorates stupas and temples. Evil...

One conceals faults with affairs and does not proclaim virtuous deeds. It is further said: "If one accords with the words and does not contradict correct principle, and is always free from contention, this is called 'protecting the True Dharma.
Furthermore, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of people who can protect the Dharma:
first, those who abide in accordance with the Dharma; second, those who recite these words. If there were no words, the Dharma could not be taught. (2)

Regarding the distinctions among persons: first is the protector of the Dharma (dharmapāla). One whose moral virtue (*śīla*) is strictly comprehensive and whose wisdom (*prajñā*) is concentrated and luminous protects the Dharma by remaining far removed from injury and destruction.
Thus, the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Now, one who protects the Dharma is said to possess right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and is able to widely proclaim and expound the Mahāyāna sūtras.
They never grasp or hold royal parasols, oil flasks, grain, rice, or seeds."
He plants fruit trees and melons not for the sake of profit or gain. Observing the local kings, ministers, elders, and patrons, his mind is free from flattery or crookedness.
He maintains perfect dignified conduct and subdues all those who break the precepts and commit evil. Such a person is called a teacher who upholds the precepts and protects the Dharma.
Later, as a lay protector of the Dharma, he acts as a wall and moat for the city of the Triple Gem, manifesting majestic power to gather and transform sentient beings.
To harbor compassion and refrain from killing is itself the protection of the Dharma. Therefore, the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I now permit those who uphold the precepts to rely upon laypeople who carry swords and staves as their companions, whether they be kings, ministers, or elders."
"Uprāsakas and others who, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, may carry swords and staves—I declare that such persons are called 'upholders of the precepts.
Although they carry swords and staves, they must not take life. If they can act in this way, they shall be named the foremost upholders of the precepts."
Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "O sons of the gods, if you are able to protect my disciples, it is equivalent to upholding my True Dharma (*saddharma*).
If one protects [the Dharma] in this way, the Dharma will abide for a long time. Regarding the second intention for protecting the Dharma:
it is because the Dharma is difficult to encounter that one protects it so as not to let it perish and to deliver all sentient beings. Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, part three...
127. It is said: To uphold and protect the True Dharma, one should not begrudge even body or life, constantly maintaining this thought:
"I would rather abandon wealth, treasures, and kinsmen than ever forsake the True Dharma of the Buddhas. Why is this?

Wealth, treasures, kinsmen, and even one's own life exist in every birth and are always easily obtained; however, the True Dharma of the Buddhas is [rare], even among hundreds of thousands of *koṭis*...
Only after *koṭi-ayuta* kalpas does one encounter it; having encountered it, for a long night one obtains great benefit and joy. Furthermore, in [the scripture] No.
572, it says: "All Tathāgatas constantly and together protect these words and letters, which neither arise nor perish."
It is eternally without concealment or extinction; the meaning it reveals likewise neither arises nor ceases, being eternally without concealment or extinction. This is why one protects the Dharma.

Furthermore, five hundred and seventy-three verses state: "In order to deliver all sentient beings, one accomplishes the power of the great compassionate vow and protects and upholds this profound essential Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Regarding those who benefit from protecting the Dharma in these three ways, they shall always be the retinue of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Firm and steadfast, their meritorious achievements are immeasurable; all depend upon the protection of the Dharma. Thus, the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"If a person can protect the Buddha’s True Dharma, they are encompassed by four things: first, they are encompassed by the Buddhas; second, they are encompassed by the devas; third, they are encompassed by merit;
and fourth, they are encompassed by wisdom. Being encompassed by the Buddhas further entails four aspects: first, one constantly attains proximity to all Buddhas; second, Māra finds no opportunity."
Third, obtaining the gate of the inexhaustible *dhāraṇī*. Fourth, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression. There are also four aspects of being embraced by the gods:
first, at the place where the Dharma is preached, various kings provide purification; second, at the time of preaching the Dharma, the assembly joyfully listens and receives it;
third, one is never harmed by causal conditions; fourth, those who lack faith come to believe. There are also four aspects of being embraced by merit: first, adorning the body.
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute two adornments of the mouth; whatever he proclaims, sentient beings delight in hearing.
The third is the adornment of the land, and the fourth is the adornment of lineage, namely that of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Wheel-Turning Kings. Wisdom is also comprised of four aspects:
first, knowing the faculties of sentient beings and teaching the Dharma according to their needs; second, knowing the illnesses of sentient beings and administering medicine according to the ailment.
Third, they attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and roam through all Buddha-lands. Fourth, they clearly and thoroughly penetrate the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Good son, if you wish to obtain such merits, you should protect the True Dharma. Furthermore, a verse says: "The atoms of the worlds may be fully recounted, But the merit of protecting the Dharma is immeasurable.
If you wish to attain that which cannot be fully described, You should protect the True Dharma with a firm mind."

Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If bodhisattvas apply themselves with diligent vigor and desire to protect the true Dharma, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the retinue they obtain shall be impossible to obstruct or destroy."

Regarding "that which is sustained by the great flavor of the Dharma and the joy of delight": the "great flavor of the Dharma" is the producing phenomenon (*janaka-dharma*), while the two types of "joy and delight" are the produced phenomena (*janya-dharma*).
Because joy and delight arise due to the great Dharma as their cause, one takes those produced phenomena as the two kinds of nutriment.

Regarding the statement "impure food and so forth": sentient beings of the desire realm are called impure because they possess both the manifest and the seeds of the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, which are themselves impure.

Conversely, those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are called pure. Those in the two upper realms who are trainees (śaikṣa) and have attained the first three fruits are called both pure and impure.
Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the upper realms who are able to suppress the afflictions of the lower realms are called pure. [This continues] accordingly...

Because sleep has not yet been severed and the afflictions of oneself and others have not yet been subdued, it is called "impure. For those in the first three fruits, although the afflictions of wrong views and the like have perished, they are called "pure";
however, because the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not yet exhausted, they are called "impure.

The Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward do not actually consume food, nor do they depend on food; their own bodies abide in natural stability. Nevertheless, in accordance with worldly custom, they manifest the act of eating.
Food. It is the manifestation of eating by means of a semblance; its body abides [thereby], which is called "manifested food. Question:
According to that treatise, there are four kinds of food, namely, the food for sustaining existence (*āhāra*) and so forth. What is this food? And what is "sustenance" (*niśraya*)? Answer:

The person is the dependent (*āśrita*); it is by depending upon food that one is able to abide. Since food is the fruit resulting from the person, it is given the name "sustenance" (*niśraya*). Thus it is named.

[The practitioner] dwells [there]. A question is asked: as in the case of the desire realm, when one is able to subdue the afflictions of the lower levels down to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), under which of the four [types of] sustenance (*āhāra*) is this dwelling sustained?
The answer is: it is included in both categories. The treatise, based on the entirety of the realms and the clarity of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), omits mentioning it here.
Question: Regarding these four nutriments, how many types among the four nutriments—edible food and so forth—are subsumed? Answer: Impure [nutriments] possess all four.
Among those that are both pure and impure, for beings of the two upper realms, three exist with the exception of edible food. Within the lower desire realm, all four types are also present.
As for the third, the pure [nutriment], whichever realm a noble being belongs to, they possess three or four; this will now be demonstrated. There are also four [aspects]. Question: How so?

Is there no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) in the higher realms? Answer: Because they have already abandoned desire, there is no solid food. This is because solid food can increase lust and other such afflictions;
furthermore, their bodies are subtle and light, being formless and shapeless, and thus neither [type of being] requires solid food. Question: That treatise speaks only of the Buddha manifesting food;
why does it also mention the noble ones of the eight stages and above? Answer: The treatise relies on the perfection of the fruit and thus briefly omits the explanation of the cause.
Indeed, this applies to the eight stages as well; for they do not depend on material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), having already definitively attained the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the statement that "it can nourish vitality until it becomes indestructible": material food nourishes physical strength, volition (*cetanā*) nourishes aspiration, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) sustains the seeds of the sense faculties.
Alternatively, one may explain this through all four [types of nutriment], as each possesses this capacity. For now, however, we rely solely on the first [explanation].
The Commentary states that there are only four because one enters the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by contemplating them.
Since one enters the foundations of mindfulness by contemplating these objects, and since the foundations of mindfulness are four, the foods that are contemplated are likewise only four.
Regarding the fact that the *Śāstra* does not include a verse for the question addressed to the assembly: in the preceding prose section, it says, "Do you see these [monks], such as Pūrṇa?

This is the Buddha questioning the assembly. Furthermore, there is a commentary which states, "It does not include a verse for the fourfold assembly," but this is an error regarding the four characters. For the prose contains no such text;
rather, it enumerates the fourfold assembly.

Regarding the statement, "Although the commentary reaches its ultimate point, it concerns the disciples who are manifestations of transformation": according to the underlying principle, this verse merely extols the virtues currently manifested by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.

Yet, upon a superficial reading of the verse, it appears to extol the virtues of all manifested disciples. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "For this reason, various Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Since the text of the question already mentions "various Bodhisattvas," why is it not permitted to interpret this as extolling [the virtues of] both [Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas]?

[The questioner] asks: Why does [the text] cite all the bodhisattvas? The intention is to reveal the reason why Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is a provisional manifestation (*upāya-nirmāṇa*), and not to reveal others.
Regarding the phrase "all the bodhisattvas, such as close associates and friends," the *Huayan* [Sūtra] speaks of ten kinds of practitioners. According to that sūtra, chapter thirty-eight:

It is said: Because one delights in hearing and receiving the Dharma; because one benefits sentient beings; because one tames one's own mind; because one teaches and brings to maturity the sentient beings of the desire realm;
because one causes [the wheel of Dharma] to turn swiftly; because one quickly accomplishes pure wisdom; because one teaches and transforms sentient beings;

because one reverently prostrates to, pays homage to, and makes offerings to all Buddhas; and because one severs the continuity of all birth and death, yet does not sever the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Because they are the practices of a bodhisattva (bodhisattvacaryā), their names are listed as in the commentary. These ten aspects of practice are assigned to their respective names in sequence.
As for why the commentary now takes this as a metaphor, it adopts the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) as its analogy.

Regarding the statement that "the coarse garment refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*"): it is called a garment because the arousal of the bodhicitta resides within the mental consciousness; thus, it is used as a metaphor for clothing.

Alternatively, the eighth consciousness is termed "mental consciousness" because it is situated within the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*); since it is the locus where seeds are perfumed (*vāsya*), it is compared to a garment.
If this were not the case, the sixth consciousness would not be an entity capable of sustaining [seeds], so how could one say, "Your garment"?
The inner pearl still exists today.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Now, as for the sixth [consciousness] and its uncommon ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*)": if the seventh consciousness remains defiled in a single mode throughout the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), how could it be said that it "arises and wanders"?
It is only the sixth consciousness that can arise in a virtuous state of mind and seek [liberation].
At the time of the supreme Dharma, it is called "arising" and there is no fault. The commentary says: The jewel of the bodhicitta arises from the sixth consciousness.
When it arises, it cannot coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*). How, then, can one say it is bound while intoxicated?

For this reason, taking the delusion (*moha*) of the seventh consciousness as the essence of intoxication is likewise without fault. The subsequent mention of "wandering" refers to the wholesome state of the sixth consciousness; nevertheless, it is also...
This refers to acting while intoxicated; it is only when one possesses true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that one is called sober.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "or the Mahāyāna [fivefold body of dharma] up to the aggregate of precepts" (*śīla-skandha*, etc.): this refers to the fivefold *dharma-kāya* of the Mahāyāna.
By citing the aggregate of precepts, the other four—wisdom, concentration, and so forth—are implied.
Regarding the statement in the *Śū* (Commentary) that "the character [宋-?][宋-? has the sound of *yǒu*": [宋-? refers to the character *yǒu*.
The author of the *Śū*, fearing that some might not recognize it, pronounced it using the modern character for *yǒu*. However, those who transcribed the *Śū* all mistakenly wrote the character *mǎo*;
this is because the character *mǎo* bears a slight resemblance to the ancient form of *yǒu*.

Regarding the phrase "the *Pusa jipin shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on the Retention of the Names of Beings), the *Gaoming ji* (Record of Illustrious Names)," and so forth: Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra alone received from the Buddha distinct particulars regarding their names, time periods, and so on;
this is termed "difference. Cundabhadrā and the five hundred [disciples] had identical Buddha-names and so forth; thus they are termed "sameness. Cundabhadrā and the five hundred attained...
Because there is a distinction between the predictions for the former and the latter, they are called "two differences.
Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "not identical names," etc.: those two thousand [disciples] received their predictions with identical names and titles, which is called "one identity.
Ānanda and Rāhula each received distinct [names], which is called "two differences."

In this commentary on the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the frequent use of the term "Dharma Master" is because those who have received the prediction in the present are already called Dharma Masters;

therefore, we know that those who uphold and recite [the sutra] in the presence of the Buddha are likewise called Dharma Masters. This is stated in terms of the majority, referring for now to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. In the present...

Regarding the passage from "acts as a disciple" through "also called a Dharma Master": this is an abbreviated statement. If one is before the Buddha, one acts as a disciple, representing the eight classes of beings;
the same applies to those who uphold the sutra. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one acts as a Dharma Master. Eight.
Recite the section and show yourself as a Dharma Master.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the Medicine King has long upheld this sutra” and so forth: the question is, since the subsequent skillful means explain the events concerning the Medicine King's past causes, why is he addressed by name right now?
The answer is that the Medicine King is present in the assembly; it was because of his past deeds that he [was able to] uphold this sutra at such an early stage.
This is why it is announced. As for the phrase "due to what loss," "due to" (*yin*) refers to the cause or reason.
Furthermore, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.

After the prose introduction and the verses have extensively explained the events of the past during the era of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja—concerning King Ratnacchattra and his son Prince Succhattra and their practice of the Dharma-offering—it is only then that the following is stated.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed eighty thousand bodhisattvas. Because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, one should know that the commentary and its explanations do not contradict the principle.
Some say that at the beginning of the "Dharma Master" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the past deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja upholding the sutra are first clarified;
thus the sutra says: "Because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, he addressed eighty thousand great beings, saying... [End of] the chapter's opening.
Although he bears the title of "Medicine King," he is in fact a Buddha and not a bodhisattva. Regarding the king and the crown prince, the sutra itself states:
"The king at that time is the present Buddha Ratnārcis; the crown prince, Suvīra, is my current self."
There is no mention whatsoever of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja; therefore, it is known that [this citation] is a misquotation.
Regarding the phrase "how much more so for those who can fully receive and uphold [the teaching]," one asks: the Dharma is fundamentally beyond words, and names cannot reach its true meaning.
If one grasps at names and characters, this is not a skillful way of seeking the Dharma. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The Dharma is not seen, heard, sensed, or known. If one acts..."

To see, hear, perceive, and know [the words] is merely to see, hear, perceive, and know; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. Now, to praise those who receive and uphold the sutras—would this not further increase their chronic ailment?
Answer: To falsely cling to the literal meaning is what all the teachings collectively condemn. To use the raft as a metaphor for the truth is what all the sages unanimously permit.
Who could emerge from the water without passing through the gate? Thus, in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Great Bodhisattva Piṭaka Sūtra):
The verse says: Just as when a person enters a dark room, Where all light is obscured and cut off, Though various forms and images are present, They cannot be seen by one without clear vision.
In the same way, though a person may possess Internal clarity and understanding, If they do not hear the True Dharma, How could they discern good from evil?

Through extensive learning, one understands the Dharma; Through extensive learning, one does not commit evil; Through extensive learning, one abandons what is meaningless; Through extensive learning, one attains...
Nirvāṇa. Listen well; hearing increases learning. Hearing can increase wisdom; wisdom can cultivate the pure meaning.

Attaining the meaning brings forth happiness. Once the wise have attained the meaning, they realize the nirvāṇa of the present life. Through association with the Dharma of pure awakening, they realize the supreme bliss.
Having heard the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they dwell securely in the True Dharma and become a great light for the world, practicing for enlightenment.
This is sublime conduct, which is why the Tathāgata has praised it so earnestly. Furthermore, according to the *Prajñā-śāstra*, merit does not itself attain bodhi;
there are two ways [to achieve this]: first, upholding [the teaching], and second, expounding it.

Regarding the passage, "The Sūtra says that one who can secretly preach [the Dharma] for a single person, etc.": Question: In what manner does one preach the Dharma for a single person so as to become a messenger of the Buddha? Answer:
If one’s preaching deviates from correct principle and lacks skillful means (upāya), then even if it is for many people, one is truly not a messenger of the Buddha;

for by such means, one does not bring about transcendence of the world. However, if one conforms to principle and possesses skillful means, then even if it is for only a single person, one is indeed a messenger of the Buddha.
It is because it enables that which is undertaken to reach its ultimate consummation. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 567, states:
"As for preaching the Dharma, to accord with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is called 'speaking in accordance with principle.

If all that is spoken does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena, is in harmony with the Dharma, can enter into equality, and manifests the underlying meaning and principles, it is called 'skillful means of speech. From this, one should know that it is not [otherwise]."
All those who preach the Dharma are called messengers of the Buddha. [Commentary:

Regarding the passage from "if one disrupts and confuses bodhisattvas" up to "destroys all Buddha-dharmas": Question: One harms the Buddha, breaks the Sangha, kills an Arhat, and burns and destroys obstacles;
why is this not called "destroying all dharmas"? Answer: Because it is of the nature of a diamond (*vajra*).
What is the harm? Even if there were such a destroyer, how could that abolish the practice of the Dharma? The breaking of the Sangha and the killing of Arhats pertain only to the Hīnayāna;
even if these were destroyed, how could the Mahāyāna Dharma perish because of them? Furthermore, this does not rely on the five heinous crimes of the Mahāyāna.
If it were a Bodhisattva who could propagate the Great Dharma, then with that person’s death, the Dharma would naturally follow in its loss.
Regarding the phrase "the extent to which self and others [benefit]," if one praises the Buddha, one can only benefit the praiser;

because the Tathāgata’s fruition is already perfected, there is nothing further to be gained. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] has "not even a little" [to gain]. If, however, one praises a holder of the Dharma, both the object of praise and the praiser obtain benefit.
This is because the fruition of the one being praised is not yet complete; upon encountering such praise, they become joyful and courageous, thereby advancing all the more.

Regarding "practice": since it accomplishes both self-benefit and benefit for others, it is called "abundant. This follows the same principle as the gravity of offenses against the Buddha mentioned previously.
As for the commentary’s phrase "non-arising yet arising," those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) have exhausted all accumulation of suffering; this is termed "non-arising."
Now, causing them to turn toward rebirth over three great kalpas is called "having birth. This is because it is like parched grain that can still sprout;
therefore, it is difficult to believe.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "the internal and external are shaped against one another and called a 'household'": the Mahāyāna is termed the "internal," while the non-Buddhist paths and the Hīnayāna are termed the "external."
It is "external" because it takes form based upon that [interior]. It is called a "house" (*śālā*) because the house constitutes the middle.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "In other lands, I dispatch emanated beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) and so forth," one asks: what is the intention behind dispatching these emanated sentient beings?
The answer briefly sets forth three points: first, to make offerings to the Dharma-preacher; second, to guide genuine persons; and third, to protect the Dharma-preacher.

Regarding the passage in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) on the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa" (Bǎotă pǐn), which asks, "How could there be a multitude?"—according to the seventh fascicle of the treatise, the text is indeed as stated in the commentary (*shù*).

As for how the commentary resolves this, the traditional explanations are difficult to understand. Answer: The treatise states that there was no request [for the preaching]. There was no request because Prabhūtaratna preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It is not that the Many-Jeweled Stūpa (Prabhūtaratna) did not preach the sūtra at all, which would constitute a lack of request. If this were not the case, there would be no one to request the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The appearance of the stūpa serves as a witness; furthermore, it does not preach other [sūtras]. Why would the stūpa not appear as a witness for other sūtras?

Since there is a distinction between what is witnessed and what is not, we know that there is preaching, though it is different from [the preaching of] other [sūtras]. When the treatise says, "There is no request and no witnessing of the Dharma," it means...
The general meaning and the specific details are distinct; since this was not difficult for the ancients to understand, there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "because they equally constitute the nature of jewels": it means that the lands are equally composed of the seven treasures, which is termed the "equality of jewels.
This explains the reason why the transformed lands mentioned in the sūtra are adorned with crystal and other such materials.

Regarding the phrase "hanging bells" (*jing xuanling*): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "a bell that hangs down. It is composed of the radical for metal (金) with the phonetic element 令 (líng).
As for the question, "If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already accommodated [the assembly], why is there a need for him to sit again?"—this is a query concerning the second sitting.

Why, then, does the response explain the reasons for the three transformations? The answer is: because the Buddha’s second sitting serves as the primary occasion for the three transformations, the response cites the reasons for those three transformations.

In response, he stated that "the three transformations leading to the Way" seem similar to the Confucian classics. According to the *Lunyu*: "If Qi undergoes one transformation, it will reach the level of Lu;
if Lu undergoes one transformation, it will reach the Way. Zheng Kangcheng commented: "This means that Qi and Lu possess the residual influence of the Duke of Tai and the Duke of Zhou.
The Duke of Tai was a great sage, and the Duke of Zhou was a saint. Although their governance and instruction have now declined, if a wise ruler were to arise—"
It may be made like that of Qi; it may be made like that of Lu.
When the Great Way was practiced, those who sat upon the Lion Throne (siṃhāsana) were the Buddhas. Because they possessed no fear and were able to subdue all things, they were called "Lions.

A throne for a lion is called a "lion-throne"; it is not an actual lion, nor is it made of gold or other such materials. It is called a lion-throne because it is fashioned in the likeness of a lion. Thus, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*...
The seventh fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "That which is called a 'lion' is not an actual lion. The Buddha is the lion among men;
wherever the Buddha sits—whether on a couch or upon the ground—it is termed a 'lion throne' (*siṃhāsana*)."
Regarding the statement that the seat was borrowed from the Lamp-King Buddha: this refers to borrowing a seat from the buddha-field of the Lamp-King Buddha in order to host a guest.

Regarding the statement that the emitted light reached only the eight directions: this explains a potential objection. The objection arises because the number of regions differs when light is emitted and the land is transformed.

Regarding the statement that "there are [mountains] in the Buddha-lands of the higher stages": this refers to the fact that the mountains exist within the lands manifested for those in the four stages of the roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).

In contrast to other ordinary beings, these are called "higher stages. Furthermore, the "higher stages" also refer to the *paranirmita-vashavartin* (other-enjoyment) lands, which likewise possess mountains.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Mahā-Meru. If it were not so, why would the term "Mahā" (Great) be prefixed?
Furthermore, the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states that [the Buddha] was on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Thus, we know that the *saṃbhogakāya* realm possesses mountains.

If this is so, why does a sūtra speak of "moving mountains"? The answer is that it refers to moving the various mountains within those transformed lands (*nirmāṇakṣetra*). Another interpretation holds that the *parasaṃbhoga* realm does not necessarily have mountains.
As for the term *mahā*, it also carries the sense of "many," just as one speaks of a "great bhikṣu" when many have attained the name.
This is also the case here.
Regarding the entry for "tóngshàn" (僮苫) in the *Shūzìlín* (疏字林), I have searched various dictionaries but have ultimately found no explanation.

Based on my own conjecture, it should refer to a servant's dwelling; a room where one resides that is covered with *tiǎn* (thatch) is called a "tóngshàn. It is established by combining a human element with a material object.
Thus it is named.

In the commentary, the statement "the manifested transformation Buddhas appear for the sake of accomplishing the Great Matter" refers collectively to the three bodies (trikāya), all of which exist for the purpose of accomplishing this one Great Matter.

Regarding the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification), both the *Mahāpiṭaka* and *Abhidharma-piṭaka* clarify this meaning in detail. Now, following the *Yogācārabhūmi*, I shall briefly present two sections: first, the definition of the names and characteristics;
second, the specific antidotes. As for the general name, it should be called *dhūta*. The correct etymological explanation is as given in the commentaries (*śāstra*).
It is also said to mean "washing" or "cleansing. Because it washes away afflictions (*kleśa*), one who cleanses their robes is called a *dhūta*. It should...
It is called "shaking off" (*dhūta*), because one shakes off dust and defilements; its meaning is similar to that of "washing. It is also said to mean "cultivating and purifying the mind.

The twelve virtues (*guṇa*) are grouped into three categories. The first is the clarification of food, which consists of four types: namely, always maintaining the practice of begging for food (*piṇḍapātika*).
1. Regarding alms-seeking: one should beg for food in successive order from house to house, eat while remaining seated in a single sitting, and eat only after first ceasing all other activities.
2. Regarding clothing: there are three types, namely, wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*), wearing garments of wool (*vārkṣa*), and wearing rag-robes from refuse heaps (*pāṃśukūla*).

3. Regarding dwellings: there are five types, namely, secluded places, at the foot of a tree, in the open air, among burial mounds, and always sitting; these are called the five dwellings. One should always maintain the practice of begging for food.

Furthermore, he constantly sets a time limit for his almsround to sustain himself. Second, regarding "sequential begging": this means entering the streets of the holy ones (*ārya-vīthi*) and begging from house to house;
as soon as food is obtained, he accepts it immediately, without raising his hand high or skipping over other houses with the wish, "May I obtain exquisite food and drink.
Third, regarding "eating at one sitting": this means sitting in a single session until one has finished all that should be eaten.
Having received all the food and risen from his seat, he must certainly not eat again. Fourth, regarding "stopping first and eating later":
for the sake of eating, he sits upon his appropriate seat; until he has eaten, he should first fully receive all the food that is to be consumed.
He should correctly understand: "I shall now receive only this much food and drink; I will sustain myself with this and eat nothing beyond it. Thus he reflects.
Only after this may one eat. Regarding "one who maintains only the three robes": this means that one sustains oneself with only the three robes.
First is the *saṃghāṭī*, which carries the sense of being "on top"; that is, when entering royal palaces or villages, it is worn as the outermost layer, hence it is called "being on top.
Second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, which likewise carries the sense of being worn on top; that is, within the monastery... [it is] precisely this.
The seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) is worn inside the monastery; it is donned over the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*). It is also called "the upper" or "the middle.
Because it is worn below the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and above the five-strip robe, it is termed "the middle. The three *antarvāsas* are translated here as "inner garments."
*Antarvāsa* (inner robe). Regarding the meaning of *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe): the single term *pāṃśukūla* below encompasses the two [other types] above;
this is a concise explanation of the skillful method. Apart from these three robes, there are none that exceed them in length. As for "those who wear only woolen robes" (*karpāsa-cīvara-dhara*):

this refers to the three robes they carry, or perhaps the extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), all of which are made of wool. There is nothing else used; specifically, fine sheep’s wool is called "wool" (*karpāsa*). Wool...
When woven into cloth, it is called "woolen clothing" (*kṣaumika*). Alternatively, fine hair alone is simply called "wool" (*kṣauma*);
this refers to the fine wool of all birds and beasts, not exclusively that of sheep. Seventh, regarding the wearer of refuse rags (*pāṃsukūlika*):

this refers to any garment that has been discarded or thrown away by others—whether in streets, alleys, marketplaces, on roads, or in non-road areas—and which has become mixed with excrement, filth, pus, blood, mucus, or saliva.
Dyeing: Taking such impure garments as these, one removes the coarse filth, washes them thoroughly, sews and dyes them, and then accepts and wears them.

Question: Regarding garments made of wool or mixed materials, they are also used to make the three robes (*tricīvara*). What is the difference between these and the aforementioned three robes? Answer:
The first three robes are woven from fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and the like; they are not made of wool or mixed materials. This is because [the Buddha] feared that [monks] might lack contentment.
As for "those who [wear robes]," they use priceless woolen cloth and the like as their garments; therefore, they use clothing made of mixed materials such as wool.
Among these three sets of three, one may maintain any one set of three; it is not required that all three sets of three robes be maintained simultaneously and in their entirety.

Regarding "the eight types of those who dwell in an araṇya," this refers to a secluded place (*śūnyāgāra*). It means dwelling in seclusion within mountain forests, wildernesses, or open plains, making use of the peripheral limits of habitation.
Regarding bedding: dwelling far removed from all villages, towns, and settlements in extremely secluded lodgings is called "living at the edge.

Dwelling outside the city walls or beyond the forests is called "living in the wilderness. Ninth, "constantly dwelling under a tree" means constantly vowing to reside beneath a tree, relying upon its roots.
Tenth, "constantly dwelling in the open air" means constantly vowing to reside in the open, without any covering or shelter.

11. Dwelling constantly among burial mounds (*śmāśānika*). "Among burial mounds" means one who makes a constant vow to dwell among graves and cemeteries, the places where the corpses of those whose lives have passed are sent.
12. Constantly remaining in a sitting posture (*naiṣadyika*).

"One who remains constantly seated" means that in large or small forests, upon seats of grass, leaves, and so forth, one sits with the body upright, passing the time and days without leaning on the back or the sides.
Sitting in a great forest, on a small rope-bench, or on grass, leaves, and so forth, is called "constant sitting.

This refers to the practice of always sitting or lying down upon seats of various grasses and leaves as they have been appropriately spread out, without repeatedly turning them over, lifting them up, or repairing them after they have been once arranged.
Regarding the second counteractive measure, first a general explanation and then a specific one: Question: What are the qualities of ascetic purification (*dhūta-guṇa*)? Answer: [As follows:]...
For example, when wool and such have not yet been carded, beaten, teased, or split, they remain clumped together, heavy, and unserviceable for making thread, yarn, blankets, or mats.
Once they have been teased and so forth, however, they become soft, light, and fit for use.

In the same way, when a practitioner’s mind is stained by attachment to food, drink, clothing, and bedding, they are able to purify and cultivate themselves through the virtues of the *dhūta* practices.
He causes them to become upright, supple, and capable; compliant and reliant [on the teachings], such that they are able to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
As for the specific remedies, there are two kinds of craving regarding food that can obstruct the cultivation of virtue.

To sever craving for fine food, he always practices begging for alms and begs from house to house in sequence. To sever craving for excessive food, he eats at a single sitting and does not eat after rising from his seat. Regarding...
Regarding clothing, there are three kinds of craving that can obstruct the cultivation of virtue: one wears only the three robes (*tricīvara*) to abandon craving for many garments;
one wears only woolen robes (*karpāsa*) to abandon craving for soft textures; and one wears rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) to abandon craving for fine and exquisite materials.

Regarding bedding and seating, there are four kinds of craving that can obstruct the cultivation of virtue: one dwells in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) to abandon craving for social clamor; [one dwells under a tree] to abandon craving for houses...

Because of the greed for dwellings and sexual indulgence, one always dwells under trees, in the open air, or at burial mounds. Because of the greed for the pleasures of reclining and lying down, one always intends to sit upright.

Because of the greed for bedding and furnishings, one remains in a place as if it were one's regular seat; alternatively, by excluding the two greeds for dwellings and sexual indulgence, these five [ascetic practices] may also be established.
Commentary, Scroll Nine, *Devadatta-parivarta*.
Regarding the phrase "bestowed by Devadatta," an ancient interpretation states: *deva* means "heaven" (*deva*), and *datta* means "heat" (*tāpa*). This is because [he] committed...

Regarding the "Heavenly Heat" (Tianre): because one falls into hell after committing the crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and undergoes sufferings such as being burned and boiled, it is called "Heavenly Heat.
Furthermore, it is said that it is so named because at the moment of birth, the minds of the various devas become heated; thus it is called "Heavenly Heat. Why do the devas' minds become heated?

Because the devas know that this person has committed three of the crimes of immediate retribution, their minds become heated upon seeing them born for the first time; it is for this reason that the name was established. The commentary states: according to the local customs of the Western Regions...
One obtained by begging from the gods is named Devadatta; one obtained through sacrificial offerings is named Yajñadatta.
Other Devadattas did not commit the crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya). For what reason, then, was the mind of the god [Śakra] distressed? It is because not all Devadattas commit such crimes.
Therefore, it is known that the ancient commentary was intended as a definitive interpretation; one should follow the correction of the sub-commentary (ṭīkā).
"Spreading vines and trailing fruits" refers to melons, gourds, and the like. "Tié" (瓞) is pronounced *zhí*. In common parlance, it refers to the small varieties of melon;
"pó" (瓟) is pronounced *pò*.

Regarding the passage in the sutra where those who were originally śrāvakas attain the meaning of the Mahāyāna emptiness, the question is asked: why does it say [that they do so] within the assembly at the Ocean of Wisdom?
Regarding the phrase "abiding in the midst of empty space," there are two interpretations. First, during his time as a śrāvaka, he contemplated the three gates of emptiness as his basis;

this is called "abiding in empty space" while expounding the practices of the śrāvakas. Second, it refers directly to those emerging from the ocean-like assembly who abide in the midst of empty space.
Question: Does this śrāvaka practice the Great Vehicle after having emerged from emptiness, or has he already turned back while still within the ocean?
If he has already turned back while in the ocean, how can he be said to be in emptiness when teaching the practice of a śrāvaka? Answer:

Even if he has already turned his mind [toward the Great Vehicle], what fault is there in him teaching the practice of a śrāvaka? How could it be that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are unable to speak of those śrāvakas?
Is it practice? Or perhaps discussing the past teachings on the practices of the śrāvakas—none of these contradict [the point].

Regarding the commentary’s statement that one "cannot become a Māra-king" and so forth: Question: One who fully cultivates the ten wholesome paths and reveres the Triple Gem—how can such a person be called a Māra? Answer:

It is because of the causes of the ten wholesome paths and the reverence for the Triple Gem that one attains the state of a Māra; it is not that having already become a Māra, one is willing to practice [the wholesome paths].
This is indeed worthy of respect. However, those in the human realm are all summoned by virtue of wholesome karma. A woman, moreover, is a specific retribution induced by delusion;
therefore, she cannot become a Māra king or the like.

In the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta-sūtra*, there are again eight thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Question: According to the previous prediction, there were not eight thousand;

from where do these [eight thousand] come? Answer: There are three explanations. First, according to the text of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there are eighty people; the character "thousand" (*qian*) must be an error.
Second, in the "Dharmabhāṇaka" chapter, they receive their prediction (vyākaraṇa). Third, there is an error of two characters; it should be two characters [instead of eight].

This refers to the two thousand people previously mentioned who were being trained as those with and without further learning (śaikṣa-aśaikṣa). According to one interpretation, within the "Dharanī" chapter, there are five types of persons. Among the first four types of persons:

The first three are bodhisattvas who proceed directly (*ekayāna-gāmin*). The latter, the bhikṣuṇī, is one who turns from the Small Vehicle and enters the Great Vehicle. The commentary states: "Regarding the first category, it is reasonable that they proceed directly.

As for the five hundred and eight thousand, since they were formerly śrāvakas and have now just begun their resolve, why should they not also be those who turn from the Small Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle?
The text is extremely clear; I do not understand why this master [Sengzhao] has made such a definitive exclusion."

Regarding the commentary's statement, "Bending the body as if there were something below [the waist] constitutes flattery of body and speech": according to the *Yùpiān* (Jade Lexicon), "chǎn" (諂) means "flattery" (*yú*).

It explains that bending the body as if there were something below is called "chǎn. The *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "To harbor expectations regarding another's intent and to express them through one's words is called 'chǎn'."

The *Śū* (Commentary) states, "Deceitfulness of body and speech," which explains the distinction between those two schools. It does not refer to what is called "body and speech" in works such as the *Zhuangzi*.

Regarding the phrase in the *Śū*, "the practitioner of the sound of the conch," according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 21, it says: "Alternatively, one may violate the *śīla* internally..."
They harbor decay within while outwardly manifesting integrity and sincerity. Like a snail born of water, they possess the sound of a conch yet the conduct of a dog;
they are not truly śramaṇas, though they claim to be so. There are briefly two interpretations [of this analogy]:

first, it is said that just as a snail in water causes the water to become turbid with its own mucus, so too do wicked bhikṣus defile the waters of the Buddha-dharma in the same manner; thus they are compared [to the snail].

The snail. However, in the customs of Western countries, they value the sound of that conch shell; yet there is the "dog-call" which resembles the sound of that conch, and the "dog-walk" [which resembles its movement].
How much more so for that bhikṣu, who inwardly harbors the unwholesome conduct of greed while outwardly manifesting the conduct of virtuous speech and upright integrity.
Second, it is said: the snail is a metaphor for the impurity of the bodily conduct of one who has left the household life, while the conch sound is a metaphor for the speech of a bhikṣu.

This is incorrect. Although this teaching appears to be well-spoken, it cannot express the cause for transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*). The metaphor of the dog’s conduct illustrates the conduct of that [person’s] mind;
just like that dog, although its outward appearance may be pleasing, it constantly harbors greed and envy. It is exactly the same with one who is not a true renunciant (*pravrajita*).
Regarding the fact that the *Śāstra* addresses Gautamī using a feminine form of address:

according to the phonological rules (*śabda-vidyā*) of the Western Regions (India), there are three general categories of sound—masculine, feminine, and neither masculine nor feminine—due to differences in weight (*gaurava*) and other qualities. Some say that "Gautamī" translates here as "Clarified Woman" (*Ming-nü*).
Thus, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states: "The Clarified Woman also obtained a small portion [of the teaching]," yet this does not exhaust the full principle.
Question: Why are Śākyamuni and Gautamī of the same clan? Is it possible for those of the same clan to form a marriage alliance? Answer:

The customs of different countries vary, so this should not be considered a difficulty. Furthermore, the name "Śākya" is a general designation; they were not married within the same immediate kinship group.
This is somewhat similar to the system of the five surnames in this land, such as the Shang (商), which comprises many distinct lineages despite sharing the same name.

She was married into a merchant family, just like the four classes such as farmers and merchants. Some say that, according to the customs of this region, when she went to her husband’s house, she was named a daughter of the Wang clan;
they claim the same applies to Gautamī. This interpretation is incorrect, as it contradicts the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (or *Mūla-prakaraṇa-sūtra*) and other texts.

Regarding the passage "having observed eighty thousand bodhisattvas and so forth," there is one interpretation which holds that this reveals that these bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties and wisdom such that they intuitively grasp the Buddha’s intention and the purport of the sutra, thereby inspiring faith in others.
This is as Zhuang Zhou said: "The Way exists where it is directly perceived by the eyes."

Regarding the phrase "due to attachment to gain and offerings," according to the tenth chapter, the Chapter on Gain and Offerings (*Liyang pin*), of the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing), the Buddha formerly spoke this verse for the sake of Devadatta:
"The plantain perishes because of its fruit; the bamboo and the reed likewise perish because of their fruit. The conch and the donkey meet their death by sitting upon it."

The gentleman loses himself through greed; such greed brings no benefit. Know that it arises from delusion. The fool, for this reason, harms the worthy, and his head and limbs are scattered upon the ground.
The foolish person craves gain and sustenance, seeking fame, promotion, and praise; while living at home, he gives rise to envy.
Constantly seeking offerings from others, yet being able to discern this clearly—such a bhikṣu is a true son of the Buddha. He does not delight in or cling to gain and honor;
he dwells in seclusion, while his wisdom remains undisturbed by worldly concerns. Furthermore, the twelfth verse of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Great Bodhisattva Treasury Sūtra) says:

"Those who desire to dwell amidst suffering and pleasure, and among various wealth and treasures, do not delight in the sphere of practice that leads to renunciation. Such irrational, foolish commoners remain established on the ground [of ignorance]."
Regarding the passage on the road before the prison:
"When evil spirits enter their bodies," this refers to external māras entering within the body to cause them to slander [the Dharma].

Alternatively, it may refer to the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth being like an "ignited house" (*āgneya-veśman*); these too are considered evil spirits. The former interpretation emphasizes the wholesome; the latter interpretation is more universally applicable.
Regarding the statement, "Because they have received the Buddha’s admonitions in the sutras, they should all endure this matter," it is asked: The original intent was to propagate the sutra;
why, then, must one practice patience? It is answered: Because one practices patience, no disputes arise. Because disputes do not arise, evil matters shall cease.
Since there are no longer any evil matters, what dharma could one not propagate?
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning the Dharma entrusted by the Buddha: Question: One may gallop through various paths and suffer all manner of injuries and destruction;
yet, what is the benefit of maintaining a firm resolve to transmit the Dharma? Answer: The Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha, and it is man who can propagate the Way.

Since the Way exists eternally, the Buddha likewise does not perish. Because it possesses manifold virtues, it is manifested through the Buddha. Therefore, the *Dhṛtīparipṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Person Who Upholds), Chapter One, states: "If there is one who upholds..."
Recite it and explain it to others. Use this elephant scripture to exhort all bodhisattvas, causing them to study, recite, and further propagate it.
Why is this? If this shadow-attendant remains long in the world, then the Buddha’s true Way will manifest eternally and far-reaching.
Since the Tathāgata abides forever, one must therefore transmit and spread it.

I argue: This is not so. To take, for instance, the *Dharmasamgīti* [or *Yogācārabhūmi*]: ... [text continues] ... 105b) states: "If one wishes to attain the supreme vehicle, one must first cultivate the three types of pure conduct (*śīla*). What are these three? First, the pure conduct of restraint; second, the pure conduct of gathering wholesome dharmas; and third, the pure conduct of benefiting sentient beings. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* says: "One who wishes to enter the Mahāyāna path should first train in the three types of pure conduct. Thus, it is clear that the three types of pure conduct encompass both right practice and auxiliary practice. Moreover, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "What is the training in superior ethics (*adhiśīla*)? It refers to the training in the three types of pure conduct. And the *Śrāvakabhūmi* says: "What is the training in superior ethics? It refers to the training in the three types of pure conduct. Therefore, the three types of pure conduct are the essence of both right and auxiliary practice. Consequently, the four practices taught in the Chapter on Peaceful Conduct are themselves the three types of pure conduct. How can they alone be designated as "right practice" while the other six chapters are designated as "auxiliary practice"? Furthermore, the *Brahmajālasūtra* says: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to quickly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they must first learn the ten major precepts. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* also says: "What is the training in superior ethics? It refers to the training in the ten major precepts. Regarding the five kinds of Dharma-preachers mentioned in the "Chapter on the Virtues of the Teacher," one seeks them through one's own effort. How so? It is because there are not only those who assist others.

One should say that those who practice correctly themselves are called "correct practice" (*samyak-pratipatti*), while those who hear [the Dharma] incidentally, rejoice in it, and so forth, are all called "auxiliary practices" (*anugata-pratipatti*).
It does not refer to a single category alone.
To explain the Mahāyāna teachings in the Commentary yet select what is not Mahāyāna reveals a perversion (*viparyāsa*).

This is called "perversion" because one refuses to accept that which truly exists—the Mahāyāna—while falsely seeking that which does not exist—the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, one's original study was of the Mahāyāna...

Having mounted [the Great Vehicle], they instead take up the small; therefore, this is called "inversion. Question: Do they immediately turn toward the small fruit upon hearing the teaching of the Great, or do they only turn toward the small fruit after first regressing from the Great?
Answer: At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those who had previously regressed from the Great are primarily addressed;

thus, it is said that after hearing the Great, they regress and seek the small fruit. However, in reality, there are also those who, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, immediately seek the small fruit. Why is this so?
This is clarified as follows. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Sixty bodhisattvas, upon hearing the teaching of Prajñā, became arhats. One might ask:
"Is it not the case that there was a deficiency or error regarding their faculties? The answer is: "Though moistened by the same rain, their growth differs.
It is called the 'Great Vehicle' (Mahāyāna) because it is intended for the majority; therefore, there is no discrepancy."

Regarding the commentary’s statement that this dharma-gate causes those of the two vehicles to be equal to those who have perfected the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*): "this dharma-gate" refers to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

By means of the One Vehicle, it is explained that the practices of the ten stages are brought to completion. Now, it is intended that these individuals, by relying upon this One Vehicle, shall attain the perfection of practice just like the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) of the ten stages;
therefore, the treatise says they are "equal. Alternatively, because this sutra is the One Vehicle, it is as follows:
Because the practices of the ten stages are fulfilled, they are called "identical. Since the crest-jewel is the most supreme and ultimate, this sutra is likewise compared to it as being the ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata secretly bestows [the jewel] and explains [the meaning]," the *Śāstra* states: "Bestowing a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*). "Bestowing a prediction" is the meaning of "explaining.

Just as a king’s intention in bestowing a pearl is to cause that person to become a king, so too does the Buddha grant him the Dharma to cause him to become a Buddha. Thus, he gives both the pearl and the Dharma.
The *Biao* (Commentary) treats this as the Buddha-king; therefore, it is termed "Esoteric" (*mi*).

Although the text of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) differs at this point, it is a continuation of the preceding meaning. The sixth [category], the Unsurpassed, and the sixth metaphor both clarify the mani-jewel.
Although they differ in their sequence, the mani-jewel is the same; thus, this is a continuation of the previous meaning.

Regarding the passage on "the body’s conduct being intimate or distant, general or specific," this refers to the sphere of intimacy (*upāsana*). That which is called "intimate" (*pratyāsanna*) is so named because it is close;

the spheres of conduct that are each distant are "distant. Thus, the distant is the general conduct, while the intimate is the specific conduct. Alternatively, that which can be approached and associated with is called "intimate," while that which cannot be approached is called "distant.
The term "space" (*ākāśa*) is the general name, while the remaining four [elements] are the specific names.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Although the subsequent verses rely on persons, they do not contradict the principle," this refers to the following verse:
"Furthermore, one does not practice even a single verse. This corresponds to the preceding prose which states, "Furthermore, one does not practice with respect to phenomena," and so forth.

The verse says, "Nor does one discriminate," etc., which corresponds to this single recitation: "Neither practicing nor discriminating," and so forth. However, observing the text of the verses, although they are expressed by way of persons...

Regarding the Dharma: it is explained through the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which collectively clarify the inclusion of non-activity within all phenomena. To say "explaining the two kinds" refers to these two textual passages:
the former statement, "furthermore, one does not engage in [activity]," and the present statement, "one practices while remaining non-discriminative. These are the two declarations.

Regarding the "Six Scripts" (*liùshū*) mentioned in the commentary: according to the *Zhou Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou), the *Bǎo Shì* (Tutor of the Household) taught the "Six Scripts" to the sons of the nobility.

First is *zhǐshì* (Indicative Writing). This refers to characters that can be recognized by looking at them and whose meaning is perceived through observation; examples include "up" (*shàng*) and "down" (*xià*). Second is *xiàngxíng* (Pictographic Writing).

Pictographic writing involves drawing the form of an object, curving the lines according to its physical shape; examples include "sun" (*rì*) and "moon" (*yuè*). Third is *xíngshēng* (Phono-semantic Compound). Phono-semantic compounds take a radical representing the meaning... [text truncated]... of a thing.

First is *ming* (name). It is formed by taking metaphors as signs; the rivers are an example. Fourth is *huiyi* (compound ideograms). As for *huiyi*, it combines categories and unites meanings to reveal the intended reference;

"direct trust" (*jingxin*) is an example. Fifth is *zhuanzhu* (transferred phonetic notes). As for *zhuanzhu*, it connects meanings under a single head, with similar meanings mutually receiving one another;
"investigation" (*kao*) and "old age" (*lao*) are examples. Sixth is *jiejie* (phonetic loans). As for *jiejie*, there was originally no character for the meaning, so it relies on sound.

"Entrusting matters" refers to the magistrates and elders. Regarding "writing" (*shū*), according to the *Guǎngyá*, "writing" means "to resemble" (*rú*) or "to record" (*jì*). Furthermore, the *Shuōwén* states:
when Cāngjié first created writing, it was based on classifying types and imitating forms; therefore, it was called "patterns" (*wén*). Subsequently, form and sound supplemented one another.
