This is what is called a "character" (zi). A character is so named because it reproduces and gradually increases. When these are inscribed upon bamboo or silk, they are called "writing" (shu).

Writing means "to resemble" (ru). Furthermore, according to the *Shiming* (Explanation of Names): "Writing is 'abundance' (shu); it records the myriad things. It also means "to record" (zhu), for by recording them upon slips of wood or paper, they shall never perish.
Regarding the ten kinds of faults for entering a royal palace mentioned in the Vinaya commentary (*śāstra*), according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), fascicle 60, it states:
"When a renunciant enters a royal palace, there are ten faults. First, if at a time when the king and his consort are in union, a bhikṣu enters the palace and goes among the women;
the consort sees the bhikṣu and smiles, and the bhikṣu sees the consort and also smiles. The king..."
He forms this thought: "If a bhikṣu has already performed such an act, he should perform it again.
Second, when a king is intoxicated, he engages in union with his consort but does not remember it; later, the consort becomes pregnant, and the king thinks:
"The bhikṣu entered the palace; this was done by that bhikṣu. Third, when the king’s crown prince intends to rebel and kill the king, the king thinks: "The bhikṣu..."
"The Bhikṣu has entered my palace; this is what he has taught. This was the secret speech of the Four Kings within, which had been heard outside.
The King thought: "The Bhikṣu has entered my palace; this is what he has transmitted. [Thinking thus,] the Five Kings lost their jewels or things resembling jewels.
The King formed this thought: "The Bhikṣu has entered my palace; this is what he has taken away. (6)
The king appointed a person of low status to a high position; those outside who were displeased said, "It is the doing of the bhikṣu that he has entered the palace.
Or, the king may have placed those in high positions in lower offices; those who were displeased said the same.
9. It is the work of the bhikṣu that he enters the palace. This is the eighth cause and condition for groundless [accusations].
When the king assembles the fourfold army at an improper time, those who are displeased say: "It is the work of the bhikṣu that he enters the palace. This is the ninth.
When the king assembles his army but returns from mid-way, those who are displeased say: "It is the work of the bhikṣu that he enters the palace. This is the tenth.
If a king stays within his palace amidst the court ladies, he sees fine horses, birds, and beautiful women; upon seeing them, attachment arises in his mind.
This is not the dharma of a bhikṣu. These constitute the ten faults.

Regarding the statement that the Ruler of Wu shared a carriage with [the monk], according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), King Sun Hao of Wu welcomed the śramaṇa Kang Senghui into the palace by means of a horse-drawn carriage;
it does not say they shared a carriage. According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Dharma Master Dao’an shared a carriage with Fu Jian, the ruler of Qin.
The biography states: "Shi Dao’an was a native of Fuli in Changshan. His family had been distinguished scholars for generations. (Seven...)
He read books every year; after reading them twice, he was able to recite them from memory. At the age of twelve, he left the household life and met Fotudeng, taking him as his teacher.
Later, fleeing the turmoil to Xiangyang, he widely propagated the Buddha-dharma and extensively established meritorious works. At that time, Fu Jian had long heard of Dao’an’s reputation.
He often remarked, "In Xiangyang there is the monk Dao’an; he is a vessel of divine talent. I intend to bring him here to assist my prayers.
Later, he dispatched Fu Pi to attack Xiangyang from the south. Dao’an and Zhu Xu were both captured by Fu Jian.
Jian said to his Vice Director Quan Yi, "With an army of one hundred thousand, I have taken Xiangyang and obtained only one person and a half. Quan Yi asked, "Who is this?"
Fu Jian said, "Master Dao’an is a whole person; Xi Zuochi is but half a person. Later, as Fu Jian was exiting the Eastern Garden, he ordered Dao’an to ascend the imperial carriage to ride with him.

The Palace Secretary Quan Yi remonstrated, saying, "Your Majesty, I have heard that for the ceremonial carriage of a Son of Heaven, the Zhongzhong (Attendant-in-Ordinary) must accompany the sovereign.

Master Dao’an has altered his physical appearance; how can he be permitted to take such a seat? Fu Jian’s expression suddenly grew stern, and he said, "Master Dao’an’s virtue and wisdom are worthy of the highest honor. I—"

To exchange the empire for the honor of riding in a carriage or palanquin would not be commensurate with his virtue; thus, he commanded the Vice President of the Secretariat to assist him in ascending the palanquin.

His other divine virtues are fully recounted in the historical records (*zhuan*); they are here omitted for brevity. The commentary states: "The account in the *Zhuan* that follows [the text] which mentions 'Wu' is merely a scribal error.
Alternatively, there may be accounts of the King of Wu in other records, or it may refer to the meeting where carriages and horses were prepared to receive him."
This matter is called "sharing the carriage.

Regarding the account of the Qin ruler yielding his wife Qianling and her subsequent disgrace, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), Kumārajīva—translated as "Child Longevity" (*Tóngshòu*)—was a native of India.
His family had served as prime ministers for generations. Kumārajīva’s father, Kumārayāna, was intelligent and possessed of noble character.

Dharmakṣema was about to succeed to the position of Chancellor when he declined the office and left home to become a monk. He traveled east across the Pamir Mountains. When the ruler of Kucha heard that he had renounced such glory, he felt profound admiration for him.

The ruler went out to the outskirts of the city to welcome him and invited him to serve as the State Preceptor. The ruler had a younger sister, twenty years of age, who was possessed of clear insight and compassion;
she became his wife, and from her was born Master Kumārajīva. At the age of seven, Kumārajīva entered the monastic order and recited a thousand stanzas daily.

The verses consist of thirty-two characters, totaling thirty-two thousand words. He was proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles and had extensively studied the four Vedas, the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), and all works on yin-yang, astrology, and mathematics;
there was nothing he did not master completely. He possessed a subtle mastery of auspiciousness and misfortune, such that his words were like a matching tally.
On the twentieth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, dispatched...
He was invited by imperial decree and arrived in Chang’an. Yao Xing received him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher and treated him with great favor.

He requested that Kumārajīva enter the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden to translate various scriptures. Later, the Ruler of Later Qin said to Kumārajīva, "The Great Master is brilliant and wise."
Chao-wu was peerless in the world; if he were to pass away one day, how could the lineage of the Dharma be left without an heir?
He therefore coerced ten courtesans into taking him as their husband. From that time on, he no longer resided in the monastic quarters but established a separate residence for himself.
Every time he gave a discourse, he would first offer this analogy: "It is like a lotus flower growing out of foul mud;
one should grasp only the lotus flower and not take up the foul mud."

Regarding the phrase "those who are negligent and frivolous," according to the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing), in its fourth and fifth chapters on Heedlessness (*pramāda*), as well as its fourteenth chapter, it says:
"A person who is heedless turns toward the performance of evil; they disregard future conditions and do not consider the next world.
It is like casting grain seeds into fire while hoping for sprouts and stalks—such a thing cannot happen. It is like trying to block [a flood] with a small clod of earth."

It is like one who wishes to stop the flow of the Yangtze River; it can never be achieved. For a person of negligence whose mind and conduct are violent and cruel, even if they seek a measure of goodness as small as a hair or a speck of dust, I do not see such a thing.

In the *Vyākhyā*, from "There are fourteen types of persons in the Abhidharma" up to "all are called those lacking restraint (*asaṃvara*)," it refers to those who, for the sake of making a living, slaughter, raise, or trade in sheep, pigs, and the like;
those who constantly catch fish and other creatures; those who dwell in mountain forests to capture and control wild elephants; those who practice incantations upon dragons and snakes;
and those who sustain themselves through amusements. Furthermore, those who use divisive speech to ruin the kin of others in order to make a living are termed "those lacking restraint."
[The Master] asks: How does one become one who possesses non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? [The Master] answers:

If one is born into such a family of non-restraint, or is born into another family, then—according to the respective order—one first establishes a firm resolve through the preliminary application of body and speech to engage in those actions;
as long as the conditions for abandoning that non-restraint have not arisen, one is called one who possesses non-restraint.

The Commentary states that one who does not aspire to the fruits of the two vehicles is a bodhisattva who has broken the precepts. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 586:
"If at any time a bodhisattva does not manifest the arousal of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), at that time they abide in a succession of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mental states.
At such a time, the bodhisattva is still said to be 'possessed of the precepts,' and is not yet said to have 'violated, abandoned, or discarded' them."

Regarding the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva: when a bodhisattva does not manifest the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) and instead turns toward the levels of the śrāvakas and so forth, that bodhisattva abandons the bodhisattva stage and loses the sphere of their own practice.

For as long as they remain turned toward the level of the śrāvakas, for that same duration, they should be known as having "died" with respect to the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttara-yāna*). Although this is not an actual death, it receives the name of "death. It is as follows:
Suppose a master illusionist takes a small child by the hand, leads him up a high ladder, and then uses his magical powers to dismember the child’s body, causing the limbs to fall away one by one.

At that time, the child’s relatives all believe that he has died. In the same way, when a Bodhisattva abandons great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and retreats to abide in the stages of a Śrāvaka or others, thereby losing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it should be understood as being like death. When those small children and their relatives perceive this as death...
Regarding the "five types of non-males" (*pañca-paṇḍaka*) mentioned in the *Vyākhyā*: the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, fascicle 8, states:
"For example, the *śaṇḍha* and the *paṇḍaka* are unfit to approach and serve *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*. It further states that there are five types of *paṇḍakas*."
Because they are equal from birth, they are the same; this sutra intends for them to be distanced [from the path]. Question:

What is the meaning of the term *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuch) and so forth? Answer: *Ṣaṇḍha* means "rootless. Even if they should possess organs in form, they ultimately lack the functional power of the male organ;
all such are named *ṣaṇḍha*. *Pandaka* means "desire" (*kāma*). It refers to one who desires others to act toward oneself...

Because it is contrary to the Dharma, or because it is defiled (*kliṣṭa*). It is called "defiled" because, by taking pleasure in others, it constitutes a fault for oneself and is capable of defiling others.
Question: Among the five types [of eunuchs], those who are removed at birth and these two types are permanently devoid of male potency.

One should call them *ṣaṇḍha*. Why, then, do you say they are *paṇḍaka*? Answer: If one lacks male potency and furthermore does not take pleasure in others, and this constitutes a fault in oneself, one is called a *ṣaṇḍha*.
Although one lacks male potency, if one takes pleasure in others and this constitutes a fault in oneself, one is therefore called a *paṇḍaka*.
According to the actual facts, with respect to that person, because they lack the function of male potency, they should properly be called a *ṣaṇḍha*. This is according to this sutra.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that those who are obstructed by others are collectively termed "pandaka" (eunuchs).
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "Those such as the 'remover' (*apanayaka*) and so forth—if they do not incur a fault upon themselves when obstructed by another, they are merely *śaṇḍha*;
if they do incur a fault upon themselves when obstructed by another, they are called *pandaka*. Among these five types, [the one who] sees another performing sexual intercourse... [is the male].
The movement of the male faculty is called "jealousy" (*īrṣyā*). When another performs non-celibate conduct (*abrahmacarya*) upon oneself, one receives the semen and blood of the other;
from this, the male faculty arises, which is termed "pouring. This male faculty only moves once every half-month, hence it receives the name "half-month.

The other two [periods] may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 50, three types are taught; these [categories] are an expansion of those [in the previous text], while that [text] is a synthesis of these. Nor... [is there contradiction].
This is contradictory.
Regarding the statement that each of the six directions has five matters, according to the *Gālavat-ṣaḍdig-pūjā-sūtra*, it says:
"As for bowing toward the east, this refers to a son serving his parents, for which there are five matters: first, one should attend to the management of livelihood. Second... [text continues].

First, rising early, one must instruct the servants to prepare food and drink at the proper time. Second, one must not increase the anxieties of one's parents. Third, one must remain mindful of one's parents' thoughts.
Fourth, when one's parents are ill, one must feel urgency and seek out physicians to treat them. Fifth, when parents look upon their child, they also have five matters [to consider]:
first, they should think of leading the child away from evil and toward goodness; second, they should teach the child calculation and writing.
Commentary: Third, one should teach them to uphold the sutras and precepts. Fourth, one should arrange for them to take a wife early.
Fifth, one should provide them with everything that belongs to the household. Regarding "bowing toward the south," this refers to the five duties a disciple owes to a teacher:
first, one should respect and praise them; second, one should be mindful of their kindness; third, one should follow whatever they instruct; fourth, one should not... [the text continues].
Disgust. Fifth, one should praise them later. There are also five matters regarding how a teacher instructs a disciple:
first, one should cause them to understand quickly; second, one should cause them to excel over the disciples of others; third, one should desire that they understand without error; fourth...
All doubts and difficulties are completely resolved. Fifth, regarding the desire to have the disciple know that she is superior to her teacher:
bowing toward the west refers to the wife serving her husband. There are five matters: first, when the husband returns from outside, she should rise to welcome him.

Second, when the husband has gone out and is not at home, she should prepare food by steaming and boiling, sweep and clean, and wait for his return. Third, she must not harbor lustful thoughts toward others. Fourth, [if] the husband scolds her... [text continues].

[The husband] should not scold her; if she cannot [be restrained], he should return his words and show a change of countenance. Fourth, he should follow the instructions and admonitions of his wife; he must not conceal any of the household utensils.
Fifth, when the husband rests, he should ensure they are well-stored before he lies down. When the husband looks upon his wife, there are likewise five matters:
first, he should treat his wife with respect when entering or leaving; second, he should provide food and drink at the proper times and give her clothing and bedding; third, he should...
Fourth, one should bestow upon them gold, silver, pearls, and fine ornaments. Fifth, one should entrust to them all that exists within the household, regardless of its quantity.
Fifth, one must not keep improper attendants or concubines outside [the home]. Regarding those who bow toward the north—meaning relatives and friends—one should observe five matters.
First, if one sees something improper, one should not treat it with indifference; rather, one should go privately to a secluded place to admonish, instruct, and restrain them. Second, ...
First, if there is an emergency, one must hasten to provide rescue and protection. Second, one must not speak ill of others behind their backs.

Third, one must not privately discuss [the master's] affairs with others. Fourth, one should mutually respect and praise one another. Fifth, one should give whatever good things one possesses to them, however much or little.
Regarding those who bow toward the ground—meaning masters who oversee slaves and servants—they also have five duties: first, they must provide food, drink, clothing, and bedding at the proper times.
Second, when he is ill or exhausted, one should call for a physician to treat him. Third, one must not strike or beat him recklessly.
Fourth, regarding his private property, one must not seize it. Fifth, when dividing shared property, one should ensure it is distributed equitably.
As for the male and female slaves who serve their masters, there are likewise five duties: first, they should rise early so that the master does not have to call them.
Second, whatever one must do, one should perform it with a sincere mind. Third, one must cherish the master’s property and must not give it away to beggars.
Fourth, when the master goes out or comes in, one should escort him and welcome him. Fifth, one should praise the master’s virtues and must not speak of his faults.
As for bowing toward the heavens, this refers to serving śramaṇas and Daoist practitioners; one should...
One employs five matters: first, to direct a virtuous mind toward them; second, to choose what is excellent with which to converse;
third, to honor them with one’s body; fourth, to feel a sense of longing and devotion for them;

and fifth, regarding the śramaṇas and practitioners as heroes among men, one should reverently serve them and inquire about matters concerning transcendence and liberation. The śramaṇas and practitioners should regard ordinary people with six intentions.
First, to teach them to practice giving, so that they do not become stingy or greedy themselves. Second, to teach them to uphold the precepts, so that they do not violate them themselves.

Third, to teach them to practice patience, so that they do not harbor resentment or anger themselves. Fourth, to teach them to practice diligence, so that they do not become indolent or arrogant themselves.
Fifth, to teach people to maintain a single-minded focus, so that they do not allow their minds to wander. Sixth, to teach people wisdom...
One attains this through one's own folly. Śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way teach people to abandon evil and practice good, revealing the True Path;
their kindness is greater than that of one's parents. If you act in this manner, it will be as if your father were still alive, following his teaching to bow in the six directions.
Why worry about not becoming wealthy? Question: For what reason are the parents equated with the six directions, and why is there such a sequence? Answer: It is intended as a metaphor.

The rising and setting of the sun, the high and low status of the noble and the base, and the fullness and deficiency of the moon serve as metaphors; reflect upon this and you will understand them all.
Regarding the distancing of oneself from the four types of evil friends: one asks, "What kind of person is called an evil friend? The answer is:
those who break the precepts, hold wrong views, and turn their backs on Bodhi are evil friends. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 568, states: "A bodhisattva does not..."

To associate with evil friends means to associate with those who break the precepts, those who cling to false views, those who lack moral discipline, those who live by wrong livelihood, those who speak meaningless words, those who dwell in indolence, those who delight in birth and death, those who turn their backs on bodhi, and those who love worldly affairs. When asked, "When should one not associate?
the answer is: "One should never associate at any time. As the aforementioned sutra states: "Even in his dreams, a bodhisattva does not associate [with them]."
How much more so during the waking state? If that is the case, how can one have compassion for sentient beings as if they were an only son?
The answer is found in that same sutra: "Although the bodhisattva always feels compassion, he does not dwell together with them.

By means of such a method, he distances himself from evil friends; he merely causes them to be free from long-term conditions of defilement and the like, rather than causing their mental roots of goodness to be separated from him."
Therefore, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "A renunciant bodhisattva should not associate with large crowds;
I should abandon them. My roots of goodness shall never be abandoned to all sentient beings."

Regarding the "seven inversions" mentioned in the commentary: these refer to the four inversions consisting of falsely conceptualizing phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure as being permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure.
Fifth is the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), which is the arising of false conceptual discrimination regarding the four [qualities] such as permanence.

Sixth is the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), which is the acceptance, desire, establishment, and attachment toward that which has been conceptually discriminated by those [inversions of perception]. Seventh is the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*)...

Regarding the inverted attachment to afflictions such as greed, the "characteristics of distraction" (*vikṣepa-nimitta*) and the "essence of distraction" (*vikṣepa-svabhāva*) refer to the five sense objects and their respective elements; these are termed the "characteristics of distraction. Here, "characteristic" (*nimitta*) means cause.

Because they are able to produce consciousness, all cognizing minds are termed the "substance of disturbance. Since their substance is delusory inversion, they are called the "substance of disturbance.

The second phrase concludes the preceding characteristics of disturbance; because they are transformations of consciousness and because they are able to produce consciousness, they do not exist apart from consciousness and so forth, and are thus termed "form-consciousness.
The third phrase concludes the preceding substance of disturbance. The fourth phrase reveals that there is nothing transformed by disturbance.
Forms and so forth, which are capable of confusing the essence, cannot exist [independently], for an effect must have its cause in order to exist.
The sūtra states, "This is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva," referring to those aforementioned stations that are not to be approached;
by reversing them, they are termed stations that are to be approached. Furthermore, according to the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there are four modes of intimacy.
He said: "There are four intimate paths for a renunciant bodhisattva, permitted by the Tathāgata: first, intimacy with the Dharma;
second, intimacy with the maturation of all sentient beings; third, making offerings to the Tathāgata; and fourth, intimacy with the non-abandonment of the mind of omniscience."

Regarding the commentary’s reference to “eating the flesh of the *kṛtānta* (wilderness-child) and so forth,” according to the first chapter, the "Chapter on Filial Piety and Support," of the *Baoen jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness), the Buddha addressed the assembly, saying:
"In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a land called Vārāṇasī. A Buddha appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Buddha.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, a king appeared in the world named King Rāja. He was the king of Vārāṇasī."
The minister, named Rāhu, conceived a rebellious and treacherous intent and took the life of the Great King.

He then departed for a frontier state and subsequently killed his two elder brothers. Regarding the third son, a guardian deity spoke to him, saying: "The minister Rāhu has plotted treason to seize the kingdom;
having already killed the father-king and his two elder brothers, he will arrive here before long. Why do you not flee to save your life?"
The king reflected on this and wished to seek refuge in a neighboring kingdom. There were two routes available: one would take seven days, while the other required twenty-four days to reach.
At that time, the king entered the palace and commanded his son, Śuklodana, to set out immediately for the road;

the queen also followed him, but her mind became utterly bewildered, and she mistakenly took the fourteen-day route. The path was perilous and their provisions were exhausted; the king intended to kill his wife in order to save his son. His...
The son remonstrated, saying, "How could there be a son who devours his mother’s flesh? May I beg for one wish? He said, "Please cut three *jin* of my flesh daily to provide food for the three of us.
His parents granted his wish, and they were able to reach their destination on the road. The king at that time was... [the Buddha].
"The father at that time was none other than my father, King Śuddhodana; the mother was none other than Māyā; and the crown prince was none other than myself.
As for the one who then drew forth [the child] and ate the flesh of his son, it was not because he found the taste sweet, but solely for the sake of life.
When a śramaṇa accepts food, it is solely for the purpose of cultivating the Way and sustaining the body, not out of greed for flavor."

Regarding the commentary on "one such as Vimalakīrti," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Kāśyapa, one who dwells in the dharma of equality should practice alms-gathering by walking sequentially.

One should practice alms-gathering for the sake of non-eating; one should accept that food for the sake of destroying the grasping at the combination of conditions and the consumption of solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra);
one should enter the village with the perception of it as an empty village, regarding whatever forms seen there as being like those of the blind."
Sounds heard are like echoes; fragrances smelled are like the wind. Regarding tastes consumed, one does not engage in discrimination. All tactile sensations are realized through wisdom.
One knows that all phenomena are like illusions, possessing neither self-nature nor other-nature; they were originally non-arising and are now non-extinguishing.
With a single meal, one gives to all, making offerings to all Buddhas as well as the multitude of worthy sages. Thus...
It may be consumed later.

Regarding the passage from "In the Sūtra of the Śrāvakas" up to "praising its meaning": the questioner asks that a Bodhisattva should extol what is good and cease what is evil, being humble, upright, and straightforward.
If the Two Vehicles are not correct, one should directly refute them; if their goodness is worthy of being recorded, then one should do so.

Regarding the prohibition of both humble speech and praise: for what reason are these two matters not permitted? Answer: When one praises or disparages, the mind will inevitably give rise to joy or aversion.

Once joy and aversion arise, the seeds of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) fail to sprout, and pure precepts (*śīla*) sink away. For this reason, they are now forbidden. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 588, states:
"If Bodhisattvas should momentarily give rise to a mind that praises or disparages the Two Vehicles, they should..."

One should know that this constitutes a transgression of the Bodhisattva’s pure precepts. Why is this? If one praises those stages, one will develop attachment to them and thus be unable to strive for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If one disparages those stages, one will develop contempt for them, which immediately obstructs the sought-after wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Thus, there is a transgression regarding the Bodhisattva precepts; for this reason, the Bodhisattva, with respect to these two—
Regarding the stages of the vehicle (*yāna-bhūmi*), one should neither praise nor disparage them; this case is likewise so. Thus, there is truly no error.
As for the scriptural analogy of the powerful Cakravartin King and so forth: there are four types of Cakravartin Kings whose respective domains differ, as explained in detail in the *Śāstra*.
What is the meaning of their "Seven Jewels" and their "virtuous transformation"? Answer: The third fascicle of the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra Sūtra*.
It is said: A Wheel-Turning Sage King is fully endowed with the seven treasures: first, the treasure of the queen; second, the treasure of the mani-jewel;
third, the treasure of the wheel; fourth, the treasure of the elephant; fifth, the treasure of the horse; sixth, the treasure of the minister; and seventh, the treasure of the master of the treasury.
As for his transformative virtue, he is fully possessed of those seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King and traverses the entire earth without any adversaries and without any enemies or thorns.
Free from all afflictions and free from weapons and staves, relying upon the True Dharma, impartial and without bias, he comforts and subdues [his enemies] and rules over the four continents;
because he has attained sovereignty, his issued commands meet with no opposition. By means of the ten paths of wholesome action...
He transforms the four continents, causing all beings to receive and uphold [the teachings], to abandon the ten unwholesome karmic paths, and to fully accomplish the ten wholesome paths;

thus he is called a Dharma King. Question: By what cause are the seven treasures produced that come to him? Answer: They are obtained by relying on the abandonment of the unwholesome karmic paths of a hateful mind.
If this is so, why does the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) state that the "superior grade of the ten wholesome [paths] results in an iron wheel"?
"O King and others," they replied, "that sūtra states this in full detail. This [present account] relies on what is most prominent; therefore, there is no fault. Question:

Regarding the manifestation of the seven treasures, these should originally belong to a noble wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). What specific virtues do they each possess? First, as for the virtues of the monarch’s consort, regarding her body, speech, and so forth—
She emanated the fragrance of priceless *candana* sandalwood and *utpala* lotuses. Her body was soft and warm; in cold weather it could provide warmth, and in hot weather it could provide coolness.
When the king beheld his wife, she was free from all fatigue, hunger, thirst, and distress, and experienced the most supreme and boundless bliss.
Furthermore, she possessed five virtues: first, she was mindful and never contravened the king’s wishes; second, she was able to give birth...
First, he is endowed with a thousand sons. Second, his nature is naturally noble and dignified. Third, he is able to cause his dwelling place to be fully provided with all necessities of life.
Fourth, when the king and his consorts enjoy sensual pleasures, they do not give rise to jealousy, malice, or ill will.
Fifth, the jewel possesses eight kinds of virtues: first, it emits great, brilliant light in the darkness of night.

Like the full moon in autumn, its radiance can illuminate a hundred *yojanas*. During the summer, when sentient beings suffer from the heat, it emits light that touches their bodies, providing coolness.

When the two kings travel through a wilderness devoid of water and sentient beings are afflicted by hunger and thirst, the jewel emits water endowed with the eight flavors and all virtues, satisfying their hunger and thirst. Whatever the three kings require—all [is provided].
All emerge from the maṇi-jewel. It has four sides with eight facets on each. From within every facet, various kinds of light radiate forth.
Fifth, wherever it is located, it can cause all sentient beings within a hundred yojanas to be free from the suffering of illness and to constantly attain a concentrated mind.

1. Whatever wholesome karma they perform shall never go to waste. 2. Within their sphere of influence, no malevolent nāgas shall be able to release poisonous vapors, hail, fierce winds, or torrential rains to harm sentient beings.
3. All mountains, rivers, ravines, valleys, and gullies whose springs have run dry shall be caused to flow once more;
forests, trees, grasses, and shrubs that have withered for lack of flowers and fruit shall be made to flourish again; and the waters of the ponds—
The Flower Forest is fully endowed with all things. In the eight locations where it resides, the people suffer no epidemics or poisons, nor do they die untimely deaths.
As for the animals—such as tigers and wolves—they do not give rise to harmful intentions toward one another.
The Wheel Treasure possesses five qualities: first, the substance of the Wheel Treasure is pure Jambūnada gold, complete with a thousand spokes, and broad...
1. It illuminates the world for five *yojanas*, appearing like a second sun. 2. It flies through the sky, moving without obstruction;

whereas a single sun can travel eight thousand *yojanas* in one day, this wheel travels according to the king’s mental intention—namely, that of the Four Heavenly Kings—as they traverse the four continents.
It flies through the sky and proceeds before them wherever the king directs his thoughts, relying upon the power of that wheel. 4. [The fourth point: Relying on the power of that wheel... (as above).
The military forces—elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and all others—will all fly up and depart.
Among the four states, there is none that will not submit to the Wheel-Turning King; if the King thinks of them, that wheel-treasure will fly to wherever he intends and cause them all to be subdued.
The power of the five wheel-treasures is without rival; all minor kings who see them will submit. As for the elephants...
As for the Jewel of the Elephant: that Great Elephant-Jewel is like a noble horse—tamed, gentle, and obedient to its master’s will.
It subdues enemy kingdoms and dwells in the sevenfold friendliness. That elephant is useful in three places: namely, in the sky, in water, and on land.
That elephant can travel with great speed; in a single day, it circles Jambudvīpa three times, and the Wheel-Turning King mounts it.
The elephant. The elephant is of one mind with the king; wherever the king directs his thoughts, it immediately departs. Its gait is level and upright, like that of a king of swans;
neither too fast nor too slow, neither crooked nor perverse. When moving among ordinary people, it does not cause them alarm or fear.
Yet when the time for battle arrives, it can manifest an appearance of extreme ferocity and harm, such that no one may approach it. As for the virtue of the horse-treasure, its color is white as...

His body is marked with the patterns of a celestial wheel like the *kumuda* flower; it is neither too small nor too large, neither too tall nor too short, and his physical form is perfectly proportioned.
His mind is supple and gentle, and he is well-able to discipline himself. Like the royal horse of the Lord Śakra at the Pāra River, he goes and stays according to his will.
Three times each day he traverses Jambudvīpa without showing any sign of fatigue. This is the Jewel of the Great Minister.
As for "Virtue" (Guṇa): he administers the state on behalf of the king exactly according to the king's mind. He is concerned for the nation and forgets his own person;
he does not pursue private affairs, but cherishes and protects the common people as if tending to plants and trees. Whatever the king intends, it is accomplished immediately upon his thought.

He is unimpeded and unattached, practicing the Right Path and remaining free from what is contrary to the Dharma. As for the "Treasury-Manager with Jewel-like Virtues": that Treasury-Manager possesses great merit. First...

Regarding all mountains, deep ravines, secluded valleys, vast wildernesses, marshes, hills, mounds, pits, hollows, and uneven places, he is able to fill them completely with all manner of precious gems, such as the vajra-jewel and the indra-nīla jewel;
yet these jewels are never exhausted. How much more so for gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, which are not even counted among them? Such is that Lord of the Treasury.
[The Buddha] said: "His mind is always joyful and free from the marks of flattery or crookedness. Question: Among the seven treasures, how many are sentient and how many are non-sentient? Answer:

The two treasures of the jewel-wheel and the precious pearl are non-sentient phenomena; the remaining five are sentient. Question: What are the characteristics of these seven treasures when they are manifested?"

Answer: According to the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama* (the eleventh of the *Madhyama-āgama*), it is said that when the King possessed the seven treasures and appeared in mid-air, there was a white elephant king who, in a mere moment, traveled across the four seas.

When the King ascended the western tower and looked toward the east, he saw a dark-blue horse king coming through the air. When the King ascended the eastern tower and looked toward the west, he saw [the same].
There was a divine pearl, one foot six inches in length, possessing eight facets and the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.
It came through the air and hung from the top of a banner, illuminating an area of twelve yojanas.

When the king ascended the eastern tower and looked toward the east, he saw a Kṣatriya maiden named Harṣa-hāriṇī (Captivator of the Heart), peerless in her beauty, who had come through the air. [When] the king ascended the northern tower and looked toward the north...
He saw him. A treasurer named Dhanadhvaja came through the air. The King ascended the southern tower and, looking toward the south, saw a great general named Abhaya coming through the air.
[The text] asks why the description of the horse’s color and the pearl’s luster differs from that in the previous scripture;
how can they be so different? It answers: because the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, what is seen and heard differs accordingly; thus, there is no error.
The remaining [jewels] are to be explained according to this principle. Question: What is the origin of the seven jewels? Answer:
According to the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, there is a garuḍa bird named Gāruḍarāja (in its original Sanskrit pronunciation). After his life has ended, fire arises and consumes him;
everything else is reduced to ashes, yet only his heart remains. The Nanda Dragon King takes this bird’s heart and makes it into a bright pearl for the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

It is obtained; it is called the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Other sūtras do not mention this. Furthermore, the traditional commentary explains: "The two treasures, the wheel and the jewel, belong to Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
[The wheel] descends to correspond with the Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*). As for the elephant, he is the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita, one of the five hundred sons."
The horse is also the dragon-horse of the Heavenly Emperor. The elephant, the woman, and the minister—these three—are likewise all subjects and attendants of the Heavenly Emperor.

As for the latter five treasures, they descend to Jambudvīpa to correspond with the appearance of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). When the transformation of the Wheel-Turning King ceases, they return to have no dwelling place in heaven.
The other two [beings] should descend only from among the devas. Question: The *Nirgrantha-sūtra* states that they are like those given by King Śakra;

does this not constitute a contradiction? Answer: The various teachings differ according to the specific capacities of their audiences; thus, there is no fault. Question: What are the virtues of the king’s thousand sons? Answer:
According to the *Nirgrantha-sūtra*, the thousand sons of a wheel-turning monarch have massive and robust bodies and are courageous and fierce.
Magnificent and heroic, he subdues the world and accords with the king’s commands; he is able to protect the Great Dharma and accords with the practice of the Dharma.
His mind is capable of compassion for all sentient beings, and he extensively synthesizes the various teachings as well as the meanings of other gateways, as detailed in the respective chapters.

Regarding the three types of māras mentioned in the commentary: both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) [māras] each have three kinds; thus, they are categorized into three classes.
Since the sūtra mentions only "three māras," the commentary refers to them as "three. Because the *devaputra-māra* is explained separately, the word "and" (*bing*) is used.

The commentary on the "six constant abidings" (*ṣaḍ-āryavaṃśa*) states that an Arhat dwells amidst the six sense objects without experiencing joy or sorrow. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 50, says:
"It refers to the Arhat whose outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted; he constantly and uninterruptedly dwells for the most part in the six constant abidings.
That is to say, having seen a form with the eye, he is neither joyful nor sorrowful, but dwells in sublime equanimity (*upekṣā*), with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension."
In this way, having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, and cognized mental objects with the mind,
one is neither glad nor sad, but dwells in sublime equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

Regarding the passage "the noble ones of the two vehicles [attain] partial destruction up to total destruction": those still in training (*śaikṣa*) achieve partial destruction, while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) achieve total destruction.

Because the followers of the two vehicles cannot spontaneously and ultimately eliminate the celestial Māras, only three are mentioned here; as for the mention of four below, it refers to the following.
Regarding its preparatory practices (*prayoga*) and its provisional teaching:

as for the commentary’s refutation of the sequence of the destruction of Māra, and the fact that the commentary is also titled *The Lotus*, this explains away an anticipated objection. The objection states:

"If the Two Vehicles destroy the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence and are granted the *Dharmapada* (Lotus), why are Bodhisattvas—who destroy the *pariṇāmika* (transformative) existence—not granted the *Dharmapada*? Therefore, it is now said: the *Immeasurable Sūtra* is itself the *Dharma*.

Regarding the passage in the *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra) that says, "As if in a dream," etc.: Question: Since external objects fundamentally do not exist, by what cause does a dream arise? Answer:

Through the power of other conditions (*pratyaya*), although no real object exists, the dreaming mind can arise. Thus, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are five kinds of dreams."
First, when the heat-element is predominant, one frequently dreams of fire, seeing yellow and red. Second, when the cold-element is predominant, one frequently sees water and white.
Third, when the wind-element is predominant, one frequently sees flying and black. Fourth, because of the frequent contemplation and recollection of things heard and seen.
Thus, dreams are seen. Dreams and the five destinies are intended to make one know future events; what is clarified in the present sutra is precisely the fifth [category].
Even if Buddhas or Bodhisattvas add to them to induce dreams, these are likewise subsumed under the fifth, as they are of a similar nature.

Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattvas and others who have come from other lands" in the *Cūḍā-paṭala* (Chapter on the Emergence): it is asked when these bodhisattvas arrived, as there is no textual evidence clarifying this in either the preceding or following sections of the sūtra.
The answer is that there is a certain interpretation: since the *Stūpa-paṭala* (Chapter on the Stūpas) commands those who uphold the sūtra, all the bodhisattvas... [text continues].

"Sa. This refers to those who, having been summoned, intended to uphold [the Dharma] upon reaching this stage. Furthermore, another interpretation is that these are the bodhisattvas from the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings);

because the scribe highlights their excellence, they are not listed or praised at the beginning of the sutra. Alternatively, they may be the retinue from which the two sages, Gadgadasvara and Samantabhadra, departed. One might ask:

since Gadgadasvara and the others only arrive after the "Emergence" chapter (*Dharanirutsarga-parivarta*), how can there be eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sands) [of bodhisattvas] among them? It is they.

[Question: Is this not in vain? [Answer: In truth, it is because the Bodhisattvas such as Gadgadasvara emerged and arrived earlier, yet the compilers of the sutra arranged their sequence and placed them later.

If it were not so, what would have been the purpose of Gadgadasvara and the others coming here after the essential intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* had already been expounded? For this reason, we know that they had already [arrived] prior to the emergence.
[The Buddha] arrived. The discussion states: First, [the Buddha] refuted the errors of Śāriputra; second, the latter two [cases] were not as [they appeared]. Reflect on this.

Regarding the passage where the Sūtra says, "Stop, Subhūti, you do not need these people," the question is: Even if they were upholding the Sūtra, why would it be harmful to not permit them? The answer is that there is a specific meaning:
Bodhisattvas from other directions are not those transformed by Śākyamuni, and thus they cannot manifest the lifespan of Śākyamuni. For this reason, [Subhūti] was told to stop.
[He] permitted it. The bodhisattvas of this land were transformed by Śākyamuni; because this serves to manifest the lifespan of Śākyamuni, he therefore granted permission.
The commentary (*shu*) explains this as per the text. The discussion states: Although the wording differs from the original commentary’s explanation, the underlying intent is similar.

Question: The commentary says, "In order to manifest the Buddha’s transformative power (*nenghua gongneng*). Could it be that one desires to boast of one's own virtues while merely obstructing others? Answer: If...
He does not manifest his own merit so that no doubts may arise. Since there are no doubts, for what purpose would he manifest the Buddha’s lifespan as long and far-reaching?
This is done to still the views of others, not out of a desire for self-display.
Regarding those who dwell in the space of this realm: A question is raised that since it is called "space," it must be beneath the Golden Wheel;

how, then, can it be included within this realm? The answer is: the sphere of influence (*pradeśa*) of this realm is also included within this realm. It is like the sphere of influence established when demarcating a boundary (*sīmā*) according to the Vinaya;
though it is divided by distance, whether far or near, it still belongs to the proximate realm.
Regarding the phrase "having little illness and little affliction": one may ask, what is the distinction between illness and affliction that they are both inquired about?
The answer is that body and mind are different. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In accordance with worldly convention, there are two kinds of inquiries:
first, an inquiry concerning the mind, called 'little affliction'; second, an inquiry concerning the body, called 'little illness.'"

The Sūtra states: "Not recognizing even a single person. [The questioner asks: Maitreya is to attain the wondrous enlightenment of a Buddha; since his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have long since been eliminated, why is it that this assembly does not recognize him?
[The answer: Based on the principle of ultimate reality (*tattva*), there is no duality of self and other.

Since the characteristics of self and other do not exist, one cannot say, "I recognize him. Alternatively, all phenomena transcend verbal expression and cannot yet be described in terms of recognition or non-recognition.
"Recognize. Alternatively, it is based on the manifestation of signs. Thus, the sutra below states: "Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds may not believe or accept [this].

This clarifies that those who have already believed and known also include those who recognize. One interpretation holds that the Bodhisattvas who emerge [from the earth] are for the purpose of revealing the characteristics of the Dharma-body;

since the Dharma-body is not something realized by the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that "not a single person was recognized. The commentary says: the intent is to clarify that they did not recognize the one capable of revealing [the Dharma-body].

People do not understand the essence of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) that is revealed, nor do they recognize the Dharma-body; how, then, could this be related to the matter of the Bodhisattva’s miraculous emergence?
As for the statement in the Commentary that "from this place at Gayā to this city is likewise," it may be that the name Gayā already existed prior to [the Buddha's arrival].

He has been here for a long time; he attained enlightenment through transformation-birth. To dispel Maitreya’s doubt, it is said that in this present age he attained enlightenment and transformed beings while residing in the city of Gayā.
Therefore, [Maitreya] folded his hands and questioned him.
The Commentary states that the Buddha’s words are not empty and are free from the four errors. To speak falsely regarding the four matters is called having the four errors;

therefore, Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "By means of the Tathāgata’s true wisdom, he does not falsely speak of the matters concerning the prediction of Buddhahood for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or those of the Small and Great Vehicles.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, and speaks without deviation."

The four are explained in their respective order: because he teaches the dharmas of the Small Vehicle, such as the Truth of Suffering, as being exclusively truths, it is called "not falsely teaching the Small.
Because he teaches the Mahāyāna as the *tathatā* (suchness) of the selflessness of phenomena, it is called "not falsely teaching the Great.

Because he bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon all [beings] of the past, future, and present, it is called "not falsely teaching predictions. Question: For what reason does the Tathāgata possess...
Regarding these four phrases, according to the commentary by the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha:

Among those in the world who seek fame and profit, there are those who have not realized the qualities of a superior person (*uttarapudgala-dharma*) yet claim to have realized them. The Buddha speaks "true words" because he differs from such people.

Furthermore, there are those with lustful desires who are full of arrogance and delusion; having once attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they know for themselves that they have lost them. When someone comes to question them, they simply say:

First, one attains this state by distancing oneself from such a mind and speaking words of truth. Furthermore, there are those who have attained mundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through cultivation;
their minds temporarily do not arise, resembling cessation (*nirvāṇa*), and they claim to others, "I have realized nirvāṇa.
To eliminate this error, [the Buddha] spoke these words of reality. For ordinary beings cling to things such as a city of Gandharvas exactly as they appear before them.
That which is called "different from suchness" is not the case for the Buddhas; therefore, they speak words that are not different from suchness.

What ordinary beings grasp at—such as cities and so forth being non-cities and so forth—is called "different. That which is realized by the Tathāgata is not falsely existent and possesses a non-deceptive nature;

thus, it is called "not different from suchness. Furthermore, with respect to the Tathāgata’s realization of the principle of the Four Noble Truths, he speaks of the Four Noble Truths without error or delusion.
These correspond respectively to the "True Speaker" and so forth.

In the commentary on the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, from the phrase "those of the first vehicle" up to "those with overweening pride," it says: "those who do not accumulate merit" refers to those who do not accumulate the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Regarding the First Vehicle, they do not accumulate roots of goodness; thus it is said they do not 'take' [it].

This explains that for such individuals, this constitutes a perversion, which is the reason for their overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Because they have failed to accumulate them at both the former and present times, it is called "not accumulating."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Furthermore, one eliminates the eight obstacles": Question: What are the characteristics of the remedial practices (*pratipakṣa*)?
How can they be known? Answer: According to the *Vyūha-śāstra* (The Ornament Sutra), to speak briefly: first, eliminating the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha.

This refers to sentient beings who, upon seeing the Tathāgata—first born in a royal palace and then attaining Buddhahood under the Bodhi tree—perceive his time on the path as being too recent, and thus doubt his possession of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). To remedy this, they give rise to thoughts of contempt. [The following remedies are applied] to counteract this.
Regarding this person: therefore, the Mahāyāna sūtras state that the Buddha Vipaśyin of the past was none other than my own self;

it is with reference to the perspective of equality that such a statement is made. Second, as for those who create obstacles through minor dharmas: this refers to sentient beings who, regarding the scriptures of Śākya, grasp only at the superficial phrasing and shallow meanings.
It is not that they do not understand them, yet they consequently develop a sense of contempt for the Buddha’s teachings, treating them as trivial and disparaging them. For...

To counteract this, the Mahāyāna teaches that one must cultivate the Mahāyāna practices in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers before one can give rise to understanding.
What is called "giving rise to understanding" refers to the arising of realized understanding (*adhigama*). This statement is made according to a specific interpretive intent.

Third, regarding the removal of the obstacle of laziness: it refers to those sentient beings who, although they have already generated the resolve [for awakening], feel that the practice is difficult to perform and thus give rise to indolence.

Laziness: for those who are unwilling to advance in their practice, the Mahāyāna teaches that by generating a sense of peace and joy, and by reciting the name of the Buddha Vimalacandraprabha, one will certainly attain [the goal].
This statement was made with the intention of referring to a future time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*). Fourth, regarding the removal of obstacles such as meager merit:
this refers to sentient beings who, having already cultivated a small amount of practice, conceive the notion of attainment and thus give rise to a sense of complacency.

Furthermore, they do not proceed further. To treat such individuals, within the Mahāyāna, one may either praise or disparage a single root of virtue, hoping that sentient beings will not cling to a single dharma and develop a mind of complacency, but rather cultivate all virtues extensively according to their underlying intention.
Therefore, this statement was made. Fifth, regarding the removal of the obstacle of greedy conduct:
there are sentient beings who, being attached to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of this defiled land, do not cultivate sublime and wondrous causes.

To remedy this attachment, the Mahāyāna teaches that the Buddha-fields possess the most exquisite and blissful qualities, thereby encouraging them to seek and aspire toward them. Sixth, regarding the removal of the obstacle of prideful conduct: there are sentient beings...
Relying on their own nobility, they see that the Buddha dwells in an impure land, that his life-span is short, and that his various circumstances are inferior; thus, they treat him with contempt.

To remedy this fault, the Mahāyāna teaches that [the Buddha’s] body and life-span are long, his realm is magnificent and beautiful, and all his virtues are perfectly luminous, such that nothing is to be disparaged.
Seventh, regarding the removal of the obstacle of regretful conduct: it refers to sentient beings who slight the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and constantly...
One gives rise to regret; yet this regret serves as a basis for cultivating wholesome deeds and honoring such matters.

Since it obstructs the cultivation of superior goodness, the Mahāyāna teaches that even if one commits acts harmful to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one may still be reborn in the higher realms, let alone when cultivating wholesome deeds. This is intended to encourage the cultivation of superior goodness.

The eighth [point] removes the obstacle of indeterminate factors; this may be understood from the commentary (*śāstra*). Question: Having removed the first four obstacles and seen the four intentions (*abhiprāya*), how can it be said that these are the objects to be countered by the "secret" (*saṃdhi*) as an antidote?
Answer: When the intentions are categorized separately, they are subsumed only within the third of the four secrets; thus, there is a difference in terms of expansion and contraction.

If that is so, what is the distinction between the intention and the secret? Answer: There are two explanations. First: [...]* *Note: The bracketed portion indicates the ellipsis where the original text was truncated.*
It is said: "Intention" (*ābhiprāyika*) refers to the intention of the speaker; "secret" (*guhya*) refers to the difficulty of understanding what has been spoken. Second, it is said:
this means that the transformer must first, within the remote preliminary stage, observe the faculties of those to be transformed to determine which dharma is appropriate for them.

Because he gathers [beings] under his care, it is called "intention" (*abhiprāya*). Later, when he personally confronts those with capacity through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), teaching the Dharma to bring about awakening, it is called "secret" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
This is truly because the Tathāgata’s intentions are skillful and possess such expedient means; thus, it is based on the meaning of secrecy.

Because one speaks what is beneficial and appropriate for those faculties, all that is established as teaching is termed "esoteric" (*guhyaka*). The underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) is that which speaks, while the esoteric [teaching] is that which is spoken.
Observing the nature of the faculties from afar and establishing skillful means (*upāya*) from near at hand, one relies on the meaning of the esoteric to approach the esoteric teaching;

thus, there is a distinction between these two. The commentary states: Although they differ in being extensive or concise, their general intent is no different. Question: The sub-commentary lists eight [points].
Obstruction. Why is the second [explanation] regarding the aspects of adornment and so forth not the same? One should answer that the commentary contains a scribal error;

or, the intention of the commentary may be that since the Tathāgata Śrī-vipaśyin is none other than one's own body, all dharmas he clarifies are likewise secret and wondrous—unlike the first interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "the secret of transformation (*pariṇāma*)": within the words that express and the meanings they signify, the meaning is revealed through transformation; this constitutes the sense of "secret.

Furthermore, because the words that transform the expression to reveal the clear meaning undergo a change, they are designated as "secret. The *Asvabhāva-śāstra* states: "That is to say, regarding the words and their meanings, there is a transformation of distinctions.
As for the statement "speech and cognition are not solid," it means they are pliant and free from distraction.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is called "not firm" (*a-dṛḍha*). Because one can give rise to firm wisdom (*dṛḍha-prajñā*) within this concentration, it is said to be "firm.

Because that [wisdom] causes the mind to be rigid and unrestrained amidst distraction, it is termed "firm. Since concentration is different from that, it is named "not firm. Question: The name "not firm" refers directly to concentration itself;
why then is it called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) and further designated as "secret" (*guhya*)? Answer: The name "not firm" applies to both.
Regarding "fixed" (*sthira*) and "scattered" (*vikṣipta*): the meaning of "scattered" is manifest, while the meaning of "fixed" is hidden. Why is this so?
It is because that which is scattered flows toward objects without focusing exclusively on one; this is commonly known by the world, and is therefore called "manifest.

If, however, that concentrated mind focuses exclusively on a single object, the sense of its lack of stability is subtle; only those who skillfully understand the Dharma know that concentration possesses the quality of being pliant yet lacks the sense of stability.
It is not commonly known by the world; therefore, it is called "secret. Because those manifest words express this hidden meaning, it is called "transformation.
According to the principle, both concentration and distraction are termed "firm" or "unfirm. If one truly and exclusively maintains a single object, [it is firm].

That which is called "firm" (*sthira*) is precisely concentration (*samādhi*). If one is distracted, flowing, and agitated, causing the mind to be rigid and flighty, that which is called "firm" is actually distraction (*vikṣepa*).
If one's nature is pliant and supple, yet is called "not firm," this refers to being in a state of concentration that cannot focus on its object;
because it is not authentic, it is called "not firm," which is to say it is distraction. Therefore, the *Abhidharma* states: "Firmness is of two kinds."
Meaning: First, reality; second, distraction. Because of this distraction, it causes the mind to become rigid and unruly;

therefore, it is also called "firm. The *Treatise on the Absence of Nature* (*Wuxing lun*) states: "Rigidity and dissipation are termed 'firm. Because it is not [characterized by] this firmness, it is termed 'not firm,' which is precisely pliancy and concentration free from distraction.
Since the two treatises provide complementary explanations, we know that both concentration and distraction possess both firmness and non-firmness. This is false [discrimination].
To grasp at the conditioned as permanent, blissful, self, and pure is called "perversion.

If a person, within this perversion, understands and realizes that those [qualities of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity do not exist, it is called "abiding well. For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they practice difficult deeds with diligence over a long period;
being driven by the exhaustion of such toil, they are said to be "afflicted by afflictions" due to the preceding three phrases.
Practicing without ceasing, one attains the meaning of the *tri-sambodhi* (threefold perfect awakening) of all Buddhas;

this is called the supreme. There is a further sense: awakening to what is not firm as being firm refers to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Abiding well within the inversions refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Being thoroughly afflicted by afflictions refers to the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Because of these right efforts, one undergoes various hardships and sufferings for the sake of all sentient beings; therefore, diligence [is essential].
"Progressing" is named "extreme affliction. This is established based on reflection; the remainder is the same as before.

The commentary states that both the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are called "born" because they manifest repeatedly according to what is appropriate for sentient beings, and thus receive the name "birth-body" (*janmakāya*).
Commentary: Regarding the passage from "The Response Body is not a Transformation-Born [Body]" to "One Response Body," the question is:

On what basis is it known that persons who have attained the four roots of goodness see a single Response Buddha within the great trichiliocosm? The answer is: Although there is no explicit textual evidence, according to reasoning, this must certainly be the case.

For example, just as the Enjoyment Bodies for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) differ individually according to the distinct stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), so too should they differ according to the stages of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Since they are not identical, why is it that the bodies of the Buddhas are not different? Based on these dimensions, there would also be distinctions in size. Question:

Since there are forty distinct mental states (*citta*) in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the bodies of the Buddhas should likewise not be of a single kind. Answer: This refers to the distinction between the major stages;
it does not mean that the bodies must differ based on the variations within each minor sub-stage. Thus, the forty [states] are collectively designated as the "stage of equipment."
Therefore, regarding the commentary’s statement from "The ten Buddhas" to "subsumed under the three bodies as appropriate," the explanation is as follows:

The manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) attaining enlightenment beneath the tree is called "manifesting perfect awakening. To transform all sentient beings through the power of vows and supernatural penetrations is called "the great vow. [100]

The cultivation of karma over kalpas that brings about the physical body in a royal palace as a retribution for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) is called "maturation of karma" (*karma-vipāka*). The images of threads, silk, and so forth are called "sustaining" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The essential nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is called the "Dharma-realm Buddha" (*dharmadhātu-buddha*). The eighth [consciousness], which is untainted (*anāsrava*), is called the "Mind-Buddha.

The body of great meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called the "Concentration-Buddha. The Body of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*) is formed from its original lineage after three kalpas of cultivation; this is called...

The Buddha of Essential Nature (svabhāva-buddha). According to the different inclinations of those on the stages, he manifests different bodies; this is called the Buddha of Accordance with Inclination (yathābhiprāya-buddha). The first five are transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya);

because they abide and maintain [the teachings] like transformations, they are subsumed under "transformation. The sixth is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). The latter four are enjoyment bodies (saṃbhogakāya).
Alternatively, the first five are transformation bodies, the next two are the Dharma-body, and the last three are enjoyment bodies. Or, the first, second, fourth, and... [text fragment].
Five: four are transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). The sixth, seventh, ninth, and third are the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). The ninth, the Buddha-ground, is called the "Buddha of Original Nature.
Because the dharma body is the basis and its meaning is manifest, [it is designated thus]. The third, eighth, and thirteenth are the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

It is called the "Vipāka Buddha" because it enjoys the retribution of causes; the name and its meaning correspond. The transformation body acts as the response to others, serving as karmic retribution; however, this principle is not clearly explained.
[End of] commentary. Furthermore, following the increase of characteristics, it is divided into three explanations.

Regarding the passage in the *Lengqie jing shu* (Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra) concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), the first fascicle of the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* states:

"The Dharma-Buddha is that which is apart from the self-nature of the mind. This explains the Dharma taught by the Dharma-Buddha as being apart from the deluded mind and the characteristics of self-nature.
"Dharma" refers to the state of being free from the intrinsic characteristics of both the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived. Furthermore, it is said:

"The establishment of the agent of giving is based on the realm that is the object of the noble self-realization. Regarding the explanation of "self-realization," it means the principle realized by the wisdom of one's own awakening, which is termed the "object of perception."
He establishes the Dharma realized through self-awakening as the Dharma taught by the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*). To speak of "bestowing" and "acting" is precisely to explain this.
By citing the one who realizes it, he reveals the reason why the Dharma-Buddha teaches the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said that the Dharma-Buddha is free from objective referents (*ālambana*).
This is explained as being free from all deluded thoughts and the mind that clings to objects. It is further stated that such clinging to objects is entirely absent.

Regarding "the extinction of the characteristics of the measures of the sense-faculties produced": this explains that because one is free from the mind that grasps at objects (*ālambana*), all false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*)—including the measures of the various sense-faculties and their corresponding characteristics—are entirely extinguished.
Question: As for the teachings of the Dharma, which rely on provisional words, names, and so forth, if one is already free from grasping at objects, [how can these exist?]
All characteristics are quiescent; how, then, can they be said to be "taught"? The answer is: the fundamental intent of teaching the Dharma is to cause others to give rise to understanding.
Taking the *dharmakāya* as the object, it causes the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of bodhisattvas and others to arise; therefore, it is called "teaching. Thus, a sutra says:
"The establishment and application of the objects of perception realized by the self-awakened sages. It further says: "The *dharmakāya* Buddha teaches all dharmas. This is the explanation.

It is the recompense Buddha (*vipākabuddha*). Arising from the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is called the Dharma-reliant Buddha (*dharmāśrayabuddha*), which is precisely the Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).

It is not the Enjoyment for Self (*ātmasaṃbhogakāya*), because the Body of Enjoyment for Self does not preach the Dharma. Some say that the Dharma-reliant Buddha is the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*);

this interpretation is incorrect, because the characteristics of the Transformation Buddha are explained later in the text. Furthermore, it says: "entering into the specific and general characteristics."

Explanation: The dharmas such as the five aggregates each have their own specific names; these are called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Characteristics such as suffering and impermanence pervade all dharmas and are thus called "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṹ�aṇa*).

Question: What dharmas do they pervade? Answer: Although these four are called "common," there are differences in the breadth and narrowness of what they pervade. Suffering is the common characteristic of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas, because all that is contaminated is suffering.
Impermanence is the common characteristic of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas; for all things that are produced [by causes] are devoid of permanence.
Because they are constant, emptiness and selflessness are the two common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Since all phenomena are devoid of both self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 413, states: "Suffering is the common characteristic of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena;
impermanence is the common characteristic of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena; emptiness and selflessness are the common characteristics of all phenomena."

Question: For what reason are the five aggregates called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Answer: Because their characteristics do not interpenetrate, they are called specific characteristics.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 413, states: "Transformation and resistance are the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*). Experience is the specific characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*). Grasping signs is the specific characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Volitional activity is the specific characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*). Discernment is the specific characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*). [The following is] common to all.

To form a single body is therefore called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). This is not so; there is no textual basis for such a restricted meaning. Furthermore, it is said that "entering" (*praveśa*) means "understanding" (*avabodha*);

one understands both the particular and common characteristics as being manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya*). Alternatively, "entering" means "subsuming" (*saṃgraha*). As stated previously: "The Dharma relies on the Buddha’s teaching of all dharmas.
All these dharmas are subsumed within those [characteristics], namely, the particular and common characteristics. Or, "entering" means "understanding," which causes [the practitioner] to...
The understanding of the particular and universal characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) by those beings who are to be converted is called "entering into the particular and universal.

This is not designated as "understanding" with reference to the Buddha’s body, because the Buddha’s understanding is already perfectly established and does not depend on verbal explanation. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the cause which is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) manifested from one's own mind":

"manifested" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to manifestation through active functioning (*pravṛtti*). "Habitual tendency" refers to seeds (*bīja*). These particular and universal characteristics are manifestations of one's own mind; they perfume [the mind] to form seeds.
This very manifestation serves as the causal seed; it is called the cause of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, it is said:

"Just as a master illusionist, relying on grass, wood, tiles, and stones, produces various illusions, manifesting the diverse forms and colors of all sentient beings and giving rise to various false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*)," this is explained by way of analogy for sentient beings who, relying on the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), give rise to various false conceptualizations. It further states: "Those various false..."

Regarding "conception" (*saṃjñā*): it likewise lacks reality. Just as the phenomena conjured by a magician have no actual substance, so too the false conceptions (*vikalpa*) that arise based on dependently originated phenomena lack reality.
However, while the cited passage from the commentary takes up the general meaning, though the wording differs, the intent is the same.
The three types of Buddhas represent distinctions of coarseness and subtlety. Question: Regarding the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) teaching the six...

Regarding the dharmas such as the perfections (pāramitās): why are they called "coarse"? Answer: Although one speaks of the six perfections, one does not say they are conditioned (saṃskṛta); rather, they are all like illusions and transformations.
For this reason, they are called coarse.
Regarding the passage "such as the rishi Sarvajñāprabha and others," according to the *Sarvajñāprabha-rṣi-maitrīcitta-sūtra*, the matter is explained in detail;

here it is stated briefly. In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a world named Supuṣpita, where the Buddha was named Maitreya, who constantly [taught] the four immeasurables through a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
He taught and transformed sentient beings. The name of the sutra is *The Great Ocean Cloud of Compassion and the Light of Samādhi*.

Those who hear it will surely transcend the heavy sins of ten billion kalpas and attain Buddhahood without doubt. At that time, there was a great Brahmin named Sarvajñāprabha, skilled in the sixty-four arts.
Upon hearing that sutra from the Buddha, he immediately gave rise to objections; yet, unable to subdue [the Buddha], he then conceived faith and made this vow:

By upholding that sutra, he will certainly attain Buddhahood, named Maitreya. Having left his home to enter the mountains, he remained there for eight thousand years, begging for food and reciting the sutras.
At that time, he encountered a year of famine and was unable to obtain alms for seven days.
Then, within the forest, there were five hundred white rabbits; one pair, a mother and her offspring, seeing that the seer had no food, spoke these words regarding the Dharma:
