"The mountain is about to collapse; the Dharma-sea is about to run dry. For the sake of the Dharma, I now disregard my own life and body to make an offering to the Dharma Master.
I cast myself into the fire to serve as his meal, thereby saving the life of the Immortal. Once the meat was cooked, the various deities addressed the Immortal, saying:
"The King of Hares and his mother have cast themselves into the fire for the sake of making an offering; their meat is now ready."
"You may take this food. Upon hearing this, the rishi was overcome with grief and could not respond. After a long time, he spoke in verse:

"Better to burn one's own body and destroy one's eyes than to bear to kill and eat living beings. In the *Maitrī-bhāvanā-sūtra* taught by all Buddhas, it is said that a practitioner of loving-kindness would rather break through their marrow and extract their brains than bear to eat the flesh of living beings," as the Buddha has taught.
Regarding those who eat meat: this person’s practice of loving-kindness was not yet fulfilled. He further made a vow, saying: "In life after life, may I never give rise to the thought of killing;
may I never eat meat until I attain Buddhahood. Having established this precept against eating meat, he spoke these words and threw himself into the fire, perishing together with the rabbit.
Because of this, even after he attained Buddhahood, the Bodhisattva was still named Maitreya.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that Amitābha was once the Bhikṣu Dharmākara and so forth:
according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, after the appearance of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there appeared further immeasurable Buddhas in succession. The last of these Buddhas was named Lokeśvararāja.
At that time, there was a king who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, felt great joy in his heart and immediately resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment.

With a sincere resolve for the True Way, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship to become a śramaṇa, named Dharmākara. Possessing lofty talent and courageous wisdom, he was far superior to the world.
He went to the presence of the Buddha Vaśavartin and spoke verses to request the Dharma, saying: "I pray that the Buddha will extensively proclaim the sutras and the Dharma for me;
I shall practice it to gather a buddha-land, pure and adorned with immeasurable wondrous realms, so that I may..."
He swiftly attained perfect enlightenment in this world, uprooting the very foundation of the suffering of birth and death. Upon hearing the Dharma, Dharmākara Bodhisattva made vast and great vows.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now become a Buddha. He currently resides in the West, at a distance of ten trillion *kṣetras* from here.
That Buddha-world is named Sukhāvatī. Since his attainment of the Way, ten *kalpas* have passed."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “From this birth up to the maturation of the four sense-faculties,” it takes the body received upon first seeing a Buddha and designates it as the “first birth.
The “second birth” does not depend on seeing a Buddha; the third and fourth births likewise involve seeing one. Thus, within this very analogy, these four births exist;

In this world, the human lifespan is one hundred years. Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world; even if one were to cast forth the śarīra relics and encounter Kāśyapa Buddha, one would already have been born at the very beginning [of that era].
From then until the present Śākyamuni, how could there be only three births? If that were so, why is it that [the lifespan] alone was so long? This is truly most strange.
If it were not so, how could it be called "three births" from the time of first encountering a Buddha until the present Śākyamuni?

The answer is briefly given in two explanations. The first says: Having first encountered Kāśyapa Buddha, he was reborn in this realm; by the time he encountered Śākyamuni, many lifetimes must have elapsed.
Because the lifespan in this realm is short, if he had been born in other realms or in long-lived celestial abodes, why would it not have been more than three [lifetimes] until he met Śākyamuni?
The second says: It simply speaks from the beginning up to Śākyamuni Buddha in total.

There are three births. Why must one necessarily encounter a Buddha of this realm? If one encounters a Buddha in another realm and later arrives in this realm to again encounter Śākyamuni, these combined constitute three births;
what flaw is there in this reasoning? As for that second birth, whether it occurs in this realm or another realm, there is no loss in its being received.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "this is the fourth birth in which one encounters Maitreya Buddha": Question:

From the time Śākyamuni appeared in the world until Maitreya appears, it will be five hundred and sixty-seven million years. How can such a person encounter Maitreya after undergoing only one more birth?
If they must pass through further births, how can it be said that this is the fourth birth in which they encounter Maitreya? Answer:

From the point after three births until the meeting with Maitreya, these are collectively termed "one birth. This does not mean that after this point there is only one more birth, which would then be called the fourth birth and the meeting with Maitreya;
rather, it does not preclude the possibility that this person may undergo many more births. Question: Why are three births mentioned here?
Is it because they are spoken of in relation to the practitioner's own experience of births, whereas the "fourth birth" is not so [restricted]? Answer: Because of their sharp faculties.
The maximum limit extends to three lifetimes; therefore, it refers only to one's own [continuum]. For those of dull faculties, even at the slowest pace, it takes sixty kalpas.
Since the timing of birth is not fixed, this is stated in reference to the first three lifetimes. Birth in the subsequent lifetime when encountering Maitreya is termed the "fourth lifetime.

The commentary states: since birth is not fixed within the scriptural texts and the treatise likewise does not mention it, even if we do not rely on the number of lifetimes, its [attainment] is clarified...

As for this analogy, what fault is there? If phenomena are understood as returning to conceptual differentiation, it would provisionally give rise to an endorsement of the profound purport of the sutras.
Any objections or difficulties should be resolved as previously reconciled; how could they not be understood?
Regarding the commentary’s statement that there is "indeterminacy" and so forth: this applies not only to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), but also includes bodhisattvas.
Because of this indeterminacy, the Sūtra states that it extends even up to one hundred [kalpas].

Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva has no grasping or abandoning" in the *Vyākhyā* on the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merits": Question: While it is taught that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) sustains all remaining [beings], and by this standard it is also for the sake of Bodhisattvas, there is still the teaching of the provisional and the real regarding the vehicles (*yāna*), which involves grasping and abandoning.
How can it be said that there is no grasping or abandoning in the realization of the Path and so forth? Answer: For...
The teaching for the two vehicles is intended to cause them to relinquish their former provisional [attainments] and grasp the present reality; therefore, there are predictions and certifications.

For those who are bodhisattvas, one first causes them to grasp that greatness and then explains the provisional and the real, merely ensuring they do not regress. This is not the same as the Lesser Vehicle, and thus the two cases cannot be compared.

Regarding the phrase "non-arising is the object" (*ālambana*) and so forth: based now on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, I shall provide two brief explanations. First, the phenomenon itself is non-arising;

thus it is called the "phenomenon of non-arising. Therefore, the three hundred and seventy-sixth fascicle, as well as the fifth and sixth fascicles of the tenth volume of that sūtra, all state in unison:
"It means causing all afflictions (*kleśa*) not to arise, while subtle and wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) remains constantly uninterrupted."
To contemplate all phenomena as ultimately non-arising is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This means that the wisdom capable of severing those afflictions contemplates all that is conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*) as ultimately non-arising; this contemplating wisdom is termed "patience regarding non-arising.
Non-arising is itself the phenomenon (*dharma*); thus, "patience regarding the phenomenon of non-arising" is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. It has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because it is also called "Dharma," it is the Dharma. The afflictions severed by the two types of wisdom never arise again; this is termed "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).

Wisdom that realizes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like mirages and so forth is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*). Non-arising is itself the Dharma; thus, it is the patience regarding the non-arising Dharma.

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound), which differs from the previous [explanation]. It refers to the "dharmas that do not arise" solely by way of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Therefore, the preceding sūtra states: "By this power, even the slightest portion of evil and unwholesome dharmas cannot arise;

for this reason, it is called the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This brings all afflictions, such as the conceits of "I" and "mine," to their ultimate end.
It is tranquil. One endures it as it truly is. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like dreams, like the city of Gandharvas, and so forth. This patience is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

Because one attains this wisdom, it is termed the attainment of the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). According to another interpretation, True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) are termed "non-arising."
Because one realizes this *tathatā* (suchness) at the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is called "attaining the patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). A commentary states:
Although this principle exists, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, the meaning is not actually so. There is no fault in the fact that the sacred teachings follow many paths.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary states that it refers to the three kinds of non-arising (*trividhā-anutpatti*)," the question is: How is it known that the wisdom which takes the three as its object is called the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and does this wisdom take the three types as its objects?
The answer is: According to the third fascicle of the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi-sūtra*, it asks, "Taking what dharma as its object does one attain the patience of non-arising?

The Buddha replied, "One attains the patience of non-arising by taking the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as its object. The commentary explains: "Taking the aggregates, elements..."
[He] enters [this state]. There is no spontaneous arising; he attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). It is further said:

"He also takes the permanent, blissful, self, and pure as his object of focus (*ālambana*), and thereby attains the patience regarding dharmas (*dharma-kṣānti*). The commentary explains: By taking the permanent, blissful, and so forth as his object, afflictions and suffering do not arise, and thus he attains the patience of non-arising. It is further said:
"The object of this patience does not function in common with worldly phenomena, nor does it function in common with any phenomena whatsoever."
The commentary states: Phenomena that possess substantial existence can be said to coexist; however, the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) fundamentally lacks any essence.

For this reason, it is said not to function in conjunction with any phenomena. By taking as its object this non-existent thoroughly imagined nature, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This corresponds respectively to taking as objects the three absences of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*): the dependent (*paratantra*), the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), and the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*).

Regarding the commentary on the sixteen aspects of *nirvāṇa*, the scriptural text itself does not provide an explanation; yet, many interpretations have been offered by scholars of both ancient and modern times. I shall now briefly outline three of them.
First, it is said that these are: permanence, bliss, self, and purity; impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity. To be deluded regarding these is termed "inversion."
If one awakens to this, it is called "correct," as elucidated in *Nirvāṇa*. In its broad sense, the meaning does not exceed these eight types.
Prior to the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), if one is able to believe in and awaken to these eight types, then upon entering the Path of Vision, one immediately realizes and enters them.

There are eight distinct types for each of "seeing what has been seen" and "not yet seeing," which together constitute sixteen. Another interpretation states that there are eight inversions (*viparyāsa*) each for both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These combine to form sixteen. Reversing these sixteen inversions constitutes the sixteen meanings.

A third interpretation states that the general purport of *Nirvāṇa* clarifies that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding. Those who can understand this differ in their categories, and there are sixteen divisions.
These sixteen divisions are established as a numerical total; therefore, they are cited for the sake of enumeration, just as one *jin* (a unit of weight) consists of sixteen *liang*.

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The sixteen-fold compassion cannot be challenged by asking why it is only sixteen. Although there is ultimately this one challenge, it need not necessarily be resolved.
The commentary says: Since there is no explicit teaching regarding what was spoken of as the three virtues, there is neither the permissible nor the impermissible.
This shall be explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa-chao*.
Regarding the phrase "the king of maṇi-jewels is most supreme," there is a distinction between superior and inferior, which is divided into two types.

Alternatively, the sūtras speak of the *maṇi* as being "wish-fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*), thus providing both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms. This is because this jewel has different varieties; hence, both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are given.
The statement is made to clarify the distinction between superiority and inferiority.
Although this sutra speaks of "producing" [the One Vehicle] and so forth, the commentary explains this as a response to an anticipated objection. The objection states:

"Both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* speak of the meaning of producing the One Vehicle; why then does that sutra (*Śrīmālā*) correlate it with all six perfections, while this one excludes *prajñā*? Therefore, [this distinction is necessary].
This answer can be understood according to the text.
The commentary (*shu*) frequently states that this sutra speaks only of "arising" (*chusheng*); however, the character "only" (*wei*) is an error and should be read as "although" (*sui*).

Regarding the passage concerning "power through calculation" (*shushuli*) and so forth, according to Vasubandhu’s commentary, it says: "As for 'superiority through calculation,' it is as the sutra states: 'a hundredth part...'"
It does not equal even one part [of the former], because its number is infinite. By means of this infinity, it encompasses the remaining numbers.

The intended meaning is that the merit of upholding the sutra is such that its number is infinite; therefore, it encompasses the merit of giving. Since the measure of the merit of giving cannot reach it, it is said that "the number is superior.
Regarding "the power is superior," as the sutra says it does not equal even one *kalā* (a minute fraction), the commentary states it is "superior."
At that time, the commentary explains: "The five stages within the womb—the *kalala* is the first; it is the shortest duration.

By citing the merit of upholding this sutra for such a brief period, it is shown that what is bestowed for longer periods cannot surpass it. Because it possesses this capacity, the treatise calls it 'power' (*bala*).
Some say: 'It is like taking a single hair and dividing it into one hundred parts; one part out of those one hundred is called a *kalābhāga* (a fraction of a hair-part). "

The few surpass the many; thus, the term *liyi* (翻) is translated as "superior in power. Regarding the phrase "superior by way of non-similarity," this means that within these merits, their numbers do not correspond.
This is because these merits cannot be counted, as stated in the sutra: "numbers cannot reach them. The commentary (*shu*) says:

Regarding the phrase "because it is a superior simile" (*viśiṣṭopamā*): the intent of the commentary is that "simile" (*sādṛśya*) refers to a comparison. Because it cannot be compared [to anything else], it is called a "superior simile. Now, I shall provide an additional explanation.

The virtue of giving can be counted repeatedly; thus, it is termed "similar" (*sadṛśa*). However, the merit of upholding this sutra cannot be counted; therefore, it is said to be "without similarity" (*asādṛśya*).
Since the treatise itself separately states "because it cannot be compared," we know that "simile" here refers to that which has not yet [reached such a state].
One must certainly employ an analogy to state that cause and effect are not similar; this is because this cause and effect are superior to that cause.

As the sūtra says, "up to a fraction of an *upaniṣad*," the meaning is this: the giving of gold and other such things yields the fruits of the triple world, whereas the merit of upholding this sūtra and so forth will necessarily yield the fruit of Buddhahood; for this reason, it is called "superior."

Regarding the statement that "the monastic community of the four directions gives rise to the eight paths": this means that each of the monastic communities of the four directions individually accomplishes the eight paths;
thus, there are thirty-two. Other symbolic meanings may be understood by analogy with this.
Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit. Commentary, Volume Ten.

The sutra states that all are aged and infirm, and death will soon arrive. If one has not yet attained the stage of a sage, although one may enjoy the blissful rewards of humans and devas with joy, there is no escaping the realities of old age, sickness, and death.
Thus, one knows that the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) are deeply loathsome and to be dreaded. For this reason:
He exhorted him to cultivate and realize the fruits of sagehood. Thus, the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing) states: "From antiquity until now, there are five great fears that cannot be avoided.
The law of aging: one who wishes not to age cannot avoid it. The law of illness..."
To wish that one who is subject to illness not fall ill—this cannot be obtained. To wish that one subject to death not die—this cannot be obtained.
To wish that what is subject to decay not decay—this cannot be obtained. To wish that what is subject to exhaustion not be exhausted—this cannot be obtained.
Question: For what reason are aging and the other [afflictions] called "terrible"? Answer: Because they are capable of destroying.
It is a calamity; it is the basis for all sufferings, and is therefore called "terrible. Thus, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Sutra on Past Deeds) says:
"Old age is most terrible. Why is this? When old age arrives and presses upon one, it can snatch away youth and carry off vigor.

It withers the physical form, causing the waist and spine to bend and the back to hunch, so that one cannot walk, resembling a withered tree. Who would delight in or cling to this? This is the most terrible. Its...
That which comes as illness is called "the fearsome. Why is this? During times of health and vigor, one neither knows nor perceives it;

yet when the period of suffering arrives with its piercing intensity, one wallows in moans. What was once radiant and full of luster suddenly fades and diminishes. Beset by distress and agonizing pain, one finds no peace whether lying down or sitting up.
At such a time, who can take one's place? Lying upon a bed or couch, one’s physical condition no longer obeys the will.
For these reasons, illness is most fearsome and death is most fearsome. Why is this? On the day death arrives, it extinguishes my life-span and suddenly seizes me away.

Even if one possesses the power to rule the four continents, with a golden wheel that subdues all, and with the seven treasures, swift arrows, sharp blades, and strong troops, none can obstruct or restrain it; nor can it be contested or wrested back. For this reason, death—
Most people are terrified [of this]. When asked about those in advanced age and so forth, it is truly lamentable; yet they abandon [the practice] to cultivate [mere worldly habits].

If one were in the prime of youth, at a time when health is prized, one must weary of such afflictions and cause them to reform their training. Answer: For one who dwells in the world, nothing can be guaranteed.
Like a sliver of light through a crack or the glint on a stone, things change and perish in an instant. Therefore, the teaching calls for renunciation. Thus, the *Udānavarga* says: "In the world..."
There are four things that cannot be maintained for long: first, that which is permanent must inevitably become impermanent; second, that which is noble must inevitably become poor and lowly;
third, that which is joined together must inevitably be separated; and fourth, that which is strong and healthy must inevitably die.

Regarding the commentary on the comparison of the Buddha’s Brahma-voice characteristics: with the exception of the Brahma-voice characteristic itself, the remaining thirty characteristics do not equal even one kind—the Unseen-Upon-the-Crown characteristic.
The Infinite-Crown characteristic does not equal a single instance of the Brahma-voice. Why is this?

Because within the Brahma-voice, one can produce immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Brahma-voices and hundreds of thousands of dharma-meanings to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings; this is the intended meaning of the proof.
This can be fully understood. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Three thousand fruit-bearing trees do not equal a single wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*);
it is just as the glow of fireflies throughout the ten directions does not equal the light of a single sun, or as a thousand great-thousandfold worlds of jackals are not equal to a single lion.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 341, states: "If good sons and others, from their first generation of the mind of awakening up until their final birth..."
"Kauśika, regarding the merit of a bodhisattva’s connection [to this practice], how much merit is obtained by one who gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy? The Buddha told Kauśika:
'Suppose the trichiliocosm were joined together to form a single ocean.

If someone were able to take a single hair, split it into one hundred parts, and using the tip of one part to touch the waters of that ocean, the number of drops could be known. Yet the merit of this sympathetic joy is not [so easily measured].'"
It can be calculated. Why? Because this merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is boundless. Furthermore, it is said:

"Those sons of good family and others who give rise to sympathetic joy toward the merits and roots of goodness of all bodhisattvas and dedicate them toward enlightenment will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and will swiftly be able to fulfill all the practices of a bodhisattva. Also, [in] four hundred and thirty-two [verses], regarding what the bodhisattvas [have said]:

There is. This merit of rejoicing is the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the most sublime, the most wonderful, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all the meritorious deeds performed by ordinary worldlings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because when ordinary beings cultivate meritorious deeds, they do so solely for their own mastery, peace, and happiness.
When those of the two vehicles cultivate meritorious deeds, they do so solely for their own subduing, their own tranquility, and their own nirvāṇa.
However, all the merit of a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy is universally for the sake of the subduing, the tranquilizing, and the bringing of parinirvāṇa for all sentient beings. Thus it is said.
Regarding the merit of rejoicing by the fiftieth person mentioned here, it is difficult to find a comparison for it.

As for those confused by the "Hundred Blessings" and "Ten Wholesome Causes" in the *Commentary on the Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master*, according to the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a bodhisattva does not...
Regarding the precept against killing, there are five kinds of mental states: namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-middling, and superior-superior.
This applies likewise up to right view. These fifty mental states are called the "initially generated mind. When these fifty minds are fully perfected and determined, they are called "fulfillment.
Such one hundred mental states are called "one hundred merits. Being endowed with these one hundred merits, one accomplishes a single mark (lakṣaṇa).

Regarding the current explanation that [the vision] exists only at the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*): Question: Upon reaching the four roots of goodness, one is able to see the three thousandfold world system and so forth by oneself;

what relation does this have to the power of the sutra? Answer: Because one reaches the four roots of goodness by upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the resulting vision of the objective realm and so forth is also called the "power of the sutra.
Furthermore, for those who reach the stage of the roots of goodness without upholding the sutra, although they may see the three thousandfold world system, it is not [the same].

It is clear and sharp. If one who upholds this sutra sees it, then that vision is truly clear. Furthermore, even if one does not uphold the sutra and sees the realms and so forth, they will lack the merits such as the eight hundred [qualities].
Now, by upholding this sutra, one attains the merit of seeing the great trichiliocosm.
Regarding the commentary’s reference to the sūtra stating that “a trichiliocosm is the realm of one transformation Buddha” and so forth: the teachings on this matter are not uniform.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that upon attaining the first bhūmi, one realizes the gate of illumination of a hundred dharmas and perceives a hundred buddha-worlds; these are precisely one hundred great trichiliocosms.
Since there is one Buddha in each world, they are called “the worlds of a hundred Buddhas. This is based on what is perceived by those at the stage of the four roots of goodness.

It is called the "hundred realms" because it is the realm of the Buddha. If one speaks according to what is perceived by ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, those on the stage of accumulation, and Bodhisattvas, it should be said that they see a hundred sets of ten billion worlds; for each four-continent world is a single land of transformation of a Buddha.
Therefore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "In one flower are ten billion lands; in each land is a Śākyamuni. Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:

"Because he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood throughout all four continents [of every world-system]. These are all Buddhas perceived by ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and Bodhisattvas on the stage of accumulation (*saṃbhāra*).

Since a hundred billion sets of four continents constitute a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), and the sūtra merely says "perceived," [it refers to these conventional manifestations].
"A hundred Buddha-fields. Thus we know that this is spoken according to the realm of Buddhas perceived by those who possess such roots of goodness.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "As for the principle, there is no discrepancy," within this interpretation there are two points of textual meaning. First, it says:
"The various faculties function interchangeably, reaching beyond merely the three thousand [worlds]. The intent of this explanation is to say that one attains merit and perceives [the Buddhas].

Regarding the measure of the objective realm (*viṣaya-pramāṇa*): this belongs to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*). The mutual functioning of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃprayoga*) belongs to the stages of the grounds (*bhūmy-uttara*). This distinguishes between the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Second, as for the statement that from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward there is no deviation from principle: the intent of this explanation is that seeing the three thousandfold world system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*) also extends to the stages of the grounds; this can be understood by grasping the underlying meaning.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "If it is also attained prior to the stage of application (*prayoga-bhūmi*), it is attained in small measure through the power of application; thus, attainment prior to the stages is possible.

Regarding the phrase "this treatise [proceeds] to the section on mutual application," the intended meaning is that which was previously stated in the treatise concerning ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding these words, they apply to both the passage concerning the attainment of the superior faculty’s function and the passage concerning the mutual function of the faculties.
When the Commentary states that "in the stage of ordinary beings there is mutual function," the author of the Sub-commentary concludes that this adopts the first interpretation.

This is because the merits prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the two distinct positions of seeing the object and mutual function on the stages are different; in reality, mutual function cannot exist prior to the stages.

The commentary states: The intent of this treatise is fundamentally to clarify the merit obtained by those who uphold the sutra, as well as the scope of the six sense faculties and their objects, and the mutual functioning of the various faculties.
Since the scope of such merit belongs to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), how could the mutual functioning of the faculties pertain to them?

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas do not originally intend to clarify the stage of the *bhūmi*-entered Bodhisattvas. Therefore, the treatise again cites the sutra to prove this mutual functioning, stating: "One sees with the eyes; one hears with the nose."

Because they are known. As the *Sūtra* explains regarding Śakra Devānām Indra, and so on up to the nose faculty being known. The *Sūtra* concludes by stating that these are produced by one's parents, clarifying that they are not [the faculties] belonging to the stages (*bhūmi*).

Based on this principle, the *Śāstra* clarifies that the various faculties of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can function interchangeably. However, the intended meaning of the *Commentary* is as follows:

if one speaks of attaining a small portion through preparatory application (*prayoga*), this does not obstruct [the attainment of] mastery prior to the stages; yet it is not the case that [this mastery] is attained in its entirety.
It is not permitted for ordinary beings to use [the merits] interchangeably. The treatise relies on a partial perspective; therefore, there is no contradiction. Consider this further:

the commentary merely states that those who have practiced for a hundred kalpas are inferior to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). This refers to the "hundred kalpas" in terms of spontaneous arising (*anābhoga*).

If one includes those who engage in deliberate cultivation (*prayoga*), their number is vast and manifold; how could they possibly be compared to the two vehicles? This is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
This is explained in detail within the [text]. As for those of the Two Vehicles, they apply effort upon knowing eighty thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, the mention of "one hundred kalpas" is spoken merely in relation to the one hundred dharma-gates realized.
Regarding the statement that "the sūtra sees the entirety of the trichiliocosm": one asks why it is only the trichiliocosm and not more. The answer is as follows:

according to one interpretation, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that beyond the trichiliocosm there is a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Because this contradicts the range of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), one cannot see it.
This implies that the power of the ordinary person’s physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is such that the wind-circle obstructs it; therefore, one does not see more than that.
Regarding "Mount Meru," tradition states that its name means "Mountain of Radiance.
Regarding "Mount Sumeru," tradition states that its name means "Mountain of Tranquil Brilliance"; it is now correctly called "Wondrous High Mountain" (Mt. Meru).

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "Furthermore, obtaining the three thousand [realms] up to 'also not mutually contradictory,'" the intent clarifies that the auditory object described here pertains to all categories of objects belonging to individuals at every stage—
whether ordinary or noble, or within the vehicles of the Great or Small.

Regarding the passage from the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*): the measurement of the three-thousandfold world system is as explained in the second commentary;
the physical bases and lifespans of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) are as explained in the sixth commentary; and the individual names of the four continents and the heavens are as follows.

The commentary has never explained this; what is its meaning? The answer is: as for the four continents, first is Pūrvavideha, which means "Superior Body" (*Vijaya-kāya*), because the bodies there are superior;
alternatively, it is shaped like the south, thus receiving the name "Superior," or it is translated as "East," because it lies at the front of the other directions.
Second is Jambudvīpa, which is the name of a tree; because this tree is extremely tall, it serves as the designation for the continent. Or it is called...

It is a name for a forest, or perhaps a name designated by its fruit; as there is no equivalent for it here, it has not been translated. The old rendering "Foul Tree" (Hui-shu) is erroneous. How is this known?
Since the tree is tall and fragrant, how could it be called "foul"? Third is Aparagoyānī, which means "Cattle-Wealth" (Niuhuo).
Because beneath a tall tree there was a precious cow that provided wealth, it is thus a "Treasure Island. It is named after these two things...

It acquired its name because it was traded for cattle; thus, it is called "Cattle-Trade" (Govyūha). Fourth is Uttarakuru, which means "Superior Place," as it is the most excellent location among the four continents;
alternatively, it is called "Superior Birth," as the sentient beings there are the most superior among those of the four continents.

Next, the celestial realms will be explained. There are six heavens within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): first, the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*), as described in the second commentary; second, the Trāyastriṃśa.
"Deva. This refers to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). There are eight [divisions] on each of the four sides, plus Śakra in the center; it is named after this number.
The two heavens above these both dwell upon the earth, as they reside on Mount Sumeru. Third is the Yāma Heaven;

"Yāma" means "time division," because there are differences in the time divisions for experiencing pleasure. Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven; "Tuṣita" means "contentment," meaning that while they experience pleasure, they remain satisfied. And so forth.
Because they are content, they are called "joyful contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*). Because they possess much affection for contentment and practice fulfillment, they are called "joyful contentment.

The fifth is the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*nirmāṇarati*); they delight in transforming the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and experience pleasure therein. Although there are also objects produced by karma, this name is designated based on their predominant characteristic.
The sixth is the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*); they possess the power of mastery to cause others to transform the objects of the five senses, and...
They experience pleasure for themselves. Although they also have karma-born [bodies], they transform the objects of the five sensory realms themselves and enjoy them for their own use;

thus, they are designated by their predominant characteristic. Next, the four dhyāna heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) are explained. In the First Dhyāna, there are three: first, the Brahmakāyika (Assembly of Brahmās).

They are called Brahmakāyika because they are the retinue of Mahābrahmā, belonging to Mahābrahmā, and are those led and transformed by him. Second, the Brahmapurohita (Ministers of Brahmā). Regarding...
Before the Great Brahmā, there are those who stand in rows as attendants and serve as his assistants; they are called the Brahma-purohitas (Ministers of Brahmā). Third is the Great Brahmā himself.
Because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because he was the first to be born [in that realm], and because he is the last to pass away, his majesty and virtue are preeminent.

As the lord of the devas, he receives the name "Great Brahmā" (*Mahābrahmā*). Although the term "Brahmā" applies generally, he is the very first of them and thus alone is designated simply as "Brahmā. Second.

Regarding the three dhyānas of the third dhyāna realm: first is the "Limited Light" (Parīttābhā), so called because its radiance is slight; second is the "Immeasurable Light" (Apramāṇābhā), so called because its radiance is increasingly superior and its extent is difficult to measure;
third is the "Pervasive Pure Light" (Ābhāsvarā), so called because its pure light universally illuminates the entire sphere of its own level.

Regarding the three [subdivisions] of the third dhyāna itself: first is the "Limited Purity" (Parīttaśubhā); because the mind is free from the exultation of joy and experiences pure bliss, it is termed "pure. Within its own level, this...

The first is the Pure Heaven (*Śubhakṛtsna*), which is called "limited" because its purity is the most inferior. Second is the Immeasurable Pure Heaven (*Anabhraka*); because its purity increases further and its extent is difficult to measure, it is named "immeasurable.

Third is the Pervasive Pure Heaven (*Puṇyaprasava*); because its purity is all-pervading, it is so named. As for the nine [levels] of the fourth dhyāna: the first is the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*);
because it dwells below the empty space, the place where the gods reside is like clouds densely gathered, and it is the ultimate abode within the fourth dhyāna.
1. Anabhraka (Cloudless): Because it is unlike those clouds and because this heaven is the first [of its kind], it is named Cloudless. 2. Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born):

Because only those possessing superior merit can be born there, it is named Merit-born. 3. Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit): Because it occupies a specific location and is the most excellent among the fruits of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is named Vast Fruit.
4. Asaṃjñisattva (Non-percipient Beings): Throughout the duration of one lifetime, except for the moments of birth and death, coarse perception (*saṃjñā*) is absent.

They do not regress; thus, the name "Unconceivable" (*asaṃjñin*) is established. Fifth is "Without Affliction" (*atapa*): this refers to the bodies of those gods whose minds are free from agitation and disturbance.

Throughout their entire lifespan, they experience exclusively pure, tranquil bliss, which does not exist in the lower realms. Alternatively, because they have realized the Truths such as suffering and are free from the coarse afflictions of the lower realms, it is called "Without Affliction.
Sixth is "Without Heat" (*sudṛśa*): because they have realized the Four Noble Truths, they are free from the heat arising from the lower realms.
"Free from heat" (*atapa*) means that they are not tormented by the steaming heat, or that they are free from the sense of "heat," which signifies intense intensity.
Because they have not yet attained the superior mixed cultivation of dhyāna and its fruit, they are called "free from heat. Seventh is "Well-manifested" (*sudṛśa*).

Because the physical forms of those gods are exquisite and upright, surpassing those of the two lower heavens, and because they have attained the superior mixed cultivation of dhyāna, which is clearly and excellently manifested, they are called "well-manifested. Eighth is...
"Excellent Vision. The physical forms of those devas become increasingly exquisite and beautiful, such that they are a source of delight for all who behold them.

Furthermore, because the obstacles to the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation have been attenuated to their subtlest degree, their vision is extremely clear and refined. Moreover, having attained the superior and perfect meditative absorptions of mixed cultivation, the wholesome dharmas they have acquired become increasingly prominent and manifest;
therefore, it is called "Excellent Vision. Ninth is Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate Form), meaning that the physical forms of those devas are supreme...
It is supreme and wondrous, beyond the reach of all others. Furthermore, within that realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is the most honored and ultimate.

Moreover, "form" (*rūpa*) carries the meaning of accumulation; reaching the limit of such accumulation is called the "Ultimate of Form" (*Akaniṣṭha*). As for the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are as explained in the third commentary on the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

Regarding "the faculties are impaired but the objects are not": "impaired" (*bhraṣṭa*) means mixed impairment; it carries the sense of being corrupted and disordered. All subsequent instances should be understood accordingly.
The meaning of their mutual application is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Weishi chao).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This is the realm of wisdom because it is known by the olfactory faculty": this refers to the wisdom associated with the sixth consciousness;
because it relies upon the olfactory faculty to know that [object], it is also said to be "known by the olfactory faculty."
Regarding the statement, "The commentary [states that] one attains a semblance of artificial fragrance, etc.": Question: In various scriptures, no mention is made of artificial fragrance;

how then can it be said that one attains a semblance of such artificial fragrance? Answer: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fragrances such as those that are pleasant or unpleasant are termed "real," whereas blended or compounded fragrances are "artificial.
Thus, the fifty-fourth fascicle states: "In the winds moving through space, there is no innate fragrance; it exists only by reference [to other factors]."
Regarding "conjoined by conditions" (*prajñapti-saṃghāta*): since it is said to be conjoined by conditions, one knows that it is provisional. Question:

What are the characteristics of fragrance conjoined by conditions within the wind that moves through space? Answer: Within the wind there is no fundamental fragrance. Just as when the wind passes over a tree, the fragrance of the tree’s flowers and so forth comes along with the wind;
because the wind possesses fragrance only due to the flowers and other such factors, it is called "conjoined by conditions. Because it is conjoined by conditions...

"Provisional. The commentary states that "obtaining what resembles [it]" refers to the wind and fragrance of the *yoga* of emptiness. "Not obtaining the real" means not obtaining the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the fundamental fragrance.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "this is based on the form and so forth," this refers to the arising of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) based upon a substantial body in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), which then transforms and arises [as fragrance].
Regarding "fragrance" and so forth:

concerning the passage in the sutra that states one knows the presence of hidden treasures beneath the earth by smelling their fragrance, a question is raised based on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "Gold and silver have no fragrance; the diamond (vajra) has no taste.

Does this not contradict [the sutra]? The answer is: "The faculties of those in the Hīnayāna are dull, and thus they do not perceive these things. This present sutra, however, belongs to the Mahāyāna."
How could it be the same as that? The sūtra says that the *jīvajīvaka* bird is the *sahajīvin* bird.
The sūtra refers to the *mallikā* flower as a *mālā* flower; it is suitable for making garlands.
The term *jāti* in the sūtra refers to gold and silver flowers.

Although the sūtra states that one who has not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma does not produce the nose-consciousness, the question—“Is it permitted for the five consciousnesses to be associated with the untainted?”—precisely accords with this text.
How could the position established by Dharmapāla contradict the teaching? By stating “although [the dharma] has not yet been attained,” it clearly indicates that there is indeed attainment.
Therefore, the answer merely states that the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) acts as the producer; it does not state that the produced entity itself is outflow-free.
If the entity itself were outflow-free, why would it be necessary to say "produced by the outflow-free"? Question: If it arises from the outflow-free, its entity should be outflow-free. Answer:

Just as in the case of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), where the mutual production of various minds pertains to all three natures and to both the outflowing and the outflow-free—how can there be any doubt in this case?

Furthermore, it is said that the "nose" refers to the faculty (*indriya*). Thus, the long discourse states: "The pure nose-faculty. How could it be possible for the nose-faculty itself to become untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Therefore, we know the intention of the sutra is to clarify that noble bodhisattvas give rise to the functions of the nose and other faculties by means of untainted dharmas.

This is called "arising from the untainted" (*anāsrava*). "Arising" (*sheng*) here means "to manifest. It does not refer to being produced by the direct influence of karmic retribution (*vipāka*), for such a thing is not discussed by the Sages.
The commentary on the sutra also states that the Buddha possesses the supernormal powers of the nose and tongue that surpass those of the eyes and ears.

According to the third fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, it is clearly stated that there is the supernormal power of the nose. Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmi-bandhana-vinirmukti-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the eye... [is unsurpassed].
It is inconceivable. The Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the ear is beyond all measure; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the nose is even more incalculable;
the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the tongue is vast and without limit.
Regarding the mention of "one month, four months, etc. as provisional timeframes for the duration of the months:
according to the laws of the Western Regions (India), a single year is divided into three seasons—namely, the hot, the rainy, and the cold—and each season consists of four months.
This is why the sutra speaks of "four months" and so forth.

Regarding the commentary on the "Chapter on Not Disparaging," it states that because those [previous] explanations do not correctly clarify the matter, they refer to "Not Disparaging. It is precisely because of the practice of "Not Disparaging" that the account of "Vimalacitra" (Wei-yin) is subsequently given;
it is not intended as a direct exposition of the Buddha-activities of the Buddha Vimalacitra.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "One must not slight [the assembly] at the beginning because one might later violate the precepts": at the beginning, one is a bodhisattva but not yet a bhikṣu;

thus, when prostrating to the fourfold assembly, one must not slight them. Later, one is a bhikṣu but not yet a bodhisattva; if one were to prostrate to the fourfold assembly at that stage, one would violate the precepts.
Now, however, one is neither slighted nor slighting; being both a bhikṣu and a bodhisattva, although this contravenes prohibitions, the benefit is so great that it is permissible.
This is according to the ritual protocol.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that these two are situated within the forty stages of mind: Question: Since he has already previously entered the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-śuklāṅga*), why is it now said that he is in the forty minds?
Furthermore, the "forty minds" refer to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*). Answer: It refers to the tenth stage of dedication (*daśama-praṇidhāna*).
This includes the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Thus, there is no contradiction in saying that they are now "perfected" (*pūrṇa*).
Regarding the statement in the commentary that the latter three are collectively termed "fearlessness in preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly":

these three constitute a collective name for fearlessness in preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly; however, because their specific practices differ, they are opened up into three, which together with the preceding one make four. Practice.
The meaning is easy to understand.

From the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," which spans a thousand worlds, up to the passage where the Bodhisattvas who have Leaped Forth and others ask why they have leaped forth and further request that the sutra be upheld, [the Buddha] answers.
There is an interpretation that the Bodhisattva’s emergence has two intentions: first, to open and unfold the span of his lifespan, thereby perfecting the beginning;
second, to issue a vow for its circulation, thereby completing the end.

Regarding the phrase "expeditiously and without prolonging the time," etc.: if one were to take up the extended tongue and prolong it for the duration of an *kalpa*, the Buddha’s lifespan would be immeasurable.
Now, excluding that period of extension, he is said to have lived only eighty years. Question: For what reason does he withdraw his tongue but not retract his light? Answer:

There is an interpretation stating that he withdraws the mark of the tongue to signify that the preaching of the Dharma is concluded; however, because he wishes to allow all ten directions to penetrate through so that beings may see one another, he does not retract the light.

Regarding "guang" (light) and "shu lei pin shu lei wei zhong die deng zhe" (belonging to the various chapters; "lei" refers to overlapping, etc.): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "shu" means "to connect. According to the *Guangyi*, "wei tu lei" (to entrust and accumulate). This means—
"Because matters are interconnected and entangled. (From the *Zuozhuan*): "Acting according to the timing so as not to burden future generations. Here, "burden" (*lei*) refers to a heavy load.
There is another interpretation: "burden" (*lei*) means to rely upon or depend on.

The *Yao wang pin shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on the Medicine King) explains the "eight chronic ailments of the dust" (*aṣṭau rajas-kilāsa*) as form, odor, taste, touch, earth, water, fire, and wind.

Regarding the "seven outflows" (*sapta āsrava*), according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the "Lion's Roar" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the first is the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*). Views...

1. The outflow of the path of afflictions (*mārga-āsrava*). 2. The outflow of cultivation (*bhāvanā-āsrava*), which refers to the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). 3. The outflow of the faculties (*indriya-āsrava*), referring to the faculties such as the eye, because they are able to produce outflows.

4. The outflow of evil (*pāpa-āsrava*), referring to things such as wild elephants; those that give rise to afflictions are all termed "evil outflows," and because they are able to produce outflows, they receive the name "outflow. 5.
The outflow of proximity (*upaniṣad-āsrava*), referring to clothing, food, and so forth, which serve as the causes and conditions for generating greed. Proximity...

That which can produce outflows (*āsrava*) is called "proximate outflow. Sixth is the outflow of sensation (*vedanā-āsrava*): experiencing the three types of unwholesome thoughts produces the causes of outflows;

it is not named "outflow of sensation" by virtue of being counted as a category of sensation. The three unwholesome thoughts refer to desire, hatred, and delusion. Seventh is the outflow of mindfulness (*smṛti-āsrava*):

because wrong mindfulness gives rise to outflows, it is called the "outflow of mindfulness. Among these seven, the first two constitute the essence of the outflows, while the latter five are the factors that produce them.
The conditions for the outflows are collectively termed "outflows.

Regarding the statement that one who has attained this meditative concentration can manifest a body according to their pleasure: the physical body thus produced is precisely the fruit of that concentration.

Alternatively, having attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and display various material bodies (*rūpakāya*). These bodies are subsumed under the "fruition of supernormal power" (*ṛddhiphala*).
The term "form-trance" (*rūpasamādhi*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). The others should be understood by analogy; some are *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compounds).
Regarding the terms *tūlūpa* and *pilikā*, Master Kumārajīva’s tradition states that they originate from the land of the nāgas and spirits and do not exist in this realm;
therefore, they were not translated. Furthermore, it is said that *pilikā* is translated here as "touch."

The statement that "a full twelve hundred years have passed" signifies abiding in the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*). Among the thirteen stages of abiding (*trayodaśa-vihāra*), the first twelve are all stages of the cause.
Question: According to the Vinaya rules, if one burns one's own body, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one burns an arm, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Does this not mean that Xijian (Hsien-chien) has committed a violation of the precepts? Answer: There are two ancient interpretations. One says: "It must indeed be so..."

First, householders who are bodhisattvas do not participate in the ranks of those who have committed offenses. Second, even if they have left the household life, they transform beings according to the appropriate time;

as in the case of Śāriputra and the elder Sudatta, who traveled together on a single vehicle without committing an offense. This is because their capacities differ—whether great or small—and thus there is no contradiction.

Regarding the statement in the sutra, "The Buddha-dharma has now arrived; it is also entrusted to you": Question: If one follows the Hinayana, it can be said that the Buddha has ultimately entered parinirvāṇa, and thus an entrustment is necessary.
However, in the Mahayana, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and does not perish, responding to those who have karmic affinity with him.

Why, then, would he wait for an entrustment? Answer: There are three reasons. First, when the assembly sees the Buddha’s earnest entrustment, they will [understand that... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Their reverence for the Dharma is sincere, and each desires to proclaim and uphold it. Second, they are entrusted to the Bodhisattvas so that they may practice it themselves and transform others.
Third, the Buddha knows that sentient beings have deep and profound affinities with the Bodhisattvas; therefore, he entrusts them to them to propagate the Dharma and save all beings.
Within the text of this entrustment, there are two matters: first, the Dharma; second, the persons. Thus, in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*...
The sutras and śāstras state that Bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature are entrusted to Bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature.
Regarding the passage concerning the eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas, these symbolize that the Buddha’s eighty-four thousand merits are fully perfected.

Furthermore, they signify that the eighty-four thousand defilements of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) can thereby be eliminated. One asks: how is the essence of the Tathāgata so solid as a diamond (*vajra*)?
What is it that burns and destroys? Is it by way of a majority? The answer is: in reality, there is nothing capable of destroying the essence of awakening.

It is simply because the resonance of compassion responds to sentient beings that the power of the Buddha breaks [the cycle], bestowing [liberation] upon the three realms of existence and performing all the works of a Buddha.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 129 and fascicle 503, state: "All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, originally through the Great..."
[The Buddha] felt compassion. He observed that there were sentient beings who could attain liberation by paying homage and making offerings at the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddhas.
By the power of the *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like samādhi), he shattered his diamond-like body into pieces as small as mustard seeds.

[He then] asked: "What are the benefits and merits of making offerings to the Buddha's body? This Bodhisattva extensively erected precious stupas. [The Buddha] replied: "To speak briefly, it transcends..."
The three evil realms. [By this, one] receives the bliss of humans and devas. Speaking in terms of the ultimate distance, one ascends to the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 127, states: "O sons of good family, those who offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the *śarīra* of the Buddha will certainly never again fall into the three evil realms;
they will always be born among gods and humans, experiencing all manner of happiness and prosperity."
Noble and sovereign, one proceeds toward Nirvana by means of the three dharmas according to one's own wishes. Question:
Between making offerings for oneself and giving them to others, which merit is superior? Answer: The latter is superior to the former, because it enables those [teachings] to spread widely.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 129, section 503, states: "If a son of good family or the like receives the Buddha’s śarīra from another..."

[He] offers various kinds of offerings. If a son of good family or others receives such [offerings] from another and distributes them to yet another, even as much as a mustard seed, causing that person to respectfully accept them—of these two merits, which is superior? Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the latter would be superior. Why is this? Because it enables another to obtain immeasurable merit."

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 128, it says: "The Buddha’s *śarīra* are the most perfect and profound *prajñā*."

It is the vessel upon which the profound *prajñā* relies; therefore, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of humans, asuras, and others.
