Furthermore, through the empowerment of the profound, vast, and great compassion of his supernatural power, such relics of the Buddha as even a single grain the size of a mustard seed, once obtained after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, shall allow for various offerings; the merit thereof shall be boundless.
Among gods and humans, they experience various sublime pleasures until, at the very end, they attain the exhaustion of the ancient limit.
The passage of seventy-two thousand years represents their abiding in the stage of causes, wherein their virtues are not yet perfected. Question:

Why did he burn his entire body as an offering in a previous life, whereas now he merely ignites his two arms as an offering? Answer: In his previous life, the Buddha was present and the Dharma was being widely propagated.
When one is born into the world, there must be a guide for all things; this is why one burns the body. In the present age, there is no Buddha.
If one were to burn the entire body, sentient beings would be without a guide and the Dharma would have no one to propagate it; therefore, one merely burns an arm.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The general and specific [aspects] regarding the abandonment of evil and the gathering of good,” the first phrase is termed “general” because it possesses both that abandonment of evil and the gathering of good.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “These are assigned to the preceding three phrases as appropriate,” this refers to assigning them to the three phrases within the preceding section on the Dharma. Below this...
The combined text is also to be understood according to this principle.
Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* (Sū), "hearing and writing the merit," "hearing" refers to hearing the sūtra, and "writing" refers to copying the sūtra.
Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra*, "attaining the boundless limit," the merit of that person is indeed boundless; the Buddha is able to know that it is without limit.
Regarding the merit of its limits: it is impossible to know any limit to its merit; this is called "the Buddha’s unknowability.
As for the statement in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* that one who hears it shall not receive a female body:

if one asks why hearing this chapter alone allows one to leave the female body, while hearing other chapters does not, the answer is: in truth, by hearing other chapters, one also leaves the female body; however, [this is stated] with reference to...

Regarding the category of phenomena, this [text] specifically relies on this [example] for clarification. Why? Because women by nature are prone to attachment to their own bodies and engage in various forms of adornment;
now, by clarifying that the Bodhisattva gives up his body and arms, it shatters that nature of attachment so that no defiled love arises, and thus he abandons the female body.
The commentary states that [the Buddha] employs skillful means to guide and attract them, saying, "There is no bodhisattva who is your equal.
This is because the Buddha speaks thus to lead those who hear the sutra, encouraging them to advance; it does not mean that, in reality, all bodhisattvas are inferior to you.

Regarding the passage, "Illnesses are immediately eliminated, and one neither ages nor dies": Question: Since all those with outflows (āsrava) are subject to illness, aging, and death, how can ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), upon hearing the sutra, become free from illness, aging, and death?
Answer: There have been many ancient explanations. One states: It is because, having heard the sutra, [they realize that]...

One must reach old age before dying; there are none who die prematurely. Thus it is said, "neither aging nor dying. Furthermore, it is said that the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "disease.
Having heard this sutra, one is able to sever these afflictions; therefore, it is said that "disease is eliminated.
Not giving rise to the sixty-two views is called "not aging," and not losing the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) is called "not dying. Moreover, it is said that by hearing this...
The Sūtra states: Because one knows that old age, sickness, and death are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, it says "no old age, sickness, or death. Furthermore, it says:
By upholding this Sūtra, one obtains a fine complexion and thus does not grow old; one attains longevity and thus does not die. That there is no sickness can be understood by extension.

Regarding the *cintāmaṇi* (甄叔迦寶) mentioned in the "Chapter on Wondrous Sounds" (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*): it is a red-colored gem. According to the *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions), there are many *cintāmaṇi* trees in India;
their flowers are red and as large as a hand. This gem’s color resembles that flower, and for this reason, it is so named.
It is named [after its shape]. Furthermore, tradition says it is a jade disc (*bi*). Others say it is called the "Parrot Jewel" (*śuka-ratna*) here;
this jewel resembles the beak of a parrot bird and is red in color.

Regarding the phrase in the *Pumenpin shu* (Commentary on the Universal Gate Chapter), "transforming beings by following their various types": Question: Since a Bodhisattva makes a vow to constantly attend upon the Buddha, like a shadow following a form, how can it be said that they transform beings by following their various types?

Answer: This is based on the fact that while not transforming those born of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), one speaks of not being separated from the Buddha; furthermore, the mind does not depart [from the Buddha].

The Buddha manifests his body throughout the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*). Furthermore, even while not arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he still displays his dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), and beings born through transformation (*upapāduka*) attend upon him;
both of these are never lacking.

Regarding the passage in the *Falin* [Biography] concerning "taking refuge" and so forth: according to the *Separate Biography of Dharma Master Falin*, his secular surname was Chen. He was exceptionally...
He was a native of Chuangjun. His ancestors had moved to Xiangyang due to official service. He resided at the Jifa Monastery in Chang’an.

In the first month of spring in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor, wishing to propagate the teachings of Li (Laozi) and promote the lineage of Li, issued a manifest edict ordering that Daoists and female Daoists be ranked equally in their ritual processions and standing positions, placing them before the monks and nuns. At that time, the Dharma Master [was] with the capital’s...
The monks submitted a memorial, arguing for the superiority of the Buddha’s Way over [other paths] and the authenticity of the Li family [scriptures], presenting their case with candid words.
At that time, the Emperor’s majesty was incensed, and he issued an edict to the Dharma Master, saying:

"In the 'Chapter on the Reciprocity of Faith and Slander' in your *Bianzheng lun*, you state that those who contemplate Avalokiteśvara will not be harmed even when facing the blade. Since such a miracle exists, I now grant you amnesty. Within seven days, you must..."

"Alas! When the time for execution arrives, will it not be too late to act? Since the Dharma Master was bound in fetters and further pressed by the deadline of his sentence, he was as if torn between ice and fire, with no one to whom he could appeal.
On the sixth day, at night, as he leaned against a pillar, he walked slowly under the bright moon, which seemed to burn like incense smoke.
Sighing that this floating life is but a temporary lodging, he looked up to heaven and lamented: "In the past, Zou was imprisoned in the jail of Qi; the cinnabar..."

I offer this as a pledge at the altars of Qin. How could I dare allow the summer’s warmth to shift toward frost? Since even the crest of a crow can turn white, how could it be that for Senglin alone there would be no subtle response from the unseen realm?
Having finished speaking, a divine being suddenly appeared, over ten feet tall, dressed in white robes and wearing no crown.

Leaping over the wall, he arrived and said to the Dharma Master: "Since you have declared that you will sacrifice your life for the sake of the Way, and that your entanglements are like a net, the secret protection [of the spirits] is indeed abundant."
"You need not trouble your mind with anxiety. Having spoken, he vanished. The Dharma Master prostrated himself in reverent devotion and silently recited the names of the Triple Gem.
Thereupon, his chest felt light and expansive; he was filled with joy and free from fear. On the seventh day, the Emperor issued an edict dispatching Liu Dewei, Minister of Justice, and others.
He asked the Dharma Master, "Now that the period for the amnesty has expired and the execution is imminent, what miraculous response did the bhikṣu receive from his recitation of Avalokiteśvara?

The Dharma Master replied, "For the past seven days, he has been thinking only of Your Majesty. The Emperor and his ministers asked, "Previously, we received an imperial decree ordering you to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
For what reason did he not do so, but instead say he was thinking only of Your Majesty? The Dharma Master [replied].* *(Note: The original text ends abruptly here.)*
He replied: "Senglin has heard that the holy discernment of Avalokiteśvara pervades the six realms of existence; from the heavens above to the earth below, all are taken as teachers and models.

Yet our Emperor is sagacious and wise, his brilliance encompassing the realm within the seas. The nine tribes of the East submit to their duties, and throughout the eight quarters, punishments have ceased.

With a sage ruler and worthy ministers, there is no more madness or excess. Now, Your Majesty nurtures all living beings with the same care as your own children; according to the sutras, you are indeed Avalokiteśvara."
Since these spiritual responses were in perfect accord, they thought only of Your Majesty. Wei and his colleagues recorded their accounts and presented them to the Emperor, who was delighted.

He subsequently summoned the Dharma Master and questioned him regarding the relative merits of Buddhism and Daoism. The Dharma Master cited precedents from both ancient and modern times; he was a preeminent scholar of vast erudition and profound insight.
He presented a report comparing the relative merits of the two schools to the Emperor in person. By imperial decree, the Dharma Master was summoned for interrogation;
finding him consistent, he was released.
Regarding the phrase "Sengqi and Huan relied [upon him]," according to the *Qi Shu*, during the Tianping era of the Northern Wei, there was a conscript from Dingzhou named Sun...
Jingde was building a statue of Avalokiteśvara at Fang. When the work was complete and he was about to return home, he continued to worship it at his residence.
Later, he was implicated by bandits; unable to endure the torture, he falsely confessed to the crime. The next day, he was to be executed.

That night, while performing prostrations and repentance with tears streaming down, he suddenly felt as if he were in a dream and saw a śramaṇa who instructed him to recite the "Avalokiteśvara Sūtra for Saving Life. This sūtra contained the names of various Buddhas.

He was ordered to recite [the scripture] one thousand times to escape his hardships. Jingde suddenly became aware that it was exactly as he had visualized in his dream, without a single error. He then proceeded to recite it one hundred times.

As the officials bound him and led him toward the marketplace, he continued to recite with single-minded devotion. When he reached the thousandth repetition at the site of the execution, they struck him with a blade;
the blade broke into three pieces, yet his skin and flesh remained unhurt. They changed the blade and struck again, and this occurred three times in total. The blades...

The broken pieces were restored as they were before. When the provincial inspector questioned him, he fully recounted the beginning and end of the matter and submitted a formal report to the Chancellor Qi Huan.

Huan submitted a memorial on his behalf requesting that [the monk] be granted a pardon from death. Consequently, this practice spread widely throughout the world; this is what is known as "King Qi’s Avalokiteśvara.

When Jing returned and prepared a vegetarian feast to welcome the image, he saw three knife scars upon its crown. The intent of the memorial was based on the fact that the matter had been reported by Huan.

One is thus able to escape [calamity]. The term "zhai" (齋) was subsequently established based on the state of Qi; hence it is called "zhāihuān" (齋懽). In reality, it is not a matter of "rejoicing the body," yet escaping the misfortunes of the fields is likewise not contradictory to this.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, regarding those that are fixed as karmic maturation (*vipāka*), etc.”: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, "karma that is fixed as to be experienced" (*niyatavedanīya-karman*) refers to that which, having been intentionally willed (*saṃcintya*), is either performed or increased.
This explains that because one performs it intentionally and further increases it, this karma will certainly bring about a fruit of maturation;
therefore, it is called "fixed karma. As for "karma that is not fixed as to be experienced" (*aniyatavedanīya-karman*), it refers to that which, having been intentionally willed, is not increased.

Regarding "long-term maturation" (*dīrghakālavedanīya*): although the intention (*cetanā*) is the same, it does not differ in its lack of increase. Therefore, this karma is indeterminate in its production of fruit;

it is called "karma conducive to the indeterminate" (*aniyatavipāka*). Following the intent of the treatise, I have cited [the text] here; though the wording is slightly lacking and out of order, one should understand it by following this [explanation].
Regarding the commentary on lines 89–90, "not increasing," it states according to that treatise:

"If there were no increase through the absence of action, then for those who have performed such karma, provided they feel no remorse and do not cultivate remedies, whether that karma subsequently increases or does not increase, this karma will still transform so as to result in an experience favorable to the unwholesome. Explanation.
Because one does not feel regret and because one commits the act again, that karma causes one to experience the fruits of the miserable realms (*apāya*).

However, the treatise (*śāstra*) does not explicitly state that this is called "increased karma" (*upacita-karman*); rather, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) adopts the intent of the treatise to establish the term "increased. This is because the treatise states: "If it increases further..."

Because it results in the experience of the miserable realms (*apāya*), one knows that this karma is termed "increasing" (*upacita*). The subsequent statement regarding "non-increasing karma" (*anupacita-karma*) should also be explained according to this principle.

As for the commentary’s alternative explanation—that karma which was previously increasing may later be termed non-increasing—the intention behind this is as follows: [The treatise] immediately preceding...

The Commentary says: "If one intentionally commits unwholesome karma and that karma is both performed and accumulated, it will certainly result in the maturation of suffering in the miserable realms in the future.
The Sub-commentary says: "If this person does not give rise to a mind of remorse, it is truly a fixed karma (*niyata-karma*).
However, if they encounter a virtuous friend and give rise to a mind of remorse, it is also called 'unfixed' (*aniyata*). This is illustrated by the case of Ajātaśatru."

[This is] the proof. From this, it is known that regarding determinate and indeterminate karma, there is a distinction between remorse and lack of remorse when viewed from the perspective of the "great net" (the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*).

Remorse constitutes the indeterminate; lack of remorse constitutes the determinate. This does not contradict what was stated previously in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which says that those who definitely experience [the results of] evil are based on the state of having no remorse;
for sentient beings who commit evil with such violent intensity mostly feel no remorse. Thus, there is no contradiction.

In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter Seven, regarding the five types of intentional karma (*saṃcetanīya-karman*), it asks: "What is meant by 'intentional' (*saṃcetanā*) in cases such as being commanded by another? The answer is:
Although at the outset one is commanded by another, because one subsequently gives rise to an intentional mind, it is also called "intentional. Therefore, that treatise states:
"Regarding being commanded by another, it is like a certain person who, though not desiring or wishing [the act], initiates an intentional [action] due to the forceful command of another."

Regarding volitional intention (*cetanā*): one who performs unwholesome karma upon being exhorted by another does so because, although they do not desire or find pleasure in it, they initiate volitional intention by accepting it as beneficial due to that person's persuasion.

One who lacks discernment performs unwholesome karma by initiating volitional intention through acting according to their whims, without understanding what is gained or lost and without any sense of attachment.
One who possesses inverted discrimination performs [unwholesome karma] based on an uneven [view].
Due to such views, they take delight in false teachings; seeking desirable maturation in the future, they intentionally initiate unwholesome karma.
The rest is as cited in the commentary.
Regarding the "eight intrinsic natures that are indeterminate" (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*), there are briefly two interpretations. The first states:

this refers to those that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, which are not subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*), and whose intrinsic nature is neither increased nor diminished. Because they differ from those subsumed under wholesome or unwholesome paths of action, they are called "indeterminate";
it does not refer to the category of the indeterminate among the three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*). The second states: it refers to the indeterminate nature within the three natures themselves.
Commentary on the Ninth [Point], "That Which Is Damaged by Regret": This refers to remorse (*paścāttāpa*). It is called "damage" because it prevents karma from increasing.

Commentary on the Sixth [Point], "The Increase of Karma": There are two aspects: first, preparatory application (*prayoga*); through the extremely intense application of the three poisons, various karmas are initiated.
Second, habitual practice (*abhyāsa*); throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], one draws near to and cultivates them. If one habitually practices what is unwholesome (*akuśala*)...
...karmas. Third, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): among verbal karmas, false speech is the most grave; among bodily karmas, killing is the most grave;
and among mental karmas, wrong view is the most grave. Fourth, by way of the object (*vastu*): this refers to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or any one of the objects of veneration;
whether it be for their detriment or their benefit. Fifth, by way of that which is counteracted (*pratipakṣa*): being exclusively devoted to practicing all unwholesome [states].
Karma; until the end of life, there is not a single moment of goodness. Sixth is the harm of that which is to be remedied:
by severing the various unwholesome karmas that are their opposites, one causes all wholesome karmas to become free from desire and pure.

Regarding the statement that "the ten [types] do not increase beyond the few," there are ten types of non-increase, which do not exceed the three types of non-increase in the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa).

There are six types of increase, which do not depart from the two types of increase in the *Abhidharma*. However, the author of the treatise, based on differences in the stages (*avasthā*), varies the manner of their opening and closing.
Question: How do the ten types and the three types mutually subsume one another? Answer: If considered in terms of name and essence, their characteristics...
Regarding "inclusion": the second *yoga* [of the *Yogācārabhūmi*] includes that third [category]; the seventh *yoga* includes those first two;

and as for the remaining seven types, their meaning applies to all three according to what is appropriate. These seven are distinguished based on the different states—such as sleeping versus waking, or being insane versus not insane—and thus they are opened up separately.
Question: The five types in the *Abhidharma* speak generally of "intentionality" (*saṃcetanīya*). Regarding the third among the ten [types], it says:

Regarding "absence of intentional thought" (*asaṃcetanā*): how are they subsumed? Answer: The *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada) relies on the latter [stage] and speaks generally of "intentional thought," whereas the *Yogācārabhūmi* relies on the former and speaks of "absence of intentional thought.
In the first two [stages] of the *Abhidharma*, the first is called "lack of desire," which is precisely "absence of intentional thought. Question:
The ninth and tenth [stages] have no resemblance whatsoever to that *Abhidharma*; how can they be subsumed? Answer: They are precisely those first two [stages].

Because of the impairment caused by these two, even when exhorted by others, they do not increase. Question: Regarding the [categories of] one, four, five, six, and eight, which of those five are included?
Answer: One and five are the sixth; these are its three final [members]. As for the two types, four and eight, they are subsumed under the first two.

Question: Regarding the six types of increasing karma (*upacita-karman*) and the two [types] in the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*), how do they correspond? Answer: Among the five [types], it specifically refers to unwholesome karma (*akuśala-karman*) as the mode of action;
among the six, it discusses wholesome and unwholesome karma in general. Since the general meaning of the six encompasses those two, one can see their significance by examining the text;

therefore, I shall not detail them here. Question: If there is an increase through performance (*kriyā-upacaya*), does it not necessarily entail the ripening of a fruit (*phala-vipāka*)? Is it possible...

Is there that which is accumulated but not performed? The answer is: yes. Therefore, in the sixtieth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are set forth regarding unwholesome karma induced by killing:
1. There is that which is performed but not accumulated; this refers to the ten types of non-accumulative karma performed in dreams and the like.
2. There is that which is accumulated but not performed; this refers to [karma] for the purpose of harming living beings... [in the future].
Throughout the long night, they frequently engage in vitarka and vicāra. Due to these causes and conditions, they subsequently increase the evil and unwholesome dharmas induced by killing;

yet they do not actually perform the karmic act of killing. Regarding those who both perform and increase [such karma], this excludes the first two phrases and includes all other characteristics of the karmic act of killing.
Regarding those who neither perform nor increase [such karma], this refers to excluding the aforementioned characteristics and includes the remaining nine.
The paths of karma (*karmapatha*) should be understood by analogy with this.

Regarding the "thirteen karmas" and so forth mentioned in the Commentary (*śāstra*): the number of karmas—three, four, or five—varies across different teachings due to differences in how they are expanded or condensed.
These could be discussed in full detail; since the Commentary already provides the necessary pointers, one may understand them by consulting it directly, and thus I shall not elaborate further here.
The Commentary states that by this one knows the first interpretation to be correct;

that is to say, the previous interpretations—including those established by citing the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-saṃgraha* in the preceding commentary—are all termed the "first interpretation."
Regarding the phrase "to examine, bind, and collect," according to the *Guǎpǐ* (Broad Lexicon), it means to extend or to encompass; that is, to enclose and restrain.
The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states that it means "prohibition," referring to confinement; that is, instructing beings so that they do not expose themselves.
Regarding the "Great General Who Transcends Heaven," some say he is a celestial warrior (*deva-malla*), such as the *Bhṛtya* class, or of the lineage of Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa is simply a name for a deity.

Regarding the term *zǎi* (宰) used for those who occupy positions of authority: furthermore, according to the *Shēnglèi* (Classified Lexicon), *zǎi* means "to govern. This refers to officials who administer districts.
According to the *Guǎngpǐ* (Extended Glossary), it means "to regulate," referring to the regulation of affairs.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Fearing that [if one did not accept] the threefold offering would contradict their intention”: Question: Since it is said that [the recipient] does not accept, with what then would one perform the threefold offering? Answer:
It is explained that one accepts the gift out of fear that such an act would contradict their intention, and subsequently performs the threefold offering; thus, this is also called "non-acceptance."
Regarding the reason why the Commentary does not accept [this], it generally concludes the preceding three points.

As for the passage in the Sūtra where Avalokiteśvara accepts the pearls and divides them into two portions to offer to Prabhūtaratna and others, there is an interpretation that his acceptance has two intended meanings.
First, they ascend in accordance with the Buddha’s intent; second, they descend out of compassion for all living beings.

Desiring to cause the merit of the donors to increase progressively, they divide themselves into two parts to manifest the equality of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, honoring only these two venerable ones.

Furthermore, the birth of Śākyamuni represents the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna*), while the parinirvāṇa entry of Prabhūtaratna represents the perfection of cessation (*prahāṇa*). This is done to reveal that wisdom and cessation together constitute the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Moreover, it further reveals...
"The two Buddhas both accept [the offering]," which clarifies that the two Tathāgatas do not pass into extinction.
Regarding the commentary’s passage from "Like a skillful physician" to "causing them to give rise to a superior intention," there may be two meanings. First, it refers to those who practice evil.

One compares oneself with others; knowing one’s own suffering, one does not cause others to suffer. Second, one causes others to see the lack of solidity [in worldly things] and reflects inwardly so as not to engage in evil;
thus, one remains steadfast toward those very people. It is not that a bodhisattva lacks benefit for or neglects sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "the peerless (asama-sama) bodhi" in the sutra, there are briefly two interpretations. First, the Great Bodhi of the Buddha has two aspects:
because nothing below it can reach it, it is called "peerless" (asama); because there is nothing above it with which it could be equal, it is called "equal" (sama).

Second, the term "peerless" (asama) at the beginning is used to manifest that the fruit of Buddhahood transcends all things; thus it is called "peerless. The subsequent character "equal" (sama), however, refers to the cause.
The bodhicitta is called "equal" because it resembles its fruit. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment] are not two different things.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 41, says: "That which is peerless is called a Buddha. Why is this?
Because among all sentient beings and all phenomena, there is nothing equal to it. Therefore, this bodhicitta resembles the Buddha. For this reason...
Why? Because the cause resembles the fruit; this is called the "unequaled mind. The previous interpretation was incorrect, whereas the latter is complete in both principle and teaching.

Regarding the *Dhāraṇī-pāda-śū* [Commentary on the Dhāraṇī Chapter], it states that those who employ "few, brief, and esoteric words without explicit meaning" are able to contain many meanings within what is few and brief. Furthermore, it is...
Secret. When one examines its words and phrases, they appear to be without meaning; thus it is called "meaningless speech. Yet, it is not actually without meaning. Question: How is this clarified?
It is because the few encompass the vast. Furthermore, for what reason do the few contain the many? Answer:
According to the *Dharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, fascicle 2, it says: "This single dharma-phrase gives rise to immeasurable phrases; it is the Great Dhāraṇī that penetrates all."
He explains the various meanings. Why is this? It is because he wishes to enable all sentient beings to easily receive and understand them.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that "there are four types of dhāraṇī, namely dharma, meaning, and so forth," the four dhāraṇīs are: first, dharma; second, meaning; third, mantra; and fourth, *vaiśāradya* (fearlessness).

The four capacities: attaining the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Regarding the "eloquence and words" mentioned in the commentary, there are two interpretations.

First, it is an error: eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and words (*pada*) are not, in themselves, dhāraṇīs. Second, it is not an error: it refers to the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
It is subsumed within the *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma. It possesses unimpeded eloquence and penetrates the meaning of the Dharma; thus, it is included among the *dhāraṇīs* and is therefore cited here.

Regarding the statement in the preceding prose commentary that this is called the "retention of the Dharma and its meaning" (*dharmārthadhāraṇī*), there are two senses. First, it refers to the prose section at the beginning of this chapter.
Because it precedes the mantra, it is called "the preceding section" (*shanglai*). Second, this applies generally to all the prose passages (*changxing*) of the preceding chapters.

As for the subsequent question, "Why is the verse not excluded? the answer is: it is also not excluded; rather, in contrast to the subsequent mantras, it is collectively termed "prose. Consider this further.
Regarding the phrase "the dhāraṇī of the patience of non-attainment and non-arising": this sutra does not speak of a dhāraṇī for attaining the patience of non-arising.

Question: In the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," it is stated that through hearing of the Tathāgata’s long lifespan, six hundred and eighty trillion nayutas of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," forty thousand...

Two thousand devaputras attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Within this chapter, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

How can you say there were none? Answer: The Sūtra does not clarify the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas in terms of the distinctions between stages and levels of practice;
it is called "non-non-arising" because it does not obstruct those who hear the Sūtra from attaining it. There is another interpretation: [those who] heard below the divine...

Mantra. To awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—is this not the One Vehicle? This very [mantra] also possesses the *dhāraṇī* of the patience of non-arising. The commentary says:

If one takes the patience previously attained and collectively names it a *dhāraṇī*, what fault is there in this? Consider further. Question: What is the referent of the mantra that is being elucidated?
What dharma does it elucidate? Answer: There is one interpretation which states that it does not go beyond three meanings. First, it explains the ultimate...
[It refers to] either the excellence of the fruit, or the myriad practices within the cause; secondly, it provides the names of the Three Jewels, or the names of powerful spirits and deities;
thirdly, it explains the profound principle of all phenomena as being signless (*animitta*), causing those who hear it to awaken to the Way.

Question: Why is it that in this land [China], these sounds are not translated? Answer: There is a meaningful reason. Mantras contain many layers of significance, and there is nothing here [in this land] that can serve as an equivalent for them.

If one were to translate it, the meaning would not be fully exhausted, and there is also fear that its power and function might be lost. As for the existing translations, they cannot yet be relied upon.
[The sūtra says: "If anyone should harm or destroy this Dharma Master, they are thereby harming or destroying these Buddhas. Question: For what reason?
"To harm others is to harm the Buddha. Question: "The Dharma Master is a messenger of the Tathāgata and performs the work of the Tathāgata;
therefore, to disparage him is to disparage the Buddha. Question: "What, then, are the characteristics of a true Dharma Master? Answer: "The purity of the three karmas."
His accumulated virtues are profound and far-reaching; he is truly a master of the True Dharma. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"If one wishes to expound upon the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata-garbha, and the Three Vehicles, one must first purify one's own body. Because the body is pure, one will not be subject to reproach.
Being free from reproach, one causes immeasurable people to give rise to pure faith in the Great Nirvāṇa. Because this faith arises, they will show reverence."
If one hears even a single verse, a single phrase, or a single word of this sutra, as well as the teacher who expounds it, one will immediately resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
It should be known that such a person is a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to sentient beings, a disciple of mine, and not a member of Māra’s retinue. [Commentary:

This merely cites the coarse characteristics for ease of understanding; while it says "to purify the body," it actually means to purify the three karmas. Furthermore, according to the *Mahā-...* [text].
The *Saṃyuktāgama*, fascicle seven, states: "In all that one preaches, do not do so for the sake of food; preach with a sincere heart.

When preaching, do not treat others lightly, nor exalt yourself. This is to produce skillful means so that what is heard is not lost. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle five hundred and sixty-seven, states:
"That is to say, according to those to be converted, one should mostly employ kind speech (*priyavāda*); speak first with a smile, and remain far removed from frowning or scowling."
His words possess meaning and are able to accord with reality as it is. Whatever he says does not deceive or insult others; his speech is definitive.
He delights in various forms of eloquent discourse, using gentle and warm words to bring joy to the assembly. His countenance is broad and harmonious, causing others to feel drawn to him.

He speaks in accordance with the truth, so that those who hear may awaken to understanding for their own benefit. He speaks in conformity with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), speaking with impartiality and a mind free from [bias].

Impartial and unconventional, he departs from false speech and delivers definitive teachings according to the faculties and natures of the assembly. By these causes and conditions, he causes the multitude to rejoice.
[The Chapter on King Subhavyūha]

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, because the Pure Eye has already arrived, it is not mentioned”: Question: The King Subhūṣaṇa is none other than the previously mentioned King Puṣpadhvaja;
why then is he not considered redundant? Answer: Although King Subhūṣaṇa is indeed Puṣpadhvaja, Puṣpadhvaja was not designated as a chapter title in the preceding section.
Since a formal title is established here, there is no redundancy. Furthermore, the Pure Eye is none other than the previously mentioned Bhaiṣajyarāja. As for Bhaiṣajyarāja...
The former instance used the title of the chapter as its designation; to speak of it again here would surely result in redundancy and confusion, and thus it was not adopted.
Furthermore, regarding the character *chuo* (枛) used in the commentary, it refers to the five types of rice. The pronunciation of *dao* (稻) is *ruo-ling* (若冷).

When the Sūtra says, "O Mother, we pray that you allow us to leave the home life and become śramaṇas," it asks what the faults of the household life are so that one may grow weary of it and renounce it.
The answer is: it diminishes merit, ruins goodness, and increases all conditions for evil; this is why it is to be abandoned. Thus, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"That which is called 'the household life' is named the slaughter of the roots of goodness, the non-renunciation of faults, and the destruction of that which assists wholesome karma. Therefore..."
"Householder. Why is it called a "house"? Because all fetters and afflictions dwell within it; therefore, it is called a "house.
Furthermore, as for a "house," one dwells within it and commits every kind of evil. Consequently, one does not respect or obey one's parents, nor śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Moreover, as for a "house," it is a place where the branches of long-standing attachment grow, and where sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress arise. It is not yet... [end of fragment]
They fail to cultivate roots of merit; they cause roots of merit already cultivated to be entirely dissipated and extinguished.

Furthermore, if they abide in this state, they delight in the neglect of the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

Moreover, if they abide in this state, they are gripped by craving for parents, wives, children, sisters, friends, kinsmen, and associates, constantly preoccupied with thoughts of wealth and driven by greed.
It is infinite; like the ocean swallowing rivers, it is never satisfied. Furthermore, life at home is like an illusion, for it accommodates many gatherings yet lacks any real sentient beings.
Life at home is like a dream, because of the alternating rise and fall. Life at home is like dew, because it quickly breaks.
Home is like a drop of honey, for its flavor lasts but a moment. Home is like a net of thorns, because of attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. Home is like...
Like venomous snakes, because they prey upon one another, those in the household life are beset by much fear; for they are plundered by kings, thieves, water, and fire.

Possessing such manifold calamities, one should abandon them as if discarding a worn-out sandal. Question: What benefits does one who has left the household life possess, such that one seeks to pursue it? Answer:
A true renunciant is able to block the gates of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), extinguish all worldly clamor and entanglements, and give rise to *bodhicitta*.
The Path. It gives rise to and nurtures all virtues. Thus, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Leaving the home life is sublime and excellent;

it abandons many defilements and stays far removed from the mire of craving and desire. It is the limit of *nirvāṇa*, a vessel for the nectar of immortality, difficult to encounter even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.

There are over a hundred such passages that contrast the monastic life with that of the householder to clarify their relative merits. Because it possesses such superior qualities, one seeks to leave the home life. Question: If one wishes...

Regarding renunciation: what constitutes the mind of one who is called a true renunciant? The answer is: for the sake of diminishing birth and death, for the sake of proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*, and for the sake of abandoning all attachments to matters such as fame and profit—this is true renunciation.
Thus, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* says: "For what reason does one abandon worldly affairs to renounce the home?
It is for the sake of cultivating wisdom. One should apply oneself with diligent vigor, as if putting out a fire on one's head. This is how it should be done.
This is the reflection: "I should abide in the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) and delight in practicing the dhūta ascetic virtues.

As for the four noble lineages, they are: being content with whatever robes, alms-food, and bedding one obtains; praising such contentment; and not engaging in false speech for the sake of these things.
If one does not obtain them, one does not think about them, does not dwell upon them, and does not give rise to distress. Even if one should obtain them, the mind...
One does not give rise to attachment; one is neither greedy nor dwelling [in things]. Knowing their faults and knowing the way of transcendence, one is content with this.

One does not praise oneself nor disparage others. One delights in relinquishment and detachment, and delights in cultivation. Regarding such delight in relinquishment and so forth, one does not praise oneself.
This is called abiding in the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "or by associating with virtuous friends through the sūtras and so forth," it further cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 35, which says:

"One should know that a bodhisattva is complete [in his spiritual resources] by virtue of four characteristics. The first is that the virtuous friends encountered by the bodhisattva are by nature not dull-witted."

1. Being intelligent and wise, one does not fall into wrong views. 2. Whatever good friends one encounters will never teach one to practice heedlessness, nor will they provide the requisites for such heedlessness.
3. Whatever good friends one encounters will never teach one to engage in unwholesome conduct, nor will they provide the requisites for such unwholesome conduct.
4. Whatever good friends one encounters will never encourage the abandonment of [wholesome] progress.

While possessing superior faith and aspiration, and having received and trained in the merits of diligence and skillful means, they further encourage others to cultivate inferior faith and aspiration, and to receive and train in the merits of diligence and skillful means.

That is to say, they never encourage the abandonment of the Mahāyāna to encourage the cultivation of the two vehicles; they never encourage the abandonment of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) to encourage the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

they never encourage the abandonment of the wisdom of reflection to encourage the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); and they never encourage the abandonment of the wisdom of hearing to encourage... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
To encourage the cultivation of meritorious deeds; to encourage the relinquishing of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and to encourage the practice of giving (*dāna*);

and never to encourage the relinquishing of such superior virtues while instead encouraging the practice of such inferior virtues—this is called the characteristic of being endowed with a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding the phrase "dark blue and red": according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to silk dyed blue that possesses a trace of red. The *Shiming* states: "Gan (紺) means 'to contain';
it is blue that contains red. The *Qieyun* gives its pronunciation as "chi" (赤).
Regarding the "river-moon" (*nadīcandra*), it belongs to the *śaṅkha* (conch) family; it emerges from the ocean and is as pure white as snow.

Concerning the statement that one must enter the first stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth within the "thicket of the yoga of right concentration" (*yoga-samyak-samādhi-nikāya*), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 100, the "thicket of factors of wrong and right certainty" (*mithyā-samyak-niyata-dharma-nikāya*) refers to the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*). The "thicket of factors of right certainty" (*samyaktva-niyata-dharma-nikāya*)...

"Those" refers to all dharmas belonging to the *śaikṣa* (those in training) and *aśaikṣa* (those beyond training). "The group of indeterminate dharmas" refers to the remaining dharmas that are neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*.
Question: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 394, it states:

"Whether they are bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, those at the stage of non-retrogression, or those in their final body, all abide in the fixed group of right nature (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*). How is it, then, that the treatise speaks of the *śaikṣa* and [aśaikṣa]?

[Question: Only when one studies [in this way] can it be called "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). [Answer: Briefly, there are two explanations. First, the treatise applies to all three vehicles, whereas the sutra refers only to the Mahāyāna;

this is because those of the two vehicles often regress from their resolve. Second, the sutra and the treatise are similar in meaning; the sutra’s mention of "generating the resolve" refers specifically to the "realized generation of the resolve" at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Thus, that sutra states: "A Bodhisattva abiding in right concentration no longer falls into the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties."
Difficult. One shall never again be born within the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties; this is because one has entered the stage of seeing [the Truth].

Furthermore, reflecting on it, the *Sūtra Commentary on the Chapter on Encouraging the Aspiration* states: "Regarding those people after my parinirvāṇa when the human lifespan is fifty years. Moreover, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it is also said that later...
"Fifty years. The commentary states: "After four hundred and fifty years, reaching the fifth century, the fifty years contained within that interval are called the 'final fifty years.'"
Regarding the passage in the sutra stating that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rides a six-tusked white elephant, there is an interpretation that he mounts the elephant for three reasons.
First, to manifest the Bodhisattva’s retinue and regalia. Second, because he wishes to subdue the poisons of all māras with this divine beast.

Third, because he wishes to symbolize the three vehicles—rabbit, horse, and elephant—as they correspond respectively to the capacities of those in the three vehicles. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is the rider who is able to mount the elephant.
That which he rides represents the dharmas of both the subject and the object of riding; as these are both free from defilement, it is therefore white.

Furthermore, according to the *Gosha-śāstra*, the six tusks symbolize the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the four legs symbolize the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), and the seven limbs symbolize the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*).
These are all distinct practices within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and because they possess such symbolic significance, he mounts the elephant.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the four lower heavens are also of inferior grade (*hīna-prakāra*) and so forth”: the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika-kāyika*) are called the four lower heavens.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of the Yāma Heaven up to the point where it says “the fruit is omitted from the text”: in Tuṣita Heaven, there is Maitreya Buddha, whom the various devas are able to see;
this is explicitly stated in the sūtra. As for the Yāma Heaven and the two heavens above it, there are no Buddhas therein, and the devas [do not see them].
Regarding what is seen: it is for this reason that the sūtra omits a detailed explanation of it here, as it is the fruit produced by middling-level cultivation.

The commentary states: "In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is likewise no Buddha [to be seen]. Why, then, does the sūtra say so? This is merely citing the fruits produced by lower and upper levels of cultivation to indirectly reveal the middling fruit;
it is not a matter of whether one sees or does not see the Buddha, nor is it a case of the sūtra being silent on the point.
Alternatively, it may not mention the Buddha. It states that the two heavens above Śakra constitute the middle grade; thus, the text is abbreviated and lacks explicit mention of the fruit.

Since the sutra does not speak of this, if one follows this principle, there is no error in the commentary. The text is concise yet its meaning is comprehensive; only through careful investigation and study will one realize it.
The Commentary states: "From 'as for the middle grade' down to 'each having lower and upper' intends to clarify that within each of the ten practices there are three grades.
This is because it is so explained in the case of the middle-upper grade of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting; by this, one may infer the same for the others."
The Commentary states: "Now, as for the statement that 'existence' and so forth are spoken of only in the middle grade:

just as it is said that practice actually has three grades, yet in this sutra only the middle grade is mentioned; likewise, when speaking of the lower and upper grades of practice, they are not mentioned."
Regarding the commentary’s statement that those who practice one, two, or three [of the ten] dharmas are classified as "inferior" (hīna) practitioners:
if there are individuals who, among the ten dharmas of practice, are able to cultivate only one, or two, or three practices, they are all designated as inferior practitioners.

Within this category of the inferior, there are thus three types. The middle and superior levels of practice should be understood accordingly. Question: Regarding the inferior level, what constitutes practicing two...
Regarding the three types of conduct: compared to those who possess two types of conduct of the middle grade, these are both higher and superior. Why, then, are they called "lower"? Answer:

Among the three grades of the lower category, each is designated as "lower" by corresponding respectively to the three grades of the middle category. It is not that the third [grade] of the lower category is called "lower" because it is inferior to the first grade of the middle category.
The same principle applies when the middle category is compared to the upper category. Alternatively, according to the *Śāstra*: [The text continues: ...or again, the commentary...
Regarding the mention of "one, two, and three," these refer respectively to the three grades of the lower category.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "two, four, five, and six," the term "two" refers to the second grade of the middle category; it does not denote the second of the ten practices.

Again, regarding the mention of "three, seven, eight, nine, and ten," the term "three" denotes the third grade of the upper category; it does not denote the three [phrases] within the text of the third practice.

This refers to the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*). This meaning is stated in general terms; however, according to those ten practices, there are variations in quantity, which are divided into three grades.
This interpretation is correct.

Regarding the statement in the *Qieyun* that "among the *liaoyin* (final sounds), there are no others besides the four *liao* characters": within the *liaoyin*, there are only the four characters *liao*. There are none other.
The two characters for "liǎoliǎo" (繚繚燎燎) have the pronunciation *dāoxiǎo* (刀小反); they do not have the pronunciation *liǎo* (了).
The pronunciation of *liǎo* is *lúniǎo* (盧鳥反). Furthermore, regarding *lù* (镽): *lù* (*jìqiáo*) means "long and extensive. The pronunciation of *qiáo* is *jùxiǎo* (巨小反).

Regarding the two instances of the character "liáo" (燎) in the commentary, they refer to the two occurrences of "liǎoliǎo" (繚繚). As for "liǎo" (繚), according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to wind around" (*liǎorào*) or "to entangle.
This refers to being mutually entwined.
"Loosely looking" (*shù*) means "looking inward" (*nèi-mù*). According to the *Cāngxié piān*, looking inward is called *lài*. The transcription "shù" contains many errors.
Furthermore, it is traditionally said that "inner eye" (naimoku) is what is colloquially called "eyes looking upward" (gan-gōmoku).
Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Four (End) of the Compendium of Explanations.
